docs.title: Spring WebFlux Cookbook
docs.text:
A hands-on guide to reactive programming with Spring Framework 7 and Spring Boot 4. Instead of explaining concepts in the abstract, it walks through real examples from the repository and shows how they fit together in a production-style Spring application.

If you want to learn by doing, this is the right place. Each chapter pairs a concise explanation with runnable code from the repository, so you can read a concept, open the sample, and try it immediately.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
This site covers the reactive stack from the ground up:

  • the core ideas behind Reactive Streams, Reactor, and WebFlux
  • how to build HTTP APIs with annotated controllers and functional routing
  • how to access data reactively with MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, Couchbase, Neo4j, Elasticsearch, and R2DBC
  • how to secure reactive apps and test them with realistic tools
  • how Kotlin and the broader reactive ecosystem fit into the same architecture

docs.title: Reading path
docs.text:
The chapters build on one another, but each topic is written to stand on its own:

  1. Preface — the intent behind the book and how the examples are organized.
  2. Getting Started — Reactor basics, Reactive Streams, and your first WebFlux app with and without Spring Boot.
  3. Web Programming — controllers, functional routing, error handling, uploads, SSE, WebSocket, view rendering, WebClient, and API versioning.
  4. Data Operations — reactive data access with MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, Couchbase, Neo4j, Elasticsearch, and relational databases via R2DBC.
  5. Security — ServerHttpSecurity, the built-in authentication mechanisms, method security, custom user services, and building a mechanism of your own.
  6. Testing — StepVerifier, WebTestClient, Testcontainers, and Spring Test integration.
  7. Kotlin — Kotlin-first WebFlux development with coroutines and DSLs.
  8. Reactive Ecosystem — Mutiny, RxJava 3, JDK Flow, Groovy, caching, events, scheduling, RSocket (TCP, WebSocket, CRUD, Spring Integration), Spring Session, and Spring Integration.

docs.title: Start with a sample
docs.text:
Each chapter is backed by a runnable example in the repository. Clone it, start a dependency, and run the module you want to explore.

git clone https://github.com/hantsy/spring-reactive-sample
cd spring-reactive-sample

docker-compose up mongodb   # start a backing store
cd boot-data-mongo          # choose a sample module
./mvnw spring-boot:run

docs.title: Repository status
docs.text:
The examples in this repo target Spring Framework 7 / Spring Boot 4. If you need older material, the repository still keeps tagged releases for:

  • Spring Boot 3.x
  • Spring Boot 2.x

This keeps the learning path practical: you can move from the modern stack to earlier versions when you need to compare behavior or migrate an older application.

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
When Spring introduced its reactive programming stack in the Spring 5 era, I followed it closely and wrote an early article, Reactive Programming with Spring 5, to explain the new ideas in practical terms. This site is the evolution of that work: it takes the original material, refreshes it for Spring Framework 7 and Spring Boot 4, and turns it into a more structured, hands-on guide.

The examples remain the core of the learning experience. Instead of long theoretical explanations, the book shows how reactive programming looks in real Spring applications — from a minimal HTTP service to database access, security, testing, and Kotlin integrations.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
This is a practical guide to the Spring reactive stack, especially Spring WebFlux.

It is not a full reference for the entire Spring ecosystem. If you are learning Spring for the first time, it helps to have some background in Spring MVC, dependency injection, and Java application development. A basic understanding of modern Java and Maven or Gradle will make the journey smoother.

docs.title: Why the examples matter
docs.text:
At the heart of this book is a simple idea: one runnable example is worth more than a thousand words.

Reactive features in Spring span many layers — WebFlux, Spring Data, Spring Security, Spring Session, Kotlin coroutines, and the wider reactive ecosystem. Rather than explaining every concept in isolation, the book uses small, real examples to show how they behave in context.

The source code for every chapter lives in the GitHub repository: hantsy/spring-reactive-sample. The README lists each sample and gives you a quick description, so you can jump directly to the module that matches your interest.

docs.title: How to read this book
docs.text:
You do not need to read every chapter in a single sitting. A good path is:

  1. read the core concepts in the Getting Started chapters
  2. try one WebFlux example locally
  3. move to data access, security, or testing when the use case matches your project
  4. return to the Kotlin and ecosystem chapters when you need a broader view

The goal is not to memorize APIs; it is to understand how the pieces fit together in a reactive application.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Feedback is welcome.

If you find an error in the code samples or a gap in the documentation, please open an issue. If a concept is missing or a sample would be useful, a pull request or issue report is always appreciated.

If this book has been useful to you, sharing it with others or supporting the project is a great way to keep the work going.

docs.title: Accessing Cassandra with Spring Data Cassandra
docs.text:
Cassandra is a wide-column database built for very high write throughput and linear scalability. In the Java ecosystem, its driver exposes a reactive execution model, and Spring makes it easy to use that model without giving up repository-style ergonomics.

In this chapter, we look at the two main patterns:

  • using Spring Data Cassandra repositories
  • working directly with the native reactive driver through CqlSession

The examples below follow the same practical style as the other chapters in this book: small, readable, and close to the way you would build a real application.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The fastest path is to generate a project from Spring Initializr, as described in the Getting Started chapter. Choose Spring WebFlux and Spring Data for Apache Cassandra.

If you are adding Cassandra to an existing project, include the following dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-cassandra-reactive</artifactId>
</dependency>

If you are building a plain Spring project without Boot auto-configuration, use this dependency instead:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-cassandra</artifactId>
</dependency>

You also need a configuration class to enable reactive Cassandra support:

@Configuration
@EnableReactiveCassandraRepositories(basePackageClasses = {CassandraConfig.class})
public class CassandraConfig extends AbstractReactiveCassandraConfiguration {

    @Value("${cassandra.keyspace-name}")
    String keySpace;

    @Value("${cassandra.contact-points}")
    String contactPoints;

    @Override
    protected List<CreateKeyspaceSpecification> getKeyspaceCreations() {
        CreateKeyspaceSpecification specification = CreateKeyspaceSpecification.createKeyspace(keySpace)
            .ifNotExists()
            .with(KeyspaceOption.DURABLE_WRITES, true);
        return Arrays.asList(specification);
    }

    @Override
    protected List<DropKeyspaceSpecification> getKeyspaceDrops() {
        return Arrays.asList(DropKeyspaceSpecification.dropKeyspace(keySpace));
    }

    @Override
    protected String getKeyspaceName() {
        return keySpace;
    }

    @Override
    protected String getContactPoints() {
        return contactPoints;
    }

    @Override
    public SchemaAction getSchemaAction() {
        return SchemaAction.RECREATE;
    }
}

The keyspace setup is straightforward: create the keyspace if it does not already exist, and keep the schema behavior explicit. The repository layer then handles most of the CRUD work for you.

You can explore this example in data-cassandra.

With Spring Boot, the connection is usually configured automatically from application.properties:

spring.cassandra.contact-points=localhost
spring.cassandra.keyspace-name=blog
spring.cassandra.local-datacenter=datacenter1

docs.title: Defining the table model
docs.text:
Create a Post class that maps to a Cassandra table:

@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
@Table("posts")
class Post {

    @PrimaryKey
    @Builder.Default
    private String id = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    private String title;
    private String content;
}

The annotations are simple:

  1. @Table maps the class to a Cassandra table.
  2. @PrimaryKey identifies the primary key field.
  3. @Builder.Default gives the record an ID by default.

Unlike MongoDB and some other document stores, Cassandra expects the identifier to be set before insertion. The default value covers that for us.

docs.title: Creating a repository
docs.text:
Define a repository interface by extending ReactiveCassandraRepository:

interface PostRepository extends ReactiveCassandraRepository<Post, String> {}

Once Spring creates the repository bean, it can be injected into any controller or service without additional ceremony.

docs.title: Exposing a REST API
docs.text:
A small controller is enough to expose a reactive CRUD API:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping
    public Flux<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @PostMapping
    public Mono<Post> create(@RequestBody Post post) {
        post.setId(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        return this.posts.save(post);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> get(@PathVariable("id") String id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> update(@PathVariable("id") String id, @RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.posts.findById(id)
            .map(existing -> {
                existing.setTitle(post.getTitle());
                existing.setContent(post.getContent());
                return existing;
            })
            .flatMap(this.posts::save);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Void> delete(@PathVariable("id") String id) {
        return this.posts.deleteById(id);
    }
}

Notice that the create method assigns the ID explicitly. Cassandra does not generate it for you the way some document databases do.

docs.title: Seeding sample data
docs.text:
You can use a CommandLineRunner to insert a few example records during startup:

public void init() {
    log.info("Start data initialization...");
    this.posts
        .deleteAll()
        .thenMany(
            Flux.just("Post one", "Post two")
                .flatMap(title -> this.posts.save(
                    Post.builder()
                        .title(title)
                        .content("content of " + title)
                        .build()))
        )
        .log()
        .subscribe(
            null,
            null,
            () -> log.info("Data initialization complete.")
        );
}

This pattern is useful when you want a clean, reproducible bootstrap for a demo or tutorial application.

docs.title: Running the application
docs.text:
Before starting the app, make sure Cassandra is running locally.

If you prefer Docker, you can start it directly from the repository's compose file:

docker-compose up cassandra

Then launch the application:

mvn spring-boot:run

You can test the API with curl:

curl -v http://localhost:8080/posts

docs.title: Working with the native client
docs.text: The CqlSession that Boot auto-configures can be used directly, without Spring Data repositories. Cassandra's driver includes native reactive support — the executeReactive extension returns a ReactiveResultSet, which converts to Reactor types with Mono.from(...).

docs.title: Project setup
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cassandra</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Implementing a repository with CqlSession
docs.text:
Switch from the blocking cqlSession.execute(...) to cqlSession.executeReactive(...), and leverage Mono.from(...) to transform the driver's publisher stream into a reactive flow:

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class ProductRepository {
    private final CqlSession cqlSession;

    public Mono<Product> save(Product product) {
        var id = product.id() != null ? product.id() : UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        String query = """
                INSERT INTO products(id, name, price)
                VALUES (:id, :name, :price)
                IF NOT EXISTS
                """;
        ReactiveResultSet resultSet = cqlSession.executeReactive(query, Map.of(
                "id", id,
                "name", product.name(),
                "price", product.price()
        ));

        return Mono.from(resultSet)
                .flatMap(row -> {
                    log.info("Inserted product with id {}", id);
                    if (row.wasApplied()) {
                        return Mono.just(new Product(id, product.name(), product.price()));
                    } else {
                        return Mono.empty();
                    }
                });
    }
}

docs.title: Testing with Testcontainers
docs.text:
Define a CassandraContainer bean with Spring Boot's @ServiceConnection to automatically configure the connection to the Cassandra container:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    CassandraContainer cassandraContainer() {
        return new CassandraContainer(DockerImageName.parse("cassandra:latest"))
                .withInitScript("init.cql")
                .withStartupTimeout(Duration.ofMinutes(5));
    }
}

Add the following dependencies to your pom.xml for testing with Testcontainers:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-testcontainers</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>testcontainers-cassandra</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.testcontainers</groupId>
    <artifactId>testcontainers-junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Assert the reactive pipeline with StepVerifier:

@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
@SpringBootTest
class DemoApplicationTests {

    @Autowired
    ProductRepository productRepository;

    @Test
    public void testProductRepository() {
        String insertedId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();

        productRepository.save(new Product(insertedId, "test", BigDecimal.ONE))
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(product -> {
                    assertThat(product.id()).isEqualTo(insertedId);
                    assertThat(product.name()).isEqualTo("test");
                })
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

You can explore the native-client example in boot-cassandra, and the repository-based one in boot-data-cassandra.

docs.title: Accessing Couchbase with Spring Data Couchbase
docs.text:
Couchbase blurs the line between document storage and a richer distributed data platform. It is especially useful when you want JSON documents, flexible indexing, and a lower-latency data layer without giving up the convenience of Spring abstractions.

In Spring, you usually work with Couchbase in one of two ways:

  • through Spring Data Couchbase repositories and templates
  • directly with the Java SDK's Cluster and ReactiveCollection when you need a more explicit control flow

The sample here focuses on the WebFlux-friendly path and demonstrates the patterns you would use in a real application without adding unnecessary ceremony.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The quickest way to start is to generate a project from Spring Initializr, as described in the Getting Started chapter. Select Spring WebFlux and Spring Data Couchbase (Reactive).

If you are adding Couchbase to an existing project, include the following dependency in your pom.xml:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-couchbase-reactive</artifactId>
</dependency>

If you are building a plain Spring project without Boot auto-configuration, use the following dependencies instead:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-couchbase</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.couchbase.client</groupId>
    <artifactId>java-client</artifactId>
</dependency>

In that case, you also need a configuration class extending AbstractCouchbaseConfiguration, with @EnableReactiveCouchbaseRepositories to enable reactive Repository support:

@Configuration
@EnableReactiveCouchbaseRepositories(basePackageClasses = {CouchbaseConfig.class})
public class CouchbaseConfig extends AbstractCouchbaseConfiguration {

    @Value("${couchbase.user}")
    private String user;

    @Value("${couchbase.password}")
    private String password;

    @Value("${couchbase.connection-string}")
    private String connectionString;

    @Value("${couchbase.bucket-name}")
    private String bucket;

    @Override
    public String getConnectionString() {
        return this.connectionString;
    }

    @Override
    public String getUserName() {
        return this.user;
    }

    @Override
    public String getPassword() {
        return this.password;
    }

    @Override
    public String getBucketName() {
        return this.bucket;
    }
}

You can explore this setup in data-couchbase.

With Spring Boot, the connection is usually configured automatically from application.properties:

spring.couchbase.connection-string=couchbase://localhost
spring.couchbase.username=Administrator
spring.couchbase.password=password
spring.data.couchbase.bucket-name=default

docs.title: Defining the document model
docs.text:
Create a Post class that maps to a Couchbase document:

@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
@Document
class Post {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UNIQUE)
    private String id;
    private String title;

    @Field("content")
    private String content;
}

The annotations in this example are straightforward:

  1. @Document marks the class as a Couchbase document.
  2. @Id designates the document key; @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UNIQUE) lets Spring Data generate a unique key for you.
  3. @Field maps a differently named field in the document.

docs.title: Creating a repository
docs.text:
Define a repository interface by extending ReactiveCouchbaseRepository:

@ViewIndexed(designDoc = "post", viewName = "all")
interface PostRepository extends ReactiveCouchbaseRepository<Post, String> {}

Once Spring creates the repository bean, you can inject it into controllers or services.

docs.title: Exposing a REST API
docs.text:
A small controller is enough to expose a reactive CRUD API:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping("")
    public Flux<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @PostMapping("")
    public Mono<Post> create(@RequestBody Post post) {
        post.setId(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        return this.posts.save(post);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> get(@PathVariable("id") String id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> update(@PathVariable("id") String id, @RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.posts.findById(id)
            .map(p -> {
                p.setTitle(post.getTitle());
                p.setContent(post.getContent());

                return p;
            })
            .flatMap(p -> this.posts.save(p));
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Void> delete(@PathVariable("id") String id) {
        return this.posts.deleteById(id);
    }
}

docs.text:
Before starting the app, make sure Couchbase is running locally.

If you prefer Docker, start Couchbase with the Docker Compose file in the repository root:

docs.title: Working with the native client
docs.text: The spring-boot-starter-couchbase starter auto-configures a Couchbase Cluster bean. By obtaining the collection reference, you can perform document operations directly — call .reactive() on the collection to obtain a ReactiveCollection; the SDK exposes it natively, so no additional reactive driver is needed.

docs.title: Project setup
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-couchbase</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Implementing a repository with ReactiveCollection
docs.text:
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class ProductRepository {
    private final Cluster cluster;
    private ReactiveCollection productCollection;

    @PostConstruct
    public void init() {
        this.productCollection = this.cluster
                .bucket("demo")
                .defaultCollection()
                .reactive();
    }

    public Mono<Product> save(Product product) {
        String id = product.id() != null ? product.id() : UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        return this.productCollection.upsert(id, product)
                .mapNotNull(result -> {
                    log.debug("saving product result: {}", result);
                    return new Product(id, product.name(), product.price());
                });
    }
}

docs.title: Testing with Testcontainers
docs.text:
Define a CouchbaseContainer bean with Spring Boot's @ServiceConnection — the bucket and credentials are provisioned for the ephemeral server:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    public CouchbaseContainer couchbaseContainer() {
        return new CouchbaseContainer("couchbase/server")
                .withCredentials("Administrator", "password")
                .withBucket(new BucketDefinition("demo").withPrimaryIndex(true))
                .withStartupAttempts(5)
                .withStartupTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(120));
    }
}

You can explore the native-client example in boot-couchbase, and the repository-based one in boot-data-couchbase.

docs.title: Accessing Elasticsearch with Spring Data Elasticsearch
docs.text:
Elasticsearch is a natural fit for full-text search, log analytics, and document lookup at scale. It is not the first tool many people think of for a small CRUD app, but once a service needs flexible search, ranking, and query composition, it becomes invaluable.

In Spring, there are two common ways to work with it:

  • through Spring Data Elasticsearch repositories, which sit on top of the framework's ReactiveElasticsearchClient
  • directly with the reactive client when you need finer control over the query pipeline

The example below keeps the setup intentionally lightweight while showing the practical patterns you need in a reactive WebFlux service.

Important

Unlike the other stores in this chapter, Elasticsearch is an exception: the official Elasticsearch Java Client SDK does not include a reactive client. Spring Data Elasticsearch fills this gap by providing its own ReactiveElasticsearchClient wrapper built on top of the low-level REST client. As a consequence, you cannot use a lightweight spring-boot-starter-elasticsearch alone — you must pull in the full Spring Data Elasticsearch starter to access the reactive client.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The quickest way to start is to generate a project from Spring Initializr, as described in the Getting Started chapter. Select Spring WebFlux and Spring Data Elasticsearch.

If you are adding Elasticsearch to an existing project, include the following dependency in your pom.xml:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-elasticsearch</artifactId>
</dependency>

With Spring Boot, the connection is usually configured automatically from application.properties:

spring.elasticsearch.uris=http://localhost:9200

docs.title: Defining the document model
docs.text:
Create a Post class that maps to an Elasticsearch index:

@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
@Document(indexName = "posts")
public class Post {

    @Id
    private String id;
    private String title;

    @Field("content")
    private String content;
}

The annotations in this example are straightforward:

  1. @Document marks the class as an Elasticsearch document and names the target index.
  2. @Id identifies the document ID field.
  3. @Field maps a differently named field in the document.

docs.title: Creating a repository
docs.text:

docs.title: Working with the native client
docs.text:
The ReactiveElasticsearchClient that Spring Data provides can be used directly, without repositories. Inject it and chain document operations in non-blocking Reactor streams.

Note

ElasticSearch does not provide a reactive client SDK for connecting to Elasticsearch services.

docs.title: Implementing a repository with ReactiveElasticsearchClient
docs.text:
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Slf4j
public class ProductRepository {
    private final ReactiveElasticsearchClient client;

    public Mono<Product> save(Product product) {
        var id = product.id() != null ? product.id() : UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        log.debug("Saving product with id={}", id);
        return client.index(builder -> builder.id(id).index("products").document(product))
                .mapNotNull(response -> {
                    var savedID = response.id();
                    log.debug("Saved product with id={}", savedID);
                    return new Product(savedID, product.name(), product.price());
                });
    }
}

docs.title: Testing with Testcontainers
docs.text:
Define an ElasticsearchContainer bean with Spring Boot's @ServiceConnection:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    ElasticsearchContainer elasticsearchContainer() {
        return new ElasticsearchContainer(DockerImageName.parse("docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:9.3.3"))
                .withEnv(Map.of("xpack.security.enabled", "false"));
    }
}

The image has to be a recent server. Spring Data Elasticsearch 6 talks to the cluster only through the modern co.elastic.clients Java client — the RestHighLevelClient-based ElasticsearchRestTemplate from the Elasticsearch 7 era has been removed — so an Elasticsearch 7 container fails with requests the old server rejects, such as POST /posts/_pit does not support having a body. xpack.security.enabled=false keeps the connection on plain HTTP.

You can explore the native-client example in boot-elasticsearch, and the repository-based one in boot-data-elasticsearch.

docs.title: An introduction to Spring Data (Reactive)
docs.text:
Spring Data is a family of projects that gives different data stores a consistent programming model. At its foundation is Spring Data Commons, which defines shared concepts such as repositories, paging and sorting, auditing, and mapping conventions. Individual modules build on those concepts and adapt them to a particular store, such as MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, or a relational database through R2DBC.

Understanding the common layer makes the store-specific chapters easier to follow. The database changes, but many of the choices you make in the application remain familiar.

docs.title: The repository model
docs.text:
The repository hierarchy starts with Repository<T, ID>, a marker interface that associates a repository with an entity type and its identifier type. It does not expose operations by itself. More specific interfaces add the capabilities an application needs:

Interface Role CrudRepository<T, ID> Synchronous CRUD operations PagingAndSortingRepository<T, ID> Paging and sorting operations ReactiveCrudRepository<T, ID> Reactive CRUD operations ReactiveSortingRepository<T, ID> Reactive sorting operations

ReactiveCrudRepository<T, ID> extends the common Repository<T, ID> marker and provides reactive CRUD operations. ReactiveSortingRepository<T, ID> adds reactive sorting support. These are separate interfaces rather than one inheritance chain, so a repository can compose the capabilities it needs.

For a reactive store, a repository can extend a store-specific interface such as ReactiveMongoRepository<Post, String>. That interface combines common reactive CRUD behavior with the query and mapping support of the store module. The reactive repository APIs use Reactor types: a single result is represented by Mono<T>, while a stream of results is represented by Flux<T>.

For example:

interface PostRepository extends ReactiveCrudRepository<Post, String> {
    Flux<Post> findByTitleContaining(String term);
}

The repository is an abstraction, not a requirement. You can define query methods and let Spring Data implement them, or choose a template or native driver when you need more control. When you need sorting as well as reactive CRUD, compose ReactiveSortingRepository with ReactiveCrudRepository where the store module supports it. Store-specific repository interfaces may already combine these capabilities, so check the module's API before adding both.

docs.title: Repositories, templates, and drivers
docs.text:
Spring Data modules commonly offer several levels of data access:

  • Repositories provide a focused interface for common operations, derived queries, and—where supported—paging or sorting.
  • Templates, such as ReactiveMongoTemplate or R2dbcEntityTemplate, offer a fluent API for operations that need more control over queries, mapping, or updates.
  • Native drivers expose the database vendor's API directly. They can be useful for specialized features, but leave more integration work to the application.

These approaches can coexist in one application. Use the highest-level API that fits the operation, and reach for a template or driver when the repository abstraction no longer expresses the query clearly.

docs.title: Auditing shared across stores
docs.text:
Spring Data Commons also provides auditing support for common entity metadata. Auditing can populate fields such as creation time, last-modified time, creator, and last modifier. The familiar annotations include @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, and @LastModifiedBy.

The annotations describe the fields, but auditing must also be enabled for the store module. The configuration varies by module—for example, reactive MongoDB and Neo4j use their reactive auditing enablement annotations. If the application needs to record the current user, provide an auditor provider; reactive modules support ReactiveAuditorAware so the auditor can be resolved without blocking.

Auditing is useful for operational metadata, but it does not replace domain-specific history or event logging. It answers questions such as “when was this record last changed?” rather than preserving every change.

docs.title: Reactive data access
docs.text:
Reactive Spring Data modules carry the common model into non-blocking applications. Their repository methods return reactive types rather than eagerly materialized collections or individual values. Spring Data R2DBC brings this model to relational databases; other modules integrate with reactive drivers or provide a reactive API of their own.

The rest of this chapter explores those store-specific differences, while the repository, template, and auditing concepts above provide a shared foundation.

docs.title: What this chapter covers
docs.text:
• the reactive repository pattern across the major Spring Data stores
  • MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, Couchbase, Elasticsearch, and Neo4j in a reactive setup
  • Spring Data R2DBC for relational databases
  • thin-client access to native reactive drivers and the richer Spring Data abstractions (XXXRepository, XXXTemplate)
  • mapping, pagination, auditing, and query derivation in real-world examples

docs.title: A quick rule of thumb
docs.text:
• Use traditional JDBC/JPA only when blocking access is acceptable.
  • In a reactive application, favor R2DBC or a reactive database driver.
  • Reactive repositories return Flux instead of List and Mono instead of a single entity.
  • There is no Page object in the reactive API; use Pageable parameters plus a separate count query, or skip/take operators.

docs.title: Thin client vs. rich Spring Data
docs.text:
There are two common ways to work with a database in a reactive Spring app:

  • a thin client approach, where you use the database's native SDK directly
  • a rich Spring Data approach, where you leverage Spring Data repositories, templates, and mapping support

The thin client is ideal when you want direct control over the driver and very targeted access patterns. It usually gives you maximum efficiency, but it also means more manual work for query composition, pagination, and object mapping.

The richer Spring Data abstraction is often easier to maintain when the application needs query derivation, auditing, pagination, or mapping support. You spend less time wiring infrastructure and more time modeling the domain.

Style API Best for Thin client native driver + starter autoconfiguration performance-sensitive operations, fine control, low overhead Rich Spring Data ReactiveMongoRepository, ReactiveRedisTemplate, R2dbcRepository, ... query derivation, pagination, auditing, object mapping

A good rule: if your app needs anything beyond a simple CRUD flow, Spring Data often saves time and reduces boilerplate.

docs.title: Spring Boot 4 starter landscape
docs.text:
Spring Boot 4 modularizes the old monolithic auto-configuration model into more focused starter modules. That makes it easier to include only the database and driver support your application actually needs.

Database Starter Autoconfigured Bean Reactive Pattern Cassandra spring-boot-starter-cassandra CqlSession executeReactive() → Mono.from(ReactiveResultSet) — see Cassandra Couchbase spring-boot-starter-couchbase Cluster collection.reactive() → ReactiveCollection — see Couchbase Elasticsearch spring-boot-starter-data-elasticsearch ReactiveElasticsearchClient Spring Data wrapper — see Elasticsearch MongoDB spring-boot-starter-mongodb MongoClient (reactive streams) Mono.from(...) / Flux.from(...) — see Mongo Neo4j spring-boot-starter-neo4j Driver ReactiveSession + Mono.usingWhen(...) — see Neo4j R2DBC spring-boot-starter-r2dbc DatabaseClient handwritten SQL — see R2DBC Redis via spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive reactive Redis connection and templates ReactiveRedisTemplate / Lettuce commands — see Redis

Tip

StepVerifier from the reactor-test module is invaluable for checking reactive flows in tests. Pair it with Testcontainers and @ServiceConnection to keep each integration test isolated and deterministic.

See the Spring Boot 4 Modularization guide in the companion spring7-sandbox repository.

docs.title: A practical reading path
docs.text:
A good way to use this chapter is to move from the most familiar patterns to the more specialized ones:

  • start with Accessing MongoDB with Spring Data Mongo for a clear, repository-first example that shows the reactive data model in action
  • continue with Accessing Redis with Spring Data Redis to see how a lightweight key-value store fits into a reactive app
  • then explore Accessing Cassandra with Spring Data Cassandra, Couchbase, Elasticsearch, and Neo4j for the other common NoSQL options
  • finish with Accessing RDBMS with Spring R2DBC and Spring Data R2DBC to see how reactive SQL works in the same Spring ecosystem

If you already know the basics, skip directly to the database that matches your use case. The important idea is consistent: the data access layer stays reactive, but the APIs and conventions vary depending on the store.

docs.title: Accessing MongoDB with Spring Data Mongo
docs.text:
MongoDB is one of the most natural fits for a reactive stack. It stores documents in a JSON-like shape, and its Java driver is built around streaming operations that align well with Reactor and WebFlux.

In Spring, you typically work with MongoDB in one of two ways:

  • through Spring Data MongoDB repositories and templates
  • directly with the reactive MongoDB driver via MongoClient when you need more control over the data flow

The example below keeps the focus on the real-world flow: a small reactive API, a document model, and a straightforward repository setup that you can adapt to a real service.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The quickest way to start is to generate a project from Spring Initializr, as described in the Getting Started chapter. Select Spring WebFlux and Spring Data MongoDB.

If you are adding MongoDB to an existing project, include the following dependencies in your pom.xml:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb-reactive</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
    <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
</dependency>

Lombok is optional, but it helps remove repetitive boilerplate such as getters, setters, equals, hashCode, and toString.

If you are building a plain Spring project without Boot auto-configuration, use the following dependencies instead:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-mongodb</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.mongodb</groupId>
    <artifactId>mongodb-driver-reactivestreams</artifactId>
</dependency>

In that case, you also need a small configuration class to enable reactive MongoDB support:

@EnableReactiveMongoRepositories(basePackageClasses = {MongoConfig.class})
public class MongoConfig extends AbstractReactiveMongoConfiguration {

    @Value("${mongo.uri}")
    String mongoUri;

    @Override
    public MongoClient mongoClient() {
        return MongoClients.create(mongoUri);
    }

    @Override
    protected String getDatabaseName() {
        return "blog";
    }
}

You can explore this setup in data-mongo.

With Spring Boot, the connection is usually configured automatically from application.properties or application.yml:

spring.data.mongodb.uri=mongodb://localhost:27017/blog

docs.title: Defining the document model
docs.text:
Create a Post document class that maps to a MongoDB collection:

@Document
@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
class Post {

    @Id
    private String id;
    private String title;
    private String content;
}

The annotations in this example are straightforward:

  1. @Document marks the class as a MongoDB document.
  2. @Id identifies the document ID field.
  3. @Data is from Lombok and help to generates getters, setters, equals, hashCode methods at compile time.
  4. @ToString generates a toString() implementation.
  5. @Builder enables the builder pattern.
  6. @NoArgsConstructor creates a no-args constructor.
  7. @AllArgsConstructor creates a constructor with all fields.

docs.title: Creating a repository
docs.text:
Define a repository interface by extending ReactiveMongoRepository:

interface PostRepository extends ReactiveMongoRepository<Post, String> {
}

Once Spring creates the repository bean, you can inject it into controllers or services.

docs.title: Exposing a REST API
docs.text:
A small controller is enough to expose a reactive CRUD API:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping
    public Flux<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @PostMapping
    public Mono<Post> create(@RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.posts.save(post);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> get(@PathVariable("id") String id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> update(@PathVariable("id") String id, @RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.posts.findById(id)
            .map(existing -> {
                existing.setTitle(post.getTitle());
                existing.setContent(post.getContent());
                return existing;
            })
            .flatMap(this.posts::save);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Void> delete(@PathVariable("id") String id) {
        return this.posts.deleteById(id);
    }
}

docs.title: Seeding sample data
docs.text:
You can use a CommandLineRunner to insert a few sample records when the application starts:

@Component
@Slf4j
class DataInitializr implements CommandLineRunner {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public DataInitializr(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @Override
    public void run(String[] args) {
        log.info("Start data initialization...");
        this.posts
            .deleteAll()
            .thenMany(
                Flux.just("Post one", "Post two")
                    .flatMap(title -> this.posts.save(
                        Post.builder()
                            .title(title)
                            .content("content of " + title)
                            .build()))
            )
            .log()
            .subscribe(
                null,
                null,
                () -> log.info("Data initialization complete.")
            );
    }
}

CommandLineRunner ensures the initialization logic runs once the application has started.

docs.title: Running the application
docs.text:
Before starting the app, make sure MongoDB is running locally.

Note

If MongoDB is not installed yet, visit the MongoDB download page and install it first.

If you prefer Docker, it is easy to start MongoDB with Docker Compose:

version: "3.3"

services:
  mongodb:
    image: mongo
    volumes:
      - mongodata:/data/db
    ports:
      - "27017:27017"
    command: --smallfiles --rest
    # command: --smallfiles --rest --auth

volumes:
  mongodata:

Note

The repository also includes a Docker Compose file that can start the database services for you.

Start MongoDB in a container:

docker-compose up mongodb

Then launch the application:

mvn spring-boot:run

You can test the API with curl:

curl -v http://localhost:8080/posts
