  • use suspend for single-value operations
  • use Flow for streaming collections
  • keep validation and exception handling in the usual Spring style
  • use coroutine-aware repository and transaction APIs for clean control flow

This produces code that is easier to read and maintain while preserving the performance and scalability characteristics of reactive programming.

docs.title: Kotlin DSLs
docs.text:
Spring ships Kotlin DSLs for the main configuration surfaces of a WebFlux application: bean registration, functional routing, and security. They replace verbose builder chains and annotation ceremony with typed, nested lambda blocks that read top-down, while producing exactly the same bean definitions, RouterFunctions, and filter chains as the Java APIs.

This page walks through the four DSLs used in the samples:

DSL Purpose Samples beans { } (BeanDefinitionDsl) Functional bean definitions (deprecated in 7.1) kotlin-dsl, boot-kotlin-dsl, boot-kotlin-co-dsl BeanRegistrarDsl Bean registration, Spring Framework 7+ boot-bean-registrar-kotlin-dsl router { } / coRouter { } Functional routes (Reactor / coroutines) boot-kotlin-dsl, boot-kotlin-co-dsl, boot-security-kotlin-dsl http { } (Security) SecurityWebFilterChain configuration boot-security-kotlin-dsl

docs.title: The beans DSL (BeanDefinitionDsl)
docs.text:
The beans { } function (org.springframework.context.support.beans) replaces annotation configuration with functional registration. Define it as a fun (or val) and apply it as an application context initializer:

import org.springframework.context.support.beans

@Suppress("DEPRECATION")
fun beans() = beans {
    bean {
        CommandLineRunner {
            println("start data initialization...")
            val posts = ref<PostRepository>()
            posts.deleteAll()
                .thenMany<Post>(
                    posts.saveAll(
                        arrayListOf(
                            Post(null, "my first post", "content of my first post"),
                            Post(null, "my second post", "content of my second post")
                        )
                    )
                )
                .log()
                .subscribe { println("data initialization done.") }
        }
    }

    bean {
        PostRoutes(PostHandler(ref())).routes()
    }

    bean {
        val config = CorsConfiguration().apply { /* ... */ }
        val source = UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource().apply {
            registerCorsConfiguration("/**", config)
        }
        CorsWebFilter(source)
    }
}

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    runApplication<DemoApplication>(*args) {
        addInitializers(beans())
    }
}

Reading the DSL:

  • bean { ... } registers a bean with a supplier; ref<T>() resolves another bean by type.
  • The DSL registers any bean the application needs — a CommandLineRunner for data initialization, the RouterFunction, even a CorsWebFilter.
  • With Spring Boot, apply it with addInitializers(beans()); in a plain Spring application, register the initializer on a GenericApplicationContext.

Note: In Spring Framework 7.1+, the beans { } function is deprecated in favor of BeanRegistrarDsl (see below). The samples use @Suppress("DEPRECATION") to silence the warning while staying compatible with both Spring Framework 6.x and 7.x. For new code targeting Spring Framework 7+, prefer BeanRegistrarDsl.

The kotlin-dsl sample shows the plain-Spring variant with RouterFunctions.toWebHandler(...); boot-kotlin-dsl shows the Spring Boot variant; boot-kotlin-co-dsl combines it with coroutine handlers.

docs.title: BeanRegistrarDsl
docs.text:
Spring Framework 7 evolves bean registration into the BeanRegistrar contract; BeanRegistrarDsl is its Kotlin face — a registrar class you @Import instead of an initializer. See Programmatic Bean Registration with BeanRegistrar for the Java API and the motivations behind it.

import org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanRegistrarDsl

class PostBeanRegistrar : BeanRegistrarDsl({
    registerBean { InMemoryPostRepository() }
    registerBean { PostHandler(bean()) }
    registerBean { Routes(bean()) }
    registerBean { bean<Routes>().routes() }
    registerBean {
        CommandLineRunner {
            runBlocking { bean<PostRepository>().initializeSampleData() }
        }
    }
    register(FoobarRegistrar())
})

class FoobarRegistrar : BeanRegistrarDsl({
    profile("foo") {
        registerBean<Bar> { Bar(bean<Foo>()) }
        registerBean { Foo() }
    }
})

Reading the DSL:

  • registerBean { ... } is reified — the bean type is inferred from the supplier's return value; pass an explicit type argument (registerBean<Bar> { ... }) when registering against a supertype.
  • bean<T>() inside a supplier resolves a dependency at instantiation time, the DSL equivalent of SupplierContext.bean(...).
  • Named parameters expose the bean metadata: name, autowirable, backgroundInit, description, fallback, infrastructure, lazyInit, order, primary, prototype.
  • profile("foo") { ... } scopes registrations to a profile; the expression also supports !, &, and | combinations.
  • register(other) composes another registrar, as FoobarRegistrar above.

Import the registrar on the application class — no initializer needed:

@SpringBootApplication
@Import(PostBeanRegistrar::class)
class DemoApplication

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    runApplication<DemoApplication>(*args)
}

Check the boot-bean-registrar-kotlin-dsl sample for a complete application: coroutine handlers, coRouter routes, and sample-data initialization, all registered through the DSL.

docs.title: Router DSLs: router and coRouter
docs.text:
The router { } function (RouterFunctionDsl) declares functional routes with a nesting style that reads top-down, replacing the andRoute chain from RouterFunctions:

class PostRoutes(private val postHandler: PostHandler) {
    fun routes() = router {
        "/posts".nest {
            GET("", postHandler::all)
            GET("/{id}", postHandler::get)
            POST("", postHandler::create)
            PUT("/{id}", postHandler::update)
            DELETE("/{id}", postHandler::delete)
        }
    }
}

The handlers here are ordinary Mono<ServerResponse> methods — the same shape as the kotlin-routes sample. Check boot-kotlin-dsl and boot-security-kotlin-dsl for router { } in a Boot application.

docs.title: The coroutine variant: coRouter and suspend handlers
docs.text:
coRouter { } (CoRouterFunctionDsl) is the coroutine counterpart — routes reference suspend handlers, and the DSL bridges them into the reactive runtime:

class Routes(val postHandler: PostHandler) {
    fun routes() = coRouter {
        "/posts".nest {
            "{id}".nest {
                GET(accept(APPLICATION_JSON), postHandler::get)
                PUT(contentType(APPLICATION_JSON), postHandler::update)
                DELETE(accept(APPLICATION_JSON), postHandler::delete)
            }
            GET(accept(APPLICATION_JSON), postHandler::all)
            POST(contentType(APPLICATION_JSON), postHandler::create)
        }
    }
}

class PostHandler(val posts: PostRepository) {

    suspend fun all(req: ServerRequest): ServerResponse {
        return ServerResponse.ok().bodyAndAwait(this.posts.findAll())
    }

    suspend fun create(req: ServerRequest): ServerResponse {
        val body = req.awaitBody(Post::class)
        val saved = this.posts.save(body)
        return ServerResponse.created(URI.create("/posts/$saved")).buildAndAwait()
    }

    suspend fun get(req: ServerRequest): ServerResponse {
        val id = UUID.fromString(req.pathVariable("id"))
        val found = this.posts.findById(id)
        return found?.let { ServerResponse.ok().bodyValueAndAwait(found) }
            ?: ServerResponse.notFound().buildAndAwait()
    }
}

The suspend handlers use the coroutine request/response extensions: awaitBody, bodyAndAwait, bodyValueAndAwait, and buildAndAwait. Request predicates such as accept(...) and contentType(...) work exactly as in router { }.

Check the boot-bean-registrar-kotlin-dsl sample for the routes above, and boot-kotlin-co-dsl for coRouter backed by a CoroutineCrudRepository. When the surrounding contract is blocking — a CommandLineRunner, for example — wrap coroutine work in runBlocking { ... }:

registerBean {
    CommandLineRunner {
        runBlocking { bean<PostRepository>().initializeSampleData() }
    }
}

docs.title: Security: the http DSL
docs.text:
Spring Security's reactive configuration has a Kotlin DSL too. Import the invoke operator and call http { ... } on the injected ServerHttpSecurity — the block configures the chain and the call returns the built SecurityWebFilterChain, so it fits directly as the expression body of a @Bean method:

import org.springframework.security.config.web.server.ServerHttpSecurity
import org.springframework.security.config.web.server.invoke
import org.springframework.security.web.server.SecurityWebFilterChain

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    fun securityWebFilterChain(http: ServerHttpSecurity): SecurityWebFilterChain =
        http {
            csrf { disable() }
            httpBasic {}
            authorizeExchange {
                authorize("/auth/**", authenticated)
                authorize(pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/posts/**"), permitAll)
                authorize(pathMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/posts/**"), hasRole("ADMIN"))
                authorize("/posts/**", authenticated)
                authorize(anyExchange, permitAll)
            }
        }
}

Reading the DSL:

  • csrf { }, httpBasic { }, and authorizeExchange { } mirror the Java configurer methods; an empty block (httpBasic {}) enables the feature with defaults.
  • Inside authorizeExchange, authorize(path, access) maps a pattern to an access decision — authenticated, permitAll, hasRole("ADMIN") — and anyExchange is the catch-all. Rules are evaluated in declaration order.
  • pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/posts/**") (from ServerWebExchangeMatchers) restricts a rule to one HTTP method.

Check the boot-security-kotlin-dsl sample for the complete application: in-memory users, router { } endpoints, and WebTestClient tests covering anonymous, basic-auth, and role-restricted requests. The servlet stack has an equivalent http { } DSL for HttpSecurity (org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.invoke).

docs.title: Kotlin
docs.text:
Kotlin is a modern JVM language designed for clarity, safety, and developer productivity. It runs on the Java Virtual Machine, interoperates tightly with Java libraries, and has become a natural fit for Spring applications because it preserves the Java ecosystem while making day-to-day code shorter and easier to read.

At the language level, Kotlin brings several ideas that matter in a Spring application:

  • it is built on the JVM, so it can use Spring, Reactor, and the broader Java ecosystem without friction
  • it is function-first: higher-order functions, lambdas, default arguments, and concise APIs are first-class features
  • it is null-safe: the type system distinguishes nullable and non-nullable values, reducing the classic NullPointerException problem in application code
  • it has strong support for immutable data: data class and val make domain models easier to reason about and safer to share across threads
  • it is expressive without being noisy: common boilerplate such as getters, setters, and factory methods can be kept out of the codebase

In other words, Kotlin does not replace the JVM or Spring. It gives Spring a more concise and safer language layer on top of the same runtime and ecosystem.

docs.title: Kotlin and Spring
docs.text:
Spring has treated Kotlin as a first-class language for a long time, and that support has only strengthened in the Spring 6 era. The framework integrates naturally with Kotlin features such as constructor injection, bean registration, functional routing, nullability-aware APIs, and coroutine support.

This is especially important in reactive applications: Kotlin does not fight the Reactor model; it sits on top of it and makes it easier to express. You can still work with Mono and Flux, but you can also write code in a more natural Kotlin style with suspend functions and Flow.

docs.title: Kotlin coroutines and Spring WebFlux
docs.text:
Kotlin coroutines are a way to write asynchronous code in a sequential style. Instead of manually nesting callbacks or chaining Mono/Flux, you can write code that reads like a normal function and let the coroutine runtime handle suspension and resumption.

In Spring WebFlux, this is integrated directly:

  • controller methods can be suspend fun
  • repository methods can return Flow<T>
  • filters and route handlers can also be coroutine-aware
  • Spring internally bridges coroutine-based APIs to Reactor so the non-blocking runtime remains intact

That means a Kotlin controller can look closer to ordinary application logic while still benefiting from the reactive server stack underneath.

The long-term direction is also interesting: Kotlin coroutine support is being treated less as a WebFlux-only feature and more as a general Kotlin capability. In other words, the future direction is to decouple coroutine support from the WebFlux-only layer and make it a broader language/platform feature, while Spring WebFlux remains one of the most natural places to use it.

docs.title: Java to Kotlin: a quick comparison
docs.text:
A common Java-style Spring controller looks like this:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/posts")
public class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> get(@PathVariable String id) {
        return posts.findById(id);
    }
}

The Kotlin version keeps the same Spring behavior but removes much of the ceremony:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/posts")
class PostController(private val posts: PostRepository) {

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    suspend fun get(@PathVariable id: String): Post? = posts.findById(id)
}

This is the same idea in a more compact form:

  • constructor injection becomes a primary constructor parameter
  • the class body is shorter
  • suspend removes the explicit Mono wrapper in a controller method
  • nullable return types are modeled directly in the type system instead of via extra switchIfEmpty logic

A Kotlin data model is also much more natural:

public class Post {
    private String id;
    private String title;
    private String content;

    public Post() {}
    public Post(String id, String title, String content) {
        this.id = id;
        this.title = title;
        this.content = content;
    }

    public String getId() { return id; }
    public void setId(String id) { this.id = id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public void setTitle(String title) { this.title = title; }
    public String getContent() { return content; }
    public void setContent(String content) { this.content = content; }
}

data class Post(
    val id: String? = null,
    val title: String,
    val content: String
)

The Kotlin version communicates intent immediately: it is an immutable value object, the fields are typed and explicit, and the boilerplate disappears.

docs.title: Why this matters in the reactive stack
docs.text:
Reactive programming is not just about Flux and Mono; it is about modeling asynchronous data flows with clear boundaries and safe composition. Kotlin complements that style because it makes the same ideas feel more direct:

  • Flow<T> maps naturally to streams of values
  • suspend fun reads like a regular function while still preserving asynchronous semantics
  • nullability helps prevent many runtime surprises at the edge of the application
  • domain code stays concise without losing type safety

For example, a coroutine-based repository and controller are often easier to read than a fully explicit Reactor pipeline:

interface PostRepository : CoroutineCrudRepository<Post, Long> {
    fun findByTitleContains(title: String): Flow<Post>
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/posts")
class PostController(private val posts: PostRepository) {

    @GetMapping
    fun findAll(): Flow<Post> = posts.findAll()

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    suspend fun findOne(@PathVariable id: Long): Post? = posts.findById(id)

    @PostMapping
    suspend fun save(@RequestBody post: Post): Post = posts.save(post)
}

This keeps the Spring model intact while making the code feel much more natural to Kotlin developers.

docs.title: A friendly reading path
docs.text:
If you are new to the Kotlin side of Spring, a good flow is to move from the familiar patterns to the more Kotlin-specific ones:

  • start with Annotation-Driven Controller to see the Kotlin equivalents of the usual Spring WebFlux code you already know
  • then read Coroutines to learn how suspend functions, Flow, and coroutine-aware Spring APIs make the code feel more natural
  • next, explore Kotlin DSLs for the more expressive, declarative functional style
  • finish with Events, caching, and scheduling for the practical integration details that show up in real applications

The order is intentional: it starts with the familiar Spring shape, then moves into Kotlin-native idioms, and finishes with the parts that matter most when you build real applications.

docs.title: Events, Caching, and Scheduling
docs.text: Spring's reactive support for application events, the caching abstraction, and task scheduling extends naturally to Kotlin coroutines. This page collects the coroutine-friendly patterns from the samples.

docs.title: Application events
docs.text:
An @EventListener supports suspend functions directly: since Spring Framework 6.1 the listener method can be declared suspend (or return Flow), and Spring bridges the coroutine completion into the event multicaster:

@Component
class GreetingListener {

    @EventListener
    suspend fun onGreetingEvent(event: Greeting) {
        log.debug("received event: {}", event)
        // ... suspend calls inside the listener body
    }
}

This mirrors the Java pattern in Application Events — publish with ApplicationEventPublisher, observe with @EventListener — with the handler body written in coroutine style.

When the surrounding contract requires a blocking method — Spring Boot lifecycle hooks such as CommandLineRunner, for example — wrap the coroutine work in runBlocking { ... }, as the boot-bean-registrar-kotlin-dsl sample does for data initialization:

registerBean {
    CommandLineRunner {
        runBlocking { bean<PostRepository>().initializeSampleData() }
    }
}

When the hook is an event listener, you can skip runBlocking entirely — the boot-kotlin-co sample declares its ApplicationReadyEvent listener as a suspend function, like the GreetingListener above.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
A @Scheduled method may be a suspend function that awaits a reactive pipeline with awaitSingle:

@Component
class KotlinCounter {

    private val count = AtomicInteger(0)

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5)
    suspend fun scheduled(): Void {
        return Mono.defer { Mono.just(count.incrementAndGet()) }
            .doOnNext { item: Int? -> log.debug("current count:{}", item) }
            .then()
            .awaitSingle()
    }

    suspend fun getInvocationCount(): Int {
        return count.get()
    }
}

The scheduler subscribes to the coroutine completion and waits for it before scheduling the next execution — the same semantics as the Java Scheduling example, with awaitSingle() (from kotlinx.coroutines.reactor) bridging the Mono into the coroutine world.

The test asserts the counter advanced using runTest:

@SpringJUnitConfig(value = [TestConfig::class])
class KotlinCounterTest {

    @Autowired
    lateinit var counter: KotlinCounter

    @Test
    fun givenSleepBy100ms_whenGetInvocationCount_thenIsGreaterThanZero() = runTest {
        assertThat(counter.getInvocationCount()).isGreaterThan(0)
    }
}

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
The reactive caching support added in Spring 6.1 covers Kotlin coroutines as well: @Cacheable/@CachePut/@CacheEvict apply to suspend functions and functions returning Flow, and the cache stores the completion rather than the publisher. Configure the cache manager exactly as in the Java chapter — ConcurrentMapCacheManager, async-mode CaffeineCacheManager, or RedisCacheManager — and annotate the repository or service methods:

@Cacheable(value = "posts", key = "#id")
suspend fun findById(id: UUID): Post? = ...

docs.title: JSON with kotlinx.serialization
docs.text:
Beyond Jackson, Spring Boot 4 adds a first-class starter for kotlinx.serialization: spring-boot-starter-kotlinx-serialization-json (plus its -test variant). A customizer tunes the Json instance:

@OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class)
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class CustomConfig {

    @Bean
    fun kotlinxSerializationJsonBuilderCustomizer(): KotlinxSerializationJsonBuilderCustomizer {
        return KotlinxSerializationJsonBuilderCustomizer { builder ->
            builder.apply {
                namingStrategy = JsonNamingStrategy.SnakeCase
                prettyPrint = true
                explicitNulls = false
                encodeDefaults = true
                ignoreUnknownKeys = false
            }
        }
    }
}

Annotate the DTOs with @Serializable and Spring encodes/decodes them on the HTTP boundary.

docs.title: RouterFunctions
docs.text:
The kotlin-routes sample replaces the controller with a RouterFunction bean — the Kotlin spelling of the Java RouterFunction style, using HandlerFunction references:

import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.HandlerFunction
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.RequestPredicates.*
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.RouterFunctions.route
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.RouterFunction
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.ServerResponse

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {

    @Bean
    fun routes(handler: PostHandler): RouterFunction<ServerResponse> {
        return route(GET("/posts"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::all))
                .andRoute(POST("/posts"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::create))
                .andRoute(GET("/posts/{id}"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::get))
                .andRoute(PUT("/posts/{id}"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::update))
                .andRoute(DELETE("/posts/{id}"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::delete))
    }
}

The handlers are @Component methods returning Mono<ServerResponse>:

@Component
class PostHandler(val posts: PostRepository) {

    fun all(req: ServerRequest): Mono<ServerResponse> {
        return ok().body(this.posts.findAll(), Post::class.java)
    }

    fun create(req: ServerRequest): Mono<ServerResponse> {
        return req.bodyToMono(Post::class.java)
                .flatMap { post -> this.posts.save(post) }
                .flatMap { (id) -> created(URI.create("/posts/$id")).build() }
    }

    fun get(req: ServerRequest): Mono<ServerResponse> {
        return this.posts.findById(req.pathVariable("id"))
                .flatMap { post -> ok().body(Mono.just(post), Post::class.java) }
                .switchIfEmpty(notFound().build())
    }

    fun update(req: ServerRequest): Mono<ServerResponse> {
        return this.posts.findById(req.pathVariable("id"))
                .zipWith(req.bodyToMono(Post::class.java))
                .map { it.t1.copy(title = it.t2.title, content = it.t2.content) }
                .flatMap { this.posts.save(it) }
                .flatMap { noContent().build() }
    }
}

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Coroutines — replace Mono/Flux with suspend functions and Flow.
  • Kotlin DSLs — declare the routes with router { }/coRouter { } and the beans with the Kotlin beans DSL instead of annotations.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Since Spring 6.1, the caching abstraction supports reactive return types: a @Cacheable method may return Mono or Flux, and the cache stores the completion rather than the publisher. The repository ships three samples that differ only in the CacheManager: an in-memory ConcurrentHashMap, Caffeine, and Redis. All three combine the cache with a Spring Data R2DBC backed PostRepository on PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Step 1: enable caching
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig implements CachingConfigurer {

    @Bean
    @Override
    public CacheManager cacheManager() {
        return new ConcurrentMapCacheManager();
    }

    @Bean
    @Override
    public KeyGenerator keyGenerator() {
        return new SimpleKeyGenerator();
    }

    @Bean
    @Override
    public CacheErrorHandler errorHandler() {
        return new SimpleCacheErrorHandler();
    }
}

docs.title: Step 2: annotate the reactive repository
docs.text:
Apply the caching annotations to the repository methods — the reactive signatures work exactly like the blocking ones:

public interface PostRepository extends R2dbcRepository<Post, UUID> {
    @Override
    @Cacheable(value = "posts", key = "#p0")
    Mono<Post> findById(UUID id);

    @Override
    @CachePut(value = "posts", key = "#result.id")
    Mono<Post> save(Post post);

    @Override
    @CacheEvict(value = "posts", key = "#p0")
    Mono<Void> deleteById(UUID id);

    @Override
    @CacheEvict(value = "posts", allEntries = true)
    Mono<Void> deleteAll();
}

docs.title: Caffeine (async cache mode)
docs.text:
Caffeine supports native async caches — enable them with setAsyncCacheMode(true):

@Bean
@Override
public CacheManager cacheManager() {
    CaffeineCacheManager cacheManager = new CaffeineCacheManager();
    cacheManager.setAsyncCacheMode(true);
    return cacheManager;
}

Add the dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.github.ben-manes.caffeine</groupId>
    <artifactId>caffeine</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
RedisCacheManager moves the cache across process boundaries. Declare the Redis connection factory and build the manager from it:

@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig implements CachingConfigurer {

    @Autowired
    private RedisConnectionFactory redisConnectionFactory;

    @Bean
    @Override
    public CacheManager cacheManager() {
        return RedisCacheManager.builder().fromConnectionFactory(redisConnectionFactory)
                .build();
    }
}

Add the dependencies:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.lettuce</groupId>
    <artifactId>lettuce-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

Note

If both cacheManager and cacheResolver are set, the cache manager is ignored — configure one or the other.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
The sample test performs the same findById twice and observes the cache interceptor in the logs (the org.springframework.cache category is set to TRACE in logback.xml): the second call hits the cache instead of the database, and the eviction annotations clear the entries on save/delete.

To run the application, start PostgreSQL (and Redis for the Redis variant):

docker-compose up postgres redis

You can explore the complete codes in cache, cache-caffeine, and cache-redis.

docs.title: Application Events
docs.text:
Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher/@EventListener mechanism supports reactive return types: an @EventListener method may return Mono<Void>, and Spring subscribes to the completion.

The event sample demonstrates the pattern end to end: a publisher component publishes a Greeting event, and a listener forwards each event into a Reactor Sinks.Many so any part of the application can consume the event stream as a Flux.

docs.title: Publish events
docs.text:
public record Greeting(String message) {
}

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class GreetingPublisher {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher applicationEventPublisher;

    public void publishGreetingEvent(String message) {
        applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new Greeting(message));
    }
}

docs.title: Listen reactively
docs.text:
@Component
@Slf4j
public class GreetingListener {

    public Sinks.Many<Greeting> sinks = Sinks.many().replay().latest();

    @EventListener
    public Mono<Void> onGreetingEvent(Greeting event) {
        log.debug("received event:{}", event);
        sinks.emitNext(event, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST);
        return Mono.empty();
    }
}

The Sinks.Many bridges the Spring event mechanism to the reactive world: subscribers of listener.sinks.asFlux() receive every published event, and replay().latest() lets new subscribers catch up on the most recent event.

docs.title: Drive it
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {
    var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);

    var publisher = context.getBean(GreetingPublisher.class);
    var listener = context.getBean(GreetingListener.class);
    listener.sinks.asFlux().subscribe(g -> log.debug("subscribed event: {}", g));

    IntStream.range(1, 100)
            .forEach(i -> {
                publisher.publishGreetingEvent("hello world #" + i + " at " + LocalDateTime.now());
                try {
                    Thread.sleep(100);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    throw new RuntimeException(e);
                }
            });
}

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
The test verifies both the Spring event and the sink, using @RecordApplicationEvents to capture events and Awaitility to bridge the asynchronous delivery:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = TypedGreetingEventTest.TestConfig.class)
@RecordApplicationEvents
public class TypedGreetingEventTest {

    @Autowired
    ApplicationEvents applicationEvents;

    @Autowired
    GreetingPublisher publisher;

    @Autowired
    GreetingListener listener;

    @Test
    public void testGreetingEvents() {
        publisher.publishGreetingEvent("hello world");

        Awaitility.await().atMost(Duration.ofMillis(500))
                .untilAsserted(() ->
                        assertThat(applicationEvents.stream(Greeting.class).count()).isEqualTo(1));

        Awaitility.await().atMost(Duration.ofMillis(1000))
                .untilAsserted(() ->
                        StepVerifier.create(listener.sinks.asFlux())
                                .consumeNextWith(greeting -> assertThat(greeting.message()).isEqualTo("hello world"))
                                .thenCancel()
                                .verify());
    }
}

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/event.

docs.title: Groovy
docs.text: Groovy interoperates with the Spring WebFlux stack out of the box: closures and the .& method-reference operator map naturally onto the functional routing API. The repository ships two Groovy samples, both plain Spring applications with manual wiring (see Getting Started).

docs.title: Functional routing in Groovy
docs.text:
The groovy sample builds the same blog API as the Java samples with a RouterFunction bean:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {

    @Bean
    RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes(PostHandler postHandler) {
        route(GET("/posts"), postHandler.&all)
                .andRoute(POST("/posts"), postHandler.&create)
                .andRoute(GET("/posts/{id}"), postHandler.&get)
                .andRoute(PUT("/posts/{id}"), postHandler.&update)
                .andRoute(DELETE("/posts/{id}"), postHandler.&delete)
    }
}

The .& operator creates a method reference from a Groovy method, exactly where Java uses the :: operator. The handler class is an ordinary @Component with Mono<ServerResponse> methods, and the data layer reuses ReactiveMongoRepository:

@Component
class PostHandler {

    private final PostRepository posts

    Mono<ServerResponse> all(ServerRequest req) {
        ok().body(this.posts.findAll(), Post)
    }

    Mono<ServerResponse> create(ServerRequest req) {
        req.bodyToMono(Post)
                .flatMap { this.posts.save(it) }
                .flatMap { p -> created(URI.create("/posts/${p.id}")).build() }
    }

    // get / update / delete follow the same pattern
}

The application class wires the server with the standard WebHttpHandlerBuilder + ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter combination and blocks on main.

docs.title: The Groovy bean definition DSL
docs.text:
The groovy-dsl sample declares beans in a Groovy script instead of annotations. The application imports the script with @ImportResource:

@ComponentScan
@Configuration
@ImportResource("classpath:application.groovy")
class Application {
    // ...
}

And the script registers the beans in the beans { } DSL:

import com.example.demo.DataInitializer
import com.example.demo.PostHandler
import com.example.demo.PostRepository

beans {

    postHandler(PostHandler){
        posts = ref("postRepository")
    }

    dataInitializer(DataInitializer){
        posts = ref("postRepository")
    }

    postRepository(PostRepository){
        template = ref("reactiveMongoTemplate")
    }
}

ref("...") resolves another bean by name, and property assignment wires collaborators — a concise alternative to XML or annotation configuration.

docs.title: Building with Groovy
docs.text:
Both samples compile Groovy with the GMavenPlus plugin:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.codehaus.gmavenplus</groupId>
    <artifactId>gmavenplus-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>compile</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

For the Spring Boot variant, see boot-groovy.

docs.title: The JDK Flow API
docs.text:
The java.util.concurrent.Flow API packages the Reactive Streams interfaces inside the JDK (Flow.Publisher, Flow.Subscriber, Flow.Subscription, Flow.Processor) and adds a ready-made Flow.Publisher implementation: SubmissionPublisher.

Spring WebFlux provides adapter support for it, so a Flow.Publisher can be a controller return type or parameter.

docs.title: Flow.Publisher as a return type
docs.text:
The java9 sample returns a Flow.Publisher from a controller and bridges Reactor's Flux with JdkFlowAdapter:

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
public class PostController {

    @GetMapping
    public Flow.Publisher<Post> all() {
        return JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(
                Flux.just(
                        new Post(1L, "post one", "content of post one"),
                        new Post(2L, "post two", "content of post two")
                )
        );
    }
}

Spring accepts the Flow.Publisher and drives it through the reactive request handling stack — the response is streamed exactly as with a Flux return type.

docs.title: The JDK HttpClient
docs.text:
The JDK ships a reactive java.net.http.HttpClient built on the Flow API. When you need a JDK-native client outside of Spring, it frees you from third-party HTTP client libraries:

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
        .build();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
        .uri(URI.create("http://localhost:8080/posts"))
        .build();

client.sendAsync(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
        .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
        .thenAccept(System.out::println)
        .join();

Inside a Spring application, prefer WebClient with the JDK connector, which wraps the same HttpClient behind the ClientHttpConnector abstraction.

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/java9.

docs.title: SmallRye Mutiny
docs.text:
SmallRye Mutiny is a Reactive Streams implementation from Red Hat, supported by Spring WebFlux since Spring Framework 5.3.10. Developers who prefer Mutiny's event-driven API can use its types directly in controllers and repositories.

Flow API based

Earlier versions of SmallRye Mutiny implemented the Reactive Streams API; current versions use the JDK Flow API instead.

docs.title: Add the dependency
docs.text:
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.smallrye.reactive</groupId>
            <artifactId>mutiny-bom</artifactId>
            <version>3.1.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.smallrye.reactive</groupId>
        <artifactId>mutiny</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <!-- ... -->
</dependencies>

docs.title: Core types
docs.text:
Mutiny's two core types map directly onto Reactor's:

Mutiny Reactor Emits Uni<T> Mono<T> 0..1 item (accepts null) Multi<T> Flux<T> 0..N items

Both implement the Reactive Streams Publisher contract, so Spring adapts them automatically wherever a Publisher is accepted.

docs.title: Use Mutiny in a controller
docs.text:
Return Uni and Multi from controller methods exactly as you would return Mono and Flux:

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "")
    public Multi<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}")
    public Uni<Post> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") UUID id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PostMapping(value = "")
    public Uni<ResponseEntity<?>> create(@RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.posts.save(post).map(p -> ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/posts/" + p.getId())).build());
    }
}

Spring handles the adaptation: a Multi is streamed like a Flux, a Uni resolves like a Mono, and Mutiny operators (onItem().transform(...), chain(...), and so on) work inside the methods.

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/smallrye-mutiny.

docs.title: Spring RestDocs
docs.text: Spring RestDocs generates accurate API documentation from tests. It integrates with WebTestClient, so every request a test performs contributes a documented snippet.

docs.title: Add the test dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.restdocs</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-restdocs-webtestclient</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

The sample also wires the spring-restdocs-asciidoctor artifact into the Asciidoctor Maven plugin to assemble the snippets into a document.

docs.title: Document a request in a test
docs.text:
Register the RestDocumentationExtension, configure the client with documentationConfiguration, and add the document(...) filter to each call you want documented:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
@ActiveProfiles("test")
@ExtendWith(RestDocumentationExtension.class)
public class ApiDocumentation {

    @Autowired
    ApplicationContext context;

    WebTestClient client;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup(RestDocumentationContextProvider restDocumentation) {
        this.client = WebTestClient
            .bindToApplicationContext(this.context)
            .configureClient()
            .baseUrl("https://api.example.com")
            .filter(documentationConfiguration(restDocumentation))
            .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk() throws Exception {
        this.client
            .get()
            .uri("/posts")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBody().consumeWith(document("sample"));
    }
}

Running the test produces the snippets under target/generated-snippets/sample/ — httpie-request.adoc, curl-request.adoc, response-body.adoc, and friends — which the Asciidoctor build then composes into the published API reference.

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/restdocs.

docs.title: RxJava 3
docs.text: RxJava 3 is the modern line of the ReactiveX library for the JVM. Spring WebFlux accepts its types directly in controller methods — Spring adapts them to the Reactive Streams contract internally. RxJava 2 is end of life and removed from Spring's supported adapters; prefer RxJava 3 for new work.

docs.title: Add the dependency
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.reactivex.rxjava3</groupId>
    <artifactId>rxjava</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Core types
docs.text:
RxJava's types map onto the Reactive Streams Publisher in different ways:

RxJava 3 Reactor Emits Backpressure Flowable<T> Flux<T> 0..N items, then completes or errors Yes (Publisher) Observable<T> Flux<T> 0..N items No (unbackpressured) Single<T> Mono<T> Exactly one value or an error No Maybe<T> Mono<T> 0..1 value or an error No Completable Mono<Void> Completion only No

Flowable is the Reactive Streams Publisher implementation; the other types bridge through Spring's adapters, which treat them as unbackpressured sources.

docs.title: Use RxJava in a controller
docs.text:
The rxjava3 sample returns RxJava types from a @RestController exactly where Reactor types would sit:

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "")
    public Observable<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}")
    public Maybe<Post> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") UUID id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PostMapping(value = "")
    public Single<Post> create(Post post) {
        return this.posts.save(post);
    }
}

The repository behind it mirrors the same types — and shows the full vocabulary:

@Component
class PostRepository {

    Observable<Post> findAll() {
        return Observable.fromIterable(DATA);
    }

    Flowable<Post> flowable() {
        return Flowable.fromIterable(DATA);
    }

    Maybe<Post> findById(UUID id) {
        // ...
                .switchIfEmpty(Maybe.error(new PostNotFoundException(id)));
    }

    Single<Post> save(Post post) {
        return Single.just(saved);
    }
}

Spring handles the adaptation on the HTTP boundary — an Observable/Flowable streams like a Flux, a Single/Maybe resolves like a Mono, and empty Maybe results map to the empty-response conventions described in Handling Web Exceptions.

docs.title: Verify with StepVerifier
docs.text:
Reactor's test tooling works on any Reactive Streams Publisher, so a Flowable verifies directly; adapter types go through RxJava3Adapter:

// Flowable is a Publisher — StepVerifier accepts it as is
StepVerifier.create(posts.findAll())
    .expectNextCount(2)
    .verifyComplete();

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/rxjava3.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text: Spring's @Scheduled supports reactive return types: a scheduled method may return Mono<Void> or Flux<Void>, and the scheduler subscribes to the completion. The schedule sample demonstrates a reactive scheduled task with a plain Spring application.

docs.title: Enable scheduling
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableAsync
@EnableScheduling
public class ScheduleConfig implements SchedulingConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void configureTasks(ScheduledTaskRegistrar taskRegistrar) {
        taskRegistrar.setScheduler(taskScheduler());
        taskRegistrar.addFixedDelayTask(
                () -> System.out.println("executing fixed delay task."),
                Duration.ofMillis(1000)
        );
    }

    @Bean(destroyMethod = "shutdown")
    public Executor taskScheduler() {
        return Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(100);
    }
}

docs.title: A reactive scheduled task
docs.text:
@Component
@Slf4j
public class ReactiveCounter {
    private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5)
    public Mono<Void> scheduled() {
        return Mono.defer(() -> Mono.just(count.incrementAndGet()))
                .doOnNext(item -> log.debug("current count:{}", item))
                .then();
    }

    public Mono<Integer> getInvocationCount() {
        return Mono.just(this.count.get());
    }
}

The @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5) method returns Mono<Void>: Spring subscribes on the scheduling thread and waits for completion before scheduling the next execution. Mono.defer(...) ensures the counter increments at subscription time, not assembly time.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
@SpringJUnitConfig(value = ReactiveCounterTest.TestConfig.class)
public class ReactiveCounterTest {

    @Configuration
    @ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = {ScheduleConfig.class})
    static class TestConfig {
    }

    @Autowired
    ReactiveCounter counter;

    @Test
    public void givenSleepBy100ms_whenGetInvocationCount_thenIsGreaterThanZero()
            throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(100L);
        counter.getInvocationCount()
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(count -> assertThat(count).isGreaterThan(0))
                .thenCancel()
                .verify();
    }
}

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/schedule.

docs.title: Spring Integration Java DSL
docs.text: The IntegrationFlow DSL replaces endpoint and channel beans with a fluent declaration. This page rebuilds the flow from the previous page — GET /all inbound gateway → reactive channel → WebFlux outbound gateway → GET /posts — with the DSL.

docs.title: The flow definition
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableIntegration
@IntegrationComponentScan
public class IntegrationDslConfig {

    @Bean
    public IntegrationFlow inboundChannelAdapterFlow() {
        return IntegrationFlow
                .from(
                        WebFlux
                                .inboundGateway("/all")
                                .requestMapping(m -> m.methods(HttpMethod.GET))
                )
                .channel(c -> c.flux("outboundReactive.input"))
                .get();
    }

    @Bean
    public IntegrationFlow outboundReactive() {
        return f -> f
                .handle(
                        WebFlux
                                .<MultiValueMap<String, String>>outboundGateway(
                                        m -> UriComponentsBuilder
                                                .fromUriString("http://localhost:8080/posts")
                                                .build()
                                                .toUri()
                                )
                                .httpMethod(HttpMethod.GET)
                                .expectedResponseType(String.class)
                );
    }
}

Reading the DSL:

  1. WebFlux.inboundGateway("/all") declares the HTTP entry point — equivalent to the WebFluxInboundEndpoint bean from the annotation-based version, including its RequestMapping.
  2. .channel(c -> c.flux("outboundReactive.input")) bridges the gateway to the second flow through a FluxMessageChannel created on the fly and named after the target flow's input channel. With the DSL there is no need to declare the FluxMessageChannel bean by hand.
  3. WebFlux.outboundGateway(...) is the DSL counterpart of WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler: it executes a GET http://localhost:8080/posts through a WebClient and delivers the response payload, typed by expectedResponseType, to the flow's output.

The dependency list and the application skeleton are identical to the annotation-based sample; only the configuration class changes.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
The test is the same as the annotation-based sample — both routes return 200:

@Test
public void getAllPostsWillBeOk_viaIntegration() {
    this.rest
            .get()
            .uri("/all")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk();
}

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: The DSL scales to real pipelines: add .filter(...), .transform(...), .split(...) between the gateway and the outbound gateway, and swap the outbound target for any messaging middleware. For channel patterns that connect Integration with Redis pub/sub and Reactor Sinks, see Reactive Message Channels.

docs.title: Sample
docs.text: You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/integration-dsl.

docs.title: Reactive Streams and Spring Integration
docs.text:
Spring Integration extends the Spring programming model into messaging and enterprise integration patterns — channels, endpoints, gateways, and adapters. Since Spring Integration 5, the framework participates in the reactive world: message channels can be backed by Reactor Fluxes, inbound endpoints can serve HTTP through WebFlux, and outbound handlers are driven by WebClient.

This chapter shows how the pieces fit together, using two runnable samples:

  • WebFlux endpoints with Spring Integration — an HTTP inbound endpoint wired to a reactive channel and a reactive outbound handler, assembled with annotations.
  • Spring Integration Java DSL — the same flow assembled with the fluent IntegrationFlow DSL.
  • Reactive Message Channels — reactive message channels across the ecosystem: Spring Integration's FluxMessageChannel, Redis pub/sub, and Reactor Sinks.

docs.title: How reactive support works
docs.text:
Spring Integration introduces a reactive channel type, FluxMessageChannel, which implements both MessageChannel and Publisher<Message<?>>. Producers send messages to it through the ordinary send() contract; consumers subscribe to it as a Reactive Streams Publisher and get backpressure for free.

On the web side, two components bridge Integration to WebFlux:

  • WebFluxInboundEndpoint — receives HTTP requests, maps them to Integration messages, and writes the (possibly streamed) reply back to the response.
  • WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler — the outbound counterpart; it executes HTTP requests through a WebClient and produces reactive replies.

Together they form a full reactive processing pipeline: HTTP in → message channel → HTTP out, without a blocking call anywhere.

docs.title: How the chapter's examples are structured
docs.text:
Both samples share the same skeleton — a WebFlux app serving GET /posts from an in-memory repository — and add an Integration layer on top that exposes GET /all. A request to /all travels through the Integration flow, which calls back into the same app's /posts endpoint through a WebClient, and streams the result to the caller.

GET /all ──▶ WebFluxInboundEndpoint ──▶ FluxMessageChannel ──▶ WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler ──▶ GET /posts

The samples are plain Spring applications (no Spring Boot auto-configuration) built with the manual wiring from the Getting Started chapter, with one extra dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.integration</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-integration-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• WebFlux endpoints with Spring Integration — annotation-based assembly.
  • Spring Integration Java DSL — the same flow with IntegrationFlow.from(...).
  • Reactive Message Channels — channel patterns across Spring Integration, Spring Data Redis, and Reactor.

docs.title: Reactive Message Channels
docs.text:
A message channel decouples producers from consumers: the producer hands off a message and does not know who processes it. In a reactive application, the channel itself is a stream — subscribers receive messages with backpressure, and multiple consumers can share the same source. This page compares three reactive channel mechanisms available in the Spring ecosystem, all exercised by the samples in this repository.

Mechanism Module Scope Best for FluxMessageChannel Spring Integration In-JVM, per application context Integration flows, HTTP in/out pipelines ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer Spring Data Redis Distributed (Redis pub/sub) Cross-process broadcast, lightweight messaging Sinks.Many Reactor In-JVM, per stream In-process fan-out, SSE/WebSocket feeds

docs.title: FluxMessageChannel (Spring Integration)
docs.text:
FluxMessageChannel implements both MessageChannel and Publisher<Message<?>>: producers call send(), consumers subscribe as to any Publisher. Declare it directly, or let the IntegrationFlow DSL create one:

@Bean
public MessageChannel fluxResultChannel() {
    return new FluxMessageChannel();
}

The Spring Integration chapter wires it between a WebFluxInboundEndpoint and a @ServiceActivator — a complete HTTP-to-HTTP reactive pipeline with backpressure from the HTTP response all the way back to the inbound request.

docs.title: Redis pub/sub (Spring Data Redis)
docs.text:
Redis channels work across processes: any application subscribed to the channel receives messages published by any other. Spring Data Redis exposes this through ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer, which returns a Flux of received messages — see Spring Data Redis — Redis Messaging for the full walkthrough:

@Bean
public ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer redisMessageListenerContainer(PostRepository posts, ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
    ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer container = new ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer(connectionFactory);
    container.receive(ChannelTopic.of("posts"))
        .map(p -> p.getMessage())
        // deserialize and persist each incoming message
        .flatMap(p -> posts.save(p))
        .subscribe();
    return container;
}

// publishing side, from any process:
reactiveRedisOperations.convertAndSend("posts", post);

The subscription stays open for the lifetime of the container — a stream of messages rather than a one-shot query.

docs.title: Reactor Sinks
docs.text:
When all producers and consumers live in the same process, a Reactor Sinks.Many is the simplest channel. The SSE example and the WebSocket example both use it as a broadcast hub:

@Service
public class MessageService {

    private final Sinks.Many<Message> sinks = Sinks.many().replay().latest();

    public Flux<Message> latestMessages() {
        return sinks.asFlux();   // consumer side: subscribe from anywhere
    }

    public void send(Message m) {
        sinks.emitNext(m, EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST);  // producer side
    }
}

The same pattern drives the reactive @EventListener in the Application Events sample: the listener forwards each event into a Sinks.Many so any part of the application can subscribe to the event stream as a Flux.

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
• Stay in-process and need to plug into Integration endpoints? Use FluxMessageChannel.
  • Stay in-process with a plain publisher/subscriber split? Use Sinks.Many.
  • Need messages to cross process or instance boundaries without standing up a full broker? Use Redis pub/sub.
  • Need durability, replay, and ordering guarantees at scale? Move to a real broker — Kafka or RabbitMQ — through their reactive clients (see the Spring Pulsar legacy sample for the pattern). For multiplexed messaging over TCP/WebSocket with backpressure, see the RSocket chapter.

docs.title: WebFlux endpoints with Spring Integration
docs.text: This page assembles a reactive Integration flow with annotations: a WebFluxInboundEndpoint serves GET /all, forwards each request through a FluxMessageChannel, and a WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler calls the app's own /posts endpoint through a WebClient and streams the reply back.

docs.title: Step 1: enable Integration
docs.text:
Add the dependency (see the chapter intro) and annotate a configuration class:

@Configuration
@EnableIntegration
@IntegrationComponentScan
public class IntegrationConfig {

    // endpoint beans below
}

docs.title: Step 2: declare the inbound endpoint
docs.text:
@Bean
public WebFluxInboundEndpoint jsonInboundEndpoint() {
    WebFluxInboundEndpoint endpoint = new WebFluxInboundEndpoint();
    RequestMapping requestMapping = new RequestMapping();
    requestMapping.setPathPatterns("/all");
    endpoint.setRequestMapping(requestMapping);
    endpoint.setRequestChannel(fluxResultChannel());
    return endpoint;
}

@Bean
public MessageChannel fluxResultChannel() {
    return new FluxMessageChannel();
}

The endpoint maps GET /all to Integration messages and writes the replies of fluxResultChannel to the HTTP response. Because the channel is a FluxMessageChannel, the reply can be a streamed Flux with backpressure honored end to end.

docs.title: Step 3: declare the reactive outbound handler
docs.text:
@Bean
public WebClient webClient() {
    return WebClient.builder().baseUrl("http://localhost:8080").build();
}

@ServiceActivator(inputChannel = "fluxResultChannel")
@Bean
public WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler reactiveOutbound(WebClient client) {
    WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler handler
            = new WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler("/posts", client);
    handler.setHttpMethod(HttpMethod.GET);
    handler.setExpectedResponseType(String.class);
    return handler;
}

The @ServiceActivator subscribes the handler to the fluxResultChannel: every message that arrives on the channel triggers an HTTP GET /posts through the WebClient, and the reactive reply flows back through the inbound endpoint to the original caller.

docs.title: Step 4: verify
docs.text:
The sample's repository serves two posts from memory, and the test asserts both the plain WebFlux route and the Integration route:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    HttpServer httpServer;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup() {
        this.disposableServer = this.httpServer.bindNow();
        this.client = WebTestClient
                .bindToServer()
                .responseTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(5000))
                .baseUrl("http://localhost:" + this.port)
                .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk() {
        this.client
                .get()
                .uri("/posts")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk_viaIntegration() {
        this.client
                .get()
                .uri("/all")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/integration.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: The annotation style works, but the wiring is verbose. The Spring Integration Java DSL expresses the same flow in a few fluent lines.

docs.title: Building a CRUD application with RSocket
docs.text: The TCP and WebSocket examples use routes to exchange simple greetings. The boot-rsocket-crud example demonstrates a more realistic application backed by Spring Data R2DBC, with an RSocket server exposing persistence routes and a WebFlux client calling them with RSocketRequester.

docs.title: The server application
docs.text:
Generate a project from Spring Initializr with RSocket, Spring Data R2DBC, H2 Database, and Lombok, or add the dependencies directly:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-rsocket</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-r2dbc</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.r2dbc</groupId>
    <artifactId>r2dbc-h2</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>

The server exposes the RSocket API over TCP:

spring.rsocket.server.port=7000
spring.rsocket.server.transport=tcp
spring.r2dbc.url=r2dbc:h2:mem:///blogdb?options=DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1;DB_CLOSE_ON_EXIT=FALSE;DATABASE_TO_LOWER=TRUE
spring.r2dbc.username=sa
spring.r2dbc.password=
spring.sql.init.mode=always

DATABASE_TO_LOWER=TRUE makes H2 fold unquoted identifiers to lower case, like PostgreSQL does. Spring Data R2DBC quotes the names it takes from @Table("posts") and @Column("title"), and plain H2 stores those same identifiers in upper case, so "posts" does not match POSTS without this option.

If you are new to Spring Data R2DBC, start with Accessing RDBMS with Spring R2DBC and Spring Data R2DBC.

docs.title: Defining the entity and repository
docs.text:
Create a simple POJO:

@Data
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
@Table("posts")
class Post {

    @Id
    @Column("id")
    private Integer id;

    @Column("title")
    private String title;

    @Column("content")
    private String content;
}

Then define a repository for Post:

interface PostRepository extends R2dbcRepository<Post, Integer> {
}

docs.title: Serving CRUD messaging routes
docs.text:
Create a Controller class to handle the incoming messages. Each route follows a consistent naming pattern: posts. plus the action, with .{id} carrying the path variable:

@Controller
@RequiredArgsConstructor
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    @MessageMapping("posts.findAll")
    public Flux<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @MessageMapping("posts.findById.{id}")
    public Mono<Post> get(@DestinationVariable("id") Integer id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @MessageMapping("posts.save")
    public Mono<Post> create(@Payload Post post) {
        return this.posts.save(post);
    }

    @MessageMapping("posts.update.{id}")
    public Mono<Post> update(@DestinationVariable("id") Integer id, @Payload Post post) {
        return this.posts.findById(id)
                .map(p -> {
                    p.setTitle(post.getTitle());
                    p.setContent(post.getContent());
                    return p;
                })
                .flatMap(p -> this.posts.save(p));
    }

    @MessageMapping("posts.deleteById.{id}")
    public Mono<Void> delete(@DestinationVariable("id") Integer id) {
        return this.posts.deleteById(id);
    }
}

As a bonus, add a derived query method to the repository and a route that filters posts by keyword:

interface PostRepository extends R2dbcRepository<Post, Integer> {

    Flux<Post> findByTitleContains(String name);
}

The Contains keyword lets Spring Data build the LIKE '%…%' condition for the database it is talking to. A hand-written @Query with $1 markers and a bare LIKE is PostgreSQL specific, and would not match anything without the % wildcards.

@MessageMapping("posts.titleContains")
public Flux<Post> titleContains(@Payload String title) {
    return this.posts.findByTitleContains(title);
}

docs.title: Initializing the data
docs.text:
Create a schema.sql and a data.sql file to create the table and seed the records:

-- schema.sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS posts (id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(255), content VARCHAR(255));

-- data.sql
DELETE FROM posts;
INSERT INTO posts (title, content) VALUES ('Post one', 'The content of post one');
INSERT INTO posts (title, content) VALUES ('Post two', 'The content of post two');

Note

Spring Boot runs schema.sql and data.sql for R2DBC on its own; spring.sql.init.mode=always forces it for the in-memory database. Declaring a ConnectionFactoryInitializer bean by hand on top of that — the workaround used before the R2DBC auto-configuration existed — executes the scripts a second time.

Start the server:

mvn spring-boot:run

docs.title: The client application
docs.text:
The client is a plain WebFlux application that uses RSocketRequester to talk to the RSocket server. Declare a requester bean connected to localhost:7000 over TCP:

@Bean
public RSocketRequester rSocketRequester(RSocketRequester.Builder b) {
    return b.dataMimeType(MimeTypeUtils.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .connect(TcpClientTransport.create("localhost", 7000))
            .block();
}

Create a generic RestController that forwards HTTP requests to RSocket routes:

@Slf4j
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@RestController()
@RequestMapping("/posts")
class PostClientController {

    private final RSocketRequester requester;

    @GetMapping("")
    Flux<Post> all(@RequestParam(name = "title", required = false) String title) {
        if (StringUtils.hasText(title)) {
            return this.requester.route("posts.titleContains")
                    .data(title).retrieveFlux(Post.class);
        } else {
            return this.requester.route("posts.findAll")
                    .retrieveFlux(Post.class);
        }
    }

    @GetMapping("{id}")
    Mono<Post> findById(@PathVariable Integer id) {
        return this.requester.route("posts.findById." + id)
                .retrieveMono(Post.class);
    }

    @PostMapping("")
    Mono<Post> save(@RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.requester.route("posts.save")
                .data(post)
                .retrieveMono(Post.class);
    }

    @PutMapping("{id}")
    Mono<Post> update(@PathVariable Integer id, @RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.requester.route("posts.update." + id)
                .data(post)
                .retrieveMono(Post.class);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("{id}")
    Mono<Void> delete(@PathVariable Integer id) {
        return this.requester.route("posts.deleteById." + id).send();
    }
}

The payload object travels between the client and server as a normal Java bean. Because the RSocket starter auto-configures JSON codecs, the same Post model can be encoded and decoded without any extra serialization code.

This gives you a clean, reactive CRUD flow: the client sends save, findById, findAll, and delete requests over RSocket, while the server persists them through Spring Data R2DBC and streams the results back as reactive data.

See the complete example and tests in boot-rsocket-crud.

@Data
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
class Post {
    private Integer id;
    private String title;
    private String content;
}

Start the client application (it serves on port 8080) and try the CRUD operations with curl:

# list all posts
curl http://localhost:8080/posts

# get a post by id
curl http://localhost:8080/posts/1

# save a new post
curl http://localhost:8080/posts -d "{\"title\":\"my save title\", \"content\":\"my content of my post\"}" -H "Content-Type:application/json"

# delete a post
curl http://localhost:8080/posts/4

# filter posts by keyword
curl http://localhost:8080/posts?title=one

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
In the ported module the client code becomes tests: connect a requester to the server and verify the messaging routes with StepVerifier — no client application required.

@SpringBootTest
public class IntegrationTests {

    static RSocketRequester requester;

    @BeforeAll
    public static void setup(@Autowired RSocketRequester.Builder builder) {
        requester = builder
                .dataMimeType(MimeTypeUtils.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .connect(TcpClientTransport.create("localhost", 7000)).block();
    }

    @Test
    public void willLoadPosts() {
        requester.route("posts.findAll")
                .retrieveFlux(Post.class)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .expectNextCount(2)
                .verifyComplete();
    }

    @Test
    public void testSaveAndGetAndDelete() {
        requester.route("posts.save")
                .data(Post.builder().title("test").content("content of test").build())
                .retrieveMono(Post.class)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(p -> assertEquals("test", p.getTitle()))
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

See the complete example and tests in boot-rsocket-crud.

docs.title: Declarative RSocket client
docs.text:
The WebClient chapter showed how @HttpExchange turns an annotated interface into an HTTP client proxy. RSocket has the same pattern: annotate an interface with @RSocketExchange, and RSocketServiceProxyFactory creates a proxy that sends each method call as an RSocket request.

Spring Boot auto-configures the surrounding infrastructure — the RSocket server, the Jackson CBOR strategies, and an RSocketRequester.Builder. The proxy factory itself is a single bean you declare by hand.

The complete example lives in boot-rsocketexchange: an RSocket server backed by PostgreSQL through R2DBC, and a declarative client calling it over TCP.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Add the RSocket and R2DBC starters:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-rsocket</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-r2dbc</artifactId>
</dependency>

Configure the server transport and the database in application.properties:

spring.rsocket.server.port=7000
spring.rsocket.server.transport=tcp
spring.r2dbc.url=r2dbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/blogdb
spring.r2dbc.username=user
spring.r2dbc.password=password
spring.sql.init.mode=always

Boot starts the RSocket server on port 7000 and registers the messaging infrastructure. The schema.sql and data.sql scripts initialize the database, as in the R2DBC chapter.

docs.title: Serving routes with @MessageMapping
docs.text:
The server side is a regular @Controller with @MessageMapping routes, as introduced in the RSocket over TCP chapter. Each route delegates to a DatabaseClient-based repository:

@Controller
@RequiredArgsConstructor
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    @MessageMapping("posts.findAll")
    public Flux<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @MessageMapping("posts.findById.{id}")
    public Mono<Post> get(@DestinationVariable("id") UUID id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @MessageMapping("posts.save")
    public Mono<UUID> create(@Payload Post post) {
        return this.posts.save(post);
    }

    // titleContains, update, deleteById follow the same pattern
}

docs.title: Declare the client interface
docs.text:
The client interface mirrors the server routes. @RSocketExchange sets the destination pattern; @DestinationVariable and @Payload bind the method arguments, and the reactive return type selects the interaction model:

public interface PostClient {

    @RSocketExchange("posts.findAll")
    Flux<Post> all();

    @RSocketExchange("posts.titleContains")
    Flux<Post> titleContains(@Payload String title);

    @RSocketExchange("posts.findById.{id}")
    Mono<Post> get(@DestinationVariable("id") UUID id);

    @RSocketExchange("posts.save")
    Mono<UUID> create(@Payload Post post);

    @RSocketExchange("posts.update.{id}")
    Mono<Boolean> update(@DestinationVariable("id") UUID id, @Payload Post post);

    @RSocketExchange("posts.deleteById.{id}")
    Mono<Boolean> delete(@DestinationVariable("id") UUID id);
}

docs.title: Create the proxy
docs.text:
Build the proxy from the auto-configured RSocketRequester.Builder:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class ClientConfig {

    @Bean
    @Lazy
    PostClient postClient(RSocketRequester.Builder builder) {
        var requester = builder.tcp("localhost", 7000);
        var proxyFactory = RSocketServiceProxyFactory.builder(requester)
                .blockTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(5000))
                .build();
        return proxyFactory.createClient(PostClient.class);
    }
}

Two details matter here:

  • builder.tcp(...) connects immediately. Boot starts the RSocket server after bean instantiation, so the bean is @Lazy — the connection opens on first use, when the server is already listening.
  • No manual RSocketStrategies configuration is needed. Boot registers the Jackson 3 JSON and CBOR codecs by default, and both sides of this example share them.

From this point on, inject PostClient like any other bean:

client.create(Post.of("test", "content"))
        .flatMap(id -> client.get(id))
        .subscribe(post -> log.debug("post: {}", post));

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The tests run against a real PostgreSQL instance started by Testcontainers. A @ServiceConnection bean replaces the spring.r2dbc.* settings, following the pattern from the R2DBC chapter:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    PostgreSQLContainer postgresContainer() {
        return new PostgreSQLContainer(DockerImageName.parse("postgres:latest"));
    }
}

The integration test loads the full application — server, database, and client proxy — and drives the routes through the declarative interface:

@SpringBootTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    PostClient client;

    @Test
    public void testCreateAndGet() {
        var data = Post.of("declarative client", "content of the declarative client post");

        this.client.create(data)
                .flatMap(id -> this.client.get(id))
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(post -> {
                    assertThat(post.title()).isEqualTo(data.title());
                    assertThat(post.status()).isEqualTo(Status.DRAFT);
                })
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

See the complete example and tests in boot-rsocketexchange.

docs.title: RSocket with Spring Integration
docs.text: Spring Integration adds first-class RSocket support to its messaging model: an RSocket server can act as an inbound gateway in an Integration flow, and an Integration flow can drive an outbound RSocket gateway.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Alongside the RSocket starter, add Spring Integration and its RSocket support:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-rsocket</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-integration</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.integration</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-integration-rsocket</artifactId>
</dependency>

The server exposes an RSocket endpoint over TCP on port 7000:

spring.rsocket.server.port=7000
spring.rsocket.server.transport=tcp

# auto configure spring integration rsocket server.
spring.integration.rsocket.server.messageMappingEnabled=true

docs.title: The server side: an inbound gateway
docs.text:
The application declares a ServerRSocketConnector and an IntegrationFlow with an RSocket inbound gateway. The flow receives a Flux<String> on the /uppercase route and transforms every element to uppercase:

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableIntegration
public class Application {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args);
    }

    // see PR: https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-boot/pull/18834
    @Bean
    ServerRSocketMessageHandler serverRSocketMessageHandler(RSocketStrategies rSocketStrategies) {
        var handler = new ServerRSocketMessageHandler(true);
        handler.setRSocketStrategies(rSocketStrategies);
        return handler;
    }

    @Bean
    public ServerRSocketConnector serverRSocketConnector(ServerRSocketMessageHandler serverRSocketMessageHandler) {
        return new ServerRSocketConnector(serverRSocketMessageHandler);
    }

    @Bean
    public IntegrationFlow rsocketUpperCaseFlow(ServerRSocketConnector serverRSocketConnector) {
        return IntegrationFlow
                .from(RSockets.inboundGateway("/uppercase")
                        .requestElementType(ResolvableType.forClass(String.class))
                        .interactionModels(RSocketInteractionModel.requestChannel)
                        .rsocketConnector(serverRSocketConnector)
                )
                .<Flux<String>, Flux<String>>transform((flux) -> flux.map(String::toUpperCase))
                .get();
    }
}

Reading the wiring:

  1. The custom ServerRSocketMessageHandler shares the Boot auto-configured RSocketStrategies (including codecs) with Integration's message handler.
  2. RSockets.inboundGateway("/uppercase") maps the /uppercase route to the flow; interactionModels(requestChannel) narrows it to the channel model, which means a Flux in and a Flux out.
  3. The transform step uppercases every incoming element. After that, any Integration DSL step such as .filter, .split, or .enrichHeaders can follow.

Note

Spring Integration 7 removed the IntegrationFlows factory class. Declare the flows with the static IntegrationFlow.from(...) methods instead, as shown above.

docs.title: The client side: an outbound gateway
docs.text:
The client example declares a ClientRSocketConnector pointing at the server and an outbound gateway flow that exposes the remote call as a Function<Flux<String>, Flux<String>>:

@Bean
public ClientRSocketConnector clientRSocketConnector() {
    ClientRSocketConnector clientRSocketConnector = new ClientRSocketConnector("localhost", 7000);
    clientRSocketConnector.setAutoStartup(false);
    return clientRSocketConnector;
}

@Bean
public IntegrationFlow rsocketUpperCaseRequestFlow(ClientRSocketConnector clientRSocketConnector) {
    return IntegrationFlow
            .from(Function.class)
            .handle(RSockets.outboundGateway("/uppercase")
                    .interactionModel((message) -> RSocketInteractionModel.requestChannel)
                    .expectedResponseType("T(java.lang.String)")
                    .clientRSocketConnector(clientRSocketConnector))
            .get();
}

In a single Spring Boot application, the server connector binds port 7000 and the client connector (with setAutoStartup(false)) starts on demand. The result is a bean of type Function<Flux<String>, Flux<String>> that other components can inject and call directly.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
To test the outbound gateway, start the client connector, apply the gateway function, and verify the uppercased channel result:

@SpringBootTest
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    @Qualifier("rsocketUpperCaseRequestFlow.gateway")
    Function<Flux<String>, Flux<String>> uppercaseFlow;

    @Autowired
    ClientRSocketConnector clientRSocketConnector;

    @BeforeEach
    public void startClient() {
        if (!clientRSocketConnector.isRunning()) {
            clientRSocketConnector.start();
        }
    }

    @Test
    public void testUppercaseFlow() {
        uppercaseFlow.apply(Flux.just("a", "b", "c", "d"))
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .expectNext("A", "B", "C", "D")
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

See the complete example and tests in integration-rsocket.

docs.title: RSocket
docs.text: RSocket is a binary messaging protocol that runs over transports such as TCP and WebSocket. It supports four interaction models—request/response, request/stream, fire-and-forget, and channel—while Spring provides a familiar programming model for building RSocket servers and clients.

docs.title: The four interaction models
docs.text:
Every RSocket exchange follows one of four interaction models. Each one maps neatly onto a Reactor type:

Model Direction Reactive types Route example Request/Response 1 → 1 Mono<T> → Mono<R> posts.findById.{id} Request/Stream 1 → N Mono<T> → Flux<R> greet-stream Fire-and-Forget 1 → 0 Mono<T> → Mono<Void> hello Channel N → N (bidirectional) Flux<T> → Flux<R> greet-channel

docs.title: RSsocket Java API
docs.text:
Before jumping into Spring wrapper, it is worth looking at the plain rsocket-java API.

The following code snippet demonstrates how to start an RSocket server and build a client to interact with it.

final RSocket responseHandler = new RSocket() {
    @Override
    public Mono<Payload> requestResponse(Payload payload) {
        return Mono.just(DefaultPayload.create("received (" + payload.getDataUtf8() + ") at " + Instant.now()));
    }
};

// server side: bind a socket acceptor to a TCP transport
RSocketServer.create(
        (setupPayload, reactiveSocket) -> Mono.just(responseHandler)
)
