        .bind(TcpServerTransport.create("localhost", PORT))
        .block();

// client side: connect and exchange payloads
RSocket socket = RSocketConnector.create()
        .connect(TcpClientTransport.create("localhost", PORT))
        .block();

socket.requestResponse(DefaultPayload.create("Hello"))
        .subscribe(r -> System.out.println(r.getDataUtf8()));

The types come directly from rsocket-java:

  • io.rsocket.core.RSocketServer.create() starts an RSocket server.
  • io.rsocket.core.RSocketConnector.create() starts an RSocket client.

Every interaction model follows the same pattern (requestResponse, requestStream, fireAndForget, and requestChannel on the RSocket interface).

docs.title: Spring's RSocket support
docs.text:
Spring wraps the same protocol with a familiar programming model:

  • spring-boot-starter-rsocket — starts an RSocket server over TCP or WebSocket, configures RSocketStrategies (including JSON codecs), and provides an RSocketRequester.Builder for client calls.
  • @MessageMapping — exposes incoming routes in a controller, much like @GetMapping exposes HTTP endpoints. @DestinationVariable captures route parameters.
  • RSocketRequester — the client-side fluent API: route(...), data(...), then send() for fire-and-forget calls, retrieveMono(...) for a single reply, retrieveFlux(...) for streams or channels, or data(Flux...) + retrieveFlux(...) for bidirectional channel traffic.

docs.title: A practical reading path
docs.text:
1. RSocket over TCP — the four interaction models end to end over a TCP connection.
  2. RSocket over WebSocket — the same handlers exposed over WebSocket with a mapping path.
  3. Building a CRUD application — RSocket messaging backed by Spring Data R2DBC in a more realistic application.
  4. RSocket with Spring Integration — IntegrationFlow-based inbound and outbound RSocket gateways.

docs.title: RSocket over TCP
docs.text: TCP is a reliable, connection-oriented transport. RSocket uses TCP to carry its messaging protocol between clients and servers.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The fastest way to begin is to generate a project from Spring Initializr, as described in the Getting Started chapter. Select Spring WebFlux, RSocket, and Lombok — the resulting dependency is the RSocket starter:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-rsocket</artifactId>
</dependency>

Configure the server to accept RSocket connections over TCP on port 7000 in application.properties:

spring.rsocket.server.port=7000
spring.rsocket.server.transport=tcp

docs.title: Defining the message payload
docs.text:
The client and server exchange a very small payload object:

@Data
class Greeting {
    String message;
}

docs.title: Serving routes with @MessageMapping
docs.text:
@MessageMapping handles incoming RSocket routes the same way @GetMapping handles HTTP paths. The return type tells Spring which interaction model to use:

@Controller
@Slf4j
class GreetingServerController {

    @MessageMapping("hello")
    public Mono<Void> hello(Greeting p) {
        log.info("received: {} at {}", p, Instant.now());
        return Mono.empty();
    }

    @MessageMapping("greet.{name}")
    public Mono<String> greet(@DestinationVariable String name, @Payload Greeting p) {
        log.info("received: {}, {} at {}", name, p, Instant.now());
        return Mono.just("Hello " + name + ", " + p.getMessage() + " at " + Instant.now());
    }

    @MessageMapping("greet-stream")
    public Flux<String> greetStream(@Payload Greeting p) {
        log.info("received:  {} at {}", p, Instant.now());
        return Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
                .map(i -> "greet-stream#(Hello #" + i + "," + p.getMessage() + ") at " + Instant.now());
    }

    @MessageMapping("greet-channel")
    public Flux<String> greetChannel(@Payload Flux<Greeting> p) {
        log.info("received:  {} at {}", p, Instant.now());
        return p.delayElements(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
                .map(m -> "greet-channel#(" + m + ") at " + Instant.now());
    }
}

Reading the handlers:

  1. hello — a fire-and-forget route: the Mono<Void> completes when the payload is consumed, and nothing is sent back.
  2. greet.{name} — a request/response route: @DestinationVariable captures the .{name} segment, and the Mono<String> reply is sent back to the caller.
  3. greet-stream — a request/stream route: one incoming Greeting yields an endless Flux<String> of periodic greetings.
  4. greet-channel — a channel route: the handler receives a Flux<Greeting> from the client and returns a transformed Flux<String>, creating a bidirectional exchange.

Start the server:

mvn spring-boot:run

docs.title: Calling the routes with RSocketRequester
docs.text:
The client side uses an RSocketRequester, built from the auto-configured Builder and a Netty TCP transport:

@Bean
public RSocketRequester rSocketRequester(RSocketRequester.Builder b) {
    return b.dataMimeType(MimeTypeUtils.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .connect(TcpClientTransport.create("localhost", 7000)).block();
}

Then call the routes from a REST controller — each interaction model exposed behind a tiny HTTP endpoint:

@Slf4j
@RestController()
@RequiredArgsConstructor
class GreetingController {

    private final RSocketRequester requester;

    @GetMapping("hello")
    Mono<Void> hello() {
        return this.requester.route("hello").data(new Greeting("Welcome to RSocket")).send();
    }

    @GetMapping("name/{name}")
    Mono<String> greet(@PathVariable String name) {
        return this.requester.route("greet." + name)
                .data(new Greeting("Welcome to RSocket"))
                .retrieveMono(String.class)
                .doOnNext(msg -> log.info("received message::" + msg));
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    Flux<String> greetStream() {
        return this.requester.route("greet-stream").data(new Greeting("Welcome to RSocket"))
                .retrieveFlux(String.class)
                .doOnNext(msg -> log.info("received messages::" + msg));
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "channel", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    Flux<String> greetChannel() {
        return this.requester.route("greet-channel")
                .data(Flux.range(0, 10).map(i -> new Greeting("Welcome to RSocket #" + i)))
                .retrieveFlux(String.class)
                .doOnNext(msg -> log.info("received messages::" + msg));
    }
}

The client-side verbs are straightforward: .send() for fire-and-forget calls, .retrieveMono() for a single reply, .retrieveFlux() for streams and channels, and .data(Flux...) when the upstream is a channel.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
In the ported module, the client code becomes tests. We connect with the builder and verify each interaction model with StepVerifier:

@SpringBootTest
public class IntegrationTests {

    static RSocketRequester requester;

    @BeforeAll
    public static void setup(@Autowired RSocketRequester.Builder builder) {
        requester = builder
                .dataMimeType(MimeTypeUtils.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .connect(TcpClientTransport.create("localhost", 7000)).block();
    }

    @Test
    public void testRequestResponse() {
        requester.route("greet.spring")
                .data(new Greeting("Welcome to RSocket"))
                .retrieveMono(String.class)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(msg -> assertTrue(msg.contains("Hello spring")))
                .verifyComplete();
    }

    @Test
    public void testRequestChannel() {
        Flux<Greeting> payloads = Flux.range(0, 10)
                .map(i -> new Greeting("Welcome to RSocket #" + i));

        requester.route("greet-channel")
                .data(payloads)
                .retrieveFlux(String.class)
                .take(10)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .expectNextCount(10)
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

The @LocalRSocketServerPort annotation from earlier Boot versions no longer exists in Boot 4, so the tests connect to the fixed port configured in application.properties.

See the complete example and tests in boot-rsocket-tcp.

docs.title: RSocket over WebSocket
docs.text: WebSocket provides a full-duplex connection over HTTP, making it a useful transport for browser-facing applications. RSocket can run over WebSocket just as it does over TCP.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The dependency is the same RSocket starter as in the TCP example:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-rsocket</artifactId>
</dependency>

The RSocket starter does not bring a web server of its own, and the WebSocket transport is served from the web server, so add one:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>

The transport change is mostly configuration. In application.properties, choose WebSocket as the transport and define the path under which the RSocket endpoint is exposed on the web server:

server.port=8081
# a mapping path is defined
spring.rsocket.server.mapping-path=/rsocket
# websocket is chosen as a transport
spring.rsocket.server.transport=websocket

A couple of practical notes:

  • With transport=websocket, the RSocket endpoint shares the HTTP server (server.port) instead of binding its own port.
  • spring.rsocket.server.mapping-path scopes the endpoint to /rsocket, so regular HTTP endpoints — such as a plain @GetMapping controller below — can live on the same server.
@RestController
public class HelloController {

    @GetMapping
    public String get() {
        return "server greeting at :" + Instant.now();
    }
}

The @MessageMapping handlers are the same as in the TCP example. See RSocket over TCP for the full controller.

docs.title: Connecting a client over WebSocket
docs.text:
The client side only changes the transport: WebsocketClientTransport points at the mapped path on the web server's port.

@Bean
public RSocketRequester rSocketRequester(RSocketRequester.Builder b) {
    return b.dataMimeType(MimeTypeUtils.APPLICATION_JSON)
            .connect(WebsocketClientTransport.create(URI.create("ws://localhost:8081/rsocket"))).block();
}

After that, the calls are the same as over TCP: .send() for fire-and-forget, .retrieveMono() and .retrieveFlux() for the rest.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The test boots the server on a random web port (RANDOM_PORT) and connects to the /rsocket WebSocket endpoint on that port:

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@TestInstance(TestInstance.Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)
public class IntegrationTests {

    RSocketRequester requester;

    @LocalServerPort
    int port;

    @Autowired
    RSocketRequester.Builder builder;

    @BeforeAll
    public void setup() {
        requester = builder
                .dataMimeType(MimeTypeUtils.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .connect(WebsocketClientTransport.create(
                        URI.create("ws://localhost:" + port + "/rsocket"))).block();
    }

    @Test
    public void testRequestResponseOverWebSocket() {
        requester.route("greet.spring")
                .data(new Greeting("Welcome to RSocket"))
                .retrieveMono(String.class)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(msg -> assertTrue(msg.contains("Hello spring")))
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

local.server.port is published as an environment property of the web application context, and @LocalServerPort reads it into an instance field. A static @BeforeAll cannot see that field, so the class is switched to @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS), which allows the setup method to be non-static.

See the complete example and tests in boot-rsocket-websocket.

docs.title: TCP or WebSocket?
docs.text:
TCP WebSocket Endpoint Own port (spring.rsocket.server.port) Shared with the HTTP server Path routing Not applicable spring.rsocket.server.mapping-path Typical clients JVM-to-JVM services Browsers and HTTP-based deployments Configuration spring.rsocket.server.transport=tcp spring.rsocket.server.transport=websocket

The handler and requester code stays the same either way — only the transport properties and the client transport implementation change.

docs.title: Header-based session id
docs.text:
By default, WebFlux resolves the session id from the SESSION cookie. Browser clients are fine with this, but API clients — mobile apps, server-to-server calls — often prefer to carry the session id in a header.

WebSessionIdResolver is the extension point that decides how a session id is resolved from a request and written back to a response. Spring ships CookieWebSessionIdResolver (the default) and HeaderWebSessionIdResolver.

docs.title: Step 1: register a custom resolver
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableSpringWebSession
public class SessionConfig {

    @Bean
    public ReactiveSessionRepository<?> sessionRepository() {
        return new ReactiveMapSessionRepository(new ConcurrentHashMap<>());
    }

    @Bean
    public WebSessionIdResolver headerWebSessionIdResolver() {
        HeaderWebSessionIdResolver resolver = new HeaderWebSessionIdResolver();
        resolver.setHeaderName("X-SESSION-ID");
        return resolver;
    }
}

HeaderWebSessionIdResolver reads the session id from the X-SESSION-ID request header and returns it in the same response header.

docs.title: Step 2: secure the application
docs.text:
The sample combines the header resolver with Spring Security, HTTP Basic, form login, and a session-based security context repository:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
       return http
               .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
               .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                       .anyExchange().authenticated())
               .httpBasic(basic -> basic.securityContextRepository(new WebSessionServerSecurityContextRepository()))
               .formLogin(withDefaults())
               .build();
    }

    @Bean
    public MapReactiveUserDetailsService userDetailsRepository() {
        var userBuilder = User.withDefaultPasswordEncoder();
        UserDetails user = userBuilder.username("user").password("password").roles("USER").build();
        UserDetails admin = userBuilder.username("admin").password("password").roles("USER", "ADMIN").build();
        return new MapReactiveUserDetailsService(user, admin);
    }
}

A controller exposes the current session id for verification:

@RestController
public class SessionController {

    @GetMapping("/sessionId")
    public Map<String, String> sessionId(WebSession session){
        Map<String, String> map = new HashMap<>();
        map.put("id", session.getId());
        return map;
    }
}

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
1. Authenticate and request the session id:

    curl -u user:password http://localhost:8080/sessionId
# {"id":"..."}

    The response carries the X-SESSION-ID header with the same value.

  2. Call a protected endpoint with the header instead of Basic auth:

    curl -H "X-SESSION-ID: <id>" http://localhost:8080/posts

The test in the sample asserts exactly this contract:

FluxExchangeResult<Map<String, String>> result = this.rest
        .get()
        .uri("/sessionId")
        .header("Authorization", getBasicAuth())
        .exchange()
        .returnResult(new ParameterizedTypeReference<Map<String, String>>() {});

assertThat(result.getStatus()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.OK);

List<String> sessionHeaders = result.getResponseHeaders().get("X-SESSION-ID");
assertThat(sessionHeaders.size()).isEqualTo(1);

String sessionId = result.getResponseBody().blockFirst().get("id");
assertThat(sessionHeaders.get(0)).isEqualTo(sessionId);

this.rest
        .get()
        .uri("/posts")
        .header("X-SESSION-ID", sessionId)
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isOk();

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/session-header.

docs.title: In-memory sessions
docs.text: The simplest ReactiveSessionRepository is a ConcurrentHashMap behind ReactiveMapSessionRepository. It demonstrates the full Spring Session setup without any external infrastructure.

docs.title: Step 1: add the dependency
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Step 2: enable Spring Web Session
docs.text:
Create a configuration class, annotate it with @EnableSpringWebSession, and declare the repository bean:

@Configuration
@EnableSpringWebSession
public class SessionConfig {

    @Bean
    public ReactiveSessionRepository<?> sessionRepository() {
        return new ReactiveMapSessionRepository(new ConcurrentHashMap<>());
    }
}

@EnableSpringWebSession installs the WebSessionManager that routes every WebSession interaction through the repository.

docs.title: Step 3: use WebSession in a controller
docs.text:
@Controller
public class SessionController {

    @PostMapping("/session")
    public String setAttribute(@ModelAttribute SessionAttributeForm sessionAttributeForm, WebSession session) {
        session.getAttributes().put(sessionAttributeForm.getAttributeName(), sessionAttributeForm.getAttributeValue());
        return "redirect:/";
    }

    @GetMapping("/")
    public String index(Model model, WebSession webSession) {
        model.addAttribute("webSession", webSession);
        return "index";
    }
}

A Thymeleaf form posts attribute name/value pairs, and the index page renders the current session's attributes:

<form class="form-inline" role="form" action="./session" method="post">
    <label for="attributeName">Attribute Name</label>
    <input id="attributeName" type="text" name="attributeName"/>
    <label for="attributeValue">Attribute Value</label>
    <input id="attributeValue" type="text" name="attributeValue"/>
    <input type="submit" value="Set Attribute"/>
</form>

<table class="table table-striped">
    <thead>
    <tr>
        <th>Attribute Name</th>
        <th>Attribute Value</th>
    </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
    <tr th:each="attr : ${webSession.attributes}">
        <td th:text="${attr.key}"></td>
        <td th:text="${attr.value}"></td>
    </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: Verify
docs.text: Start the application and open http://localhost:8080. Submit the form — the attribute appears in the table, and the browser stores a SESSION cookie (not JSESSIONID).

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
The sample verifies the flow with an HtmlUnit-driven test that boots the real server:

@Test
public void createAttribute() {
    HomePage home = HomePage.go(this.driver, this.port);

    home = home.form()
            .attributeName("a")
            .attributeValue("b")
            .submit(HomePage.class);

    List<Attribute> attributes = home.attributes();
    assertThat(attributes).hasSize(1);
    Attribute row = attributes.get(0);
    assertThat(row.getAttributeName()).isEqualTo("a");
    assertThat(row.getAttributeValue()).isEqualTo("b");
}

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/session.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: The in-memory map does not survive restarts and is not shared between instances. For production, use Redis or Mongo as the session store.

docs.title: Spring Session (Reactive)
docs.text:
Session management in a reactive application is not just a small variant of the servlet model. WebFlux introduces a different runtime model, so the session abstraction is also different: it is built around WebSession, non-blocking repositories, and integrations that work with the reactive pipeline.

This chapter shows how to use Spring Session in a WebFlux application without falling back to blocking servlet assumptions.

docs.title: WebSession: the reactive session
docs.text:
WebFlux does not use the Servlet HttpSession. Instead, every request can access a WebSession — a reactive abstraction whose attributes live on the server and whose id is exchanged with the client:

@Controller
public class SessionController {

    @PostMapping("/session")
    public String setAttribute(@ModelAttribute SessionAttributeForm sessionAttributeForm, WebSession session) {
        session.getAttributes().put(sessionAttributeForm.getAttributeName(), sessionAttributeForm.getAttributeValue());
        return "redirect:/";
    }

    @GetMapping("/")
    public String index(Model model, WebSession webSession) {
        model.addAttribute("webSession", webSession);
        return "index";
    }
}

Inject a WebSession as a controller method parameter and read or write attributes like a plain map. The session id is returned to the client in a SESSION cookie by default — there is no JSESSIONID cookie in the reactive stack.

docs.title: Spring Session for WebFlux
docs.text:
Spring Session replaces the default in-memory session store with a pluggable ReactiveSessionRepository. For WebFlux applications, activate it with @EnableSpringWebSession (and store-specific variants such as @EnableRedisWebSession or @EnableMongoWebSession) and provide a ReactiveSessionRepository bean.

Store Annotation Repository Extra dependency In-memory map @EnableSpringWebSession ReactiveMapSessionRepository spring-session-core Redis @EnableRedisWebSession ReactiveRedisSessionRepository (auto) spring-session-data-redis MongoDB @EnableMongoWebSession ReactiveMongoOperationsSessionRepository (auto) spring-session-data-mongodb

An external store is recommended for production: sessions survive restarts and are shared across instances.

docs.title: Choosing a session strategy
docs.text:
• Server-side sessions (this chapter) — simplest to reason about; pairs naturally with form login and HTTP Basic; use Redis or Mongo for clustered deployments.
  • Token strategies (JWT, OAuth2) — stateless; consider when the API is consumed by mobile apps or other services.

docs.title: A friendly reading path
docs.text:
The session chapter is easiest to read in the same order you would apply it in a real application:

  • start with In-memory sessions to see the basic reactive session model without adding external infrastructure
  • then read Redis-backed sessions when you want a production-friendly, shared session store
  • continue with Mongo-backed sessions for a document-store option that also fits a reactive ecosystem
  • finish with Header-based session id for API-first clients that do not want to rely on cookies

If you are already working with Spring Security, the examples in this section will feel especially relevant because they fit directly into the authenticated request flow.

docs.title: Mongo-backed sessions
docs.text: The spring-session-data-mongodb module stores sessions in MongoDB through the reactive Mongo driver — a natural choice when your application already uses Spring Data Mongo.

docs.title: Step 1: add the dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-data-mongodb</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.7</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-mongodb</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.mongodb</groupId>
    <artifactId>mongodb-driver-reactivestreams</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Step 2: configure the Mongo connection
docs.text:
@Configuration
public class MongoConfig extends AbstractReactiveMongoConfiguration {

    @Value("${mongo.uri}")
    String mongoUri;

    @Override
    public MongoClient reactiveMongoClient() {
        return MongoClients.create(mongoUri);
    }

    @Override
    protected String getDatabaseName() {
        return "blog";
    }
}

With the connection property set in application.properties:

server.port=8080
mongo.uri=mongodb://localhost:27017/

Start a MongoDB server for local development:

docker-compose up mongodb

docs.title: Step 3: enable Mongo web session
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableMongoWebSession
public class SessionConfig {
}

@EnableMongoWebSession registers a reactive session repository backed by MongoDB automatically. The controller and template code is identical to the in-memory example.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Start the application, submit the attribute form at http://localhost:8080, and inspect the blog database — the sessions live in a dedicated collection with the attributes and a TTL index for expiry.

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/session-data-mongo.

docs.title: Redis-backed sessions
docs.text: The spring-session-data-redis module stores sessions in Redis through a reactive Redis connection, so sessions survive application restarts and are shared between all instances that point at the same Redis.

docs.title: Step 1: add the dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.lettuce</groupId>
    <artifactId>lettuce-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

Lettuce is the required driver for reactive Redis support (see Spring Data Redis).

docs.title: Step 2: configure the Redis connection factory
docs.text:
@Configuration
public class RedisConfig {

    @Bean
    public LettuceConnectionFactory redisConnectionFactory() {
        return new LettuceConnectionFactory();
    }
}

The default LettuceConnectionFactory connects to localhost:6379. To start a Redis server for local development, use the docker-compose.yml in the repository root:

docker-compose up redis

docs.title: Step 3: enable Redis web session
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableRedisWebSession
public class SessionConfig {
}

@EnableRedisWebSession registers a reactive session repository backed by Redis automatically — no explicit ReactiveSessionRepository bean is needed. The controller and template code is identical to the in-memory example.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Start the application and submit the attribute form at http://localhost:8080. Then inspect Redis directly:

redis-cli keys "spring:session*"

You will find the session keyed under the spring:session prefix, storing the attributes and metadata.

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/session-data-redis.

docs.title: Built-in authentication mechanisms
docs.text:
Authorization rules decide whether a request may pass through the filter chain; authentication mechanisms establish who is making it. Every mechanism in a WebFlux application is a WebFilter inside the SecurityWebFilterChain: it converts the request's credentials into an Authentication token, passes the token to a ReactiveAuthenticationManager, and on success puts the authenticated result into the SecurityContext for the rest of the chain.

This page covers the two mechanisms you reach for first — HTTP Basic for API-style clients and form login for browser pages — and then surveys the rest of the built-in set. All of them follow the same converter → manager → context shape, which is also the shape you implement when you add a mechanism of your own; see Custom authentication.

docs.title: HTTP Basic
docs.text:
Enable HTTP Basic with httpBasic(withDefaults()):

@Bean
SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    return http
        .httpBasic(withDefaults())
        .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
            .anyExchange().authenticated())
        .build();
}

The customizer installs an AuthenticationWebFilter at the HTTP_BASIC position in the chain, wired with:

  1. A ServerHttpBasicAuthenticationConverter that decodes the Authorization: Basic ... header into a username/password token.
  2. A UserDetailsRepositoryReactiveAuthenticationManager that validates the token against the application's ReactiveUserDetailsService bean — the in-memory MapReactiveUserDetailsService used across this chapter's samples, or a custom store as described in Customize UserDetailsRepository.
  3. A NoOpServerSecurityContextRepository: the authenticated result is not persisted, so every request re-reads the header.
  4. An entry point that answers rejected requests with 401 and a WWW-Authenticate: Basic challenge — the response seen in Configuration.

Nothing about the mechanism depends on the credentials being a human's password. What makes Basic convenient for demos is that a single curl -u drives it, which is why the samples in this chapter use it; Custom authentication covers the machine-to-machine case where a header of your own design fits better.

docs.title: Form login
docs.text:
Form login is the mechanism for browser-driven pages: instead of expecting credentials on every request, it redirects unauthenticated browsers to a login page, remembers the result in the server-side session, and lets subsequent requests ride the session cookie.

The security-form sample needs only one line beyond the Basic example above:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http.authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                .anyExchange().authenticated())
                .formLogin(withDefaults())
                .build();
    }

    // ...
}

With that in place, a controller such as HomeController returning a view name ("home") and a template that renders Flux<Post> into HTML is enough — the security side is entirely configuration, and the template never needs to know about it.

formLogin(withDefaults()) installs four collaborators:

  1. LoginPageGeneratingWebFilter serves a generated /login page, so an application gets a login form without writing one.
  2. AuthenticationWebFilter at the FORM_LOGIN position, with a converter that reads the submitted username and password form fields and a success handler that redirects back into the application.
  3. RedirectServerAuthenticationEntryPoint, which answers an unauthenticated request with 302 to the login page rather than a 401 challenge.
  4. WebSessionServerSecurityContextRepository, which stores the authenticated SecurityContext in the WebSession — this is what makes the session cookie meaningful, and what distinguishes form login from Basic's NoOp repository.

Unlike the servlet stack, the WebFlux entry point does not inspect the request's Accept header. A single formLogin chain redirects every unauthenticated request, so an XMLHttpRequest or a fetch call expecting JSON also receives 302 → /login. For an API, use Basic or a token mechanism instead.

Because the flow involves a browser round trip with a form POST, CSRF protection is on by default: the generated login page embeds a hidden _csrf input whose token is stored in the WebSession alongside the session cookie. A login POST without a valid _csrf parameter is rejected with 403 before any credential is checked.

To replace the generated page with your own, point the entry point somewhere else:

.authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
        .pathMatchers("/signin").permitAll()
        .anyExchange().authenticated())
.formLogin(formLogin -> formLogin
        .loginPage("/signin"))

loginPage(String) does two things at once: unauthenticated requests now redirect to that URL, and LoginPageGeneratingWebFilter is no longer installed — Spring Security assumes your application serves the page. That makes the path part of your responsibility twice over: it needs a handler that renders the form, and it needs to be reachable without credentials. Leaving it behind .anyExchange().authenticated() redirects GET /signin to /signin, and the browser loops. The POST that the form submits is still handled by the security filter: loginPage derives the processing matcher from the same URL, so the form posts back to /signin.

docs.title: Other built-in mechanisms
docs.text:
The same DSL exposes the rest of the built-in set. Each is a method on ServerHttpSecurity, and each takes a customizer in the same shape as the two above:

Method Mechanism x509(...) Authenticates from the client certificate presented at the TLS layer, resolving the principal with an X509PrincipalExtractor oauth2Login(...) Full "Login with Google/GitHub/…" flow: authorization-code redirect, callback handling, then the same SecurityContext write oauth2Client(...) The client half on its own, for applications that call third-party APIs on a user's behalf without using OAuth2 to sign in oauth2ResourceServer(...) Validates an opaque or JWT bearer token issued by an authorization server — the usual fit for SPAs and service APIs oneTimeTokenLogin(...) Email-a-code sign-in, with a generated submit page like form login's

The reactive DSL is not a mirror of the servlet one. There is no rememberMe(...) and no oidcLogin(...) customizer on ServerHttpSecurity, so an application that needs those has to reach for the servlet stack or build the behaviour itself. Alongside authentication, redirectToHttps(...), anonymous(...), and logout(...) round out request handling.

For configuration details of any mechanism beyond the two worked through here, see the WebFlux section of the Spring Security reactive reference.

docs.title: Verify with curl
docs.text:
The redirect-then-POST-then-cookie flow is easy to confirm by hand. Start the security-form sample and follow the exchange.

An unauthenticated request is redirected, whatever it asks for in Accept:

curl -v http://localhost:8080/ -H "Accept: application/json"
< HTTP/1.1 302 Found
< Location: /login

Fetching the generated page starts a session and hands over the CSRF token:

curl -s -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8080/login

The relevant lines of the page it returns:

<form class="login-form" method="post" action="/login">
    <input type="text" id="username" name="username" placeholder="Username" required autofocus>
    <input type="password" id="password" name="password" placeholder="Password" required>
    <input name="_csrf" type="hidden" value="OodBUCNtzabGjmrbPZm52oMvTmNuliuoeHZp2UJGvBL1nv4RDbEiZxRa_pPr61zjDrSN7eccYwJX90mFSEdZ7SRx2nfAq8Zw" />

and the response sets SESSION=...; Path=/; HTTPOnly; SameSite=Lax. Pull the token out of that page and POST the form with the cookie it came from:

CSRF=$(curl -s -c cookies.txt http://localhost:8080/login \
  | grep -o 'name="_csrf" type="hidden" value="[^"]*' | sed 's/.*value="//')

curl -v -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt -X POST http://localhost:8080/login \
  -d "username=user" -d "password=password" -d "_csrf=$CSRF"
< HTTP/1.1 302 Found
< Location: /
< set-cookie: SESSION=e288933b-aae9-4cb6-86bb-c97f6948cfbc; Path=/; HTTPOnly; SameSite=Lax

The redirect to / is the success handler; note the session id changed, which is session-fixation protection rotating it at authentication. Now the cookie alone carries the identity:

curl -s -b cookies.txt http://localhost:8080/

renders the home page with the seeded posts. Two failures round out the picture: a wrong password redirects to /login?error, and dropping the _csrf parameter from the POST yields 403 without consulting the user store.

docs.title: See it in code
docs.text: security-form is the form login sample; HTTP Basic appears in security-method and security-user-properties. When none of the built-in mechanisms fits the credentials your clients actually send, build one in Custom authentication.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: In a WebFlux application, security is configured by declaring a SecurityWebFilterChain bean built from ServerHttpSecurity. That bean looks the same with or without Spring Boot; what differs is who switches WebFlux security on — you, with @EnableWebFluxSecurity, or Boot's auto-configuration.

docs.title: Without Spring Boot
docs.text:
When you are developing a Spring WebFlux application without Spring Boot, add the security dependencies from the previous page to your project.

Create a configuration class and add the @EnableWebFluxSecurity annotation to enable WebFlux support for Spring Security:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/posts/**").permitAll()
                .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/posts/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                //.pathMatchers("/users/{user}/**").access(this::currentUserMatchesPath)
                .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .build();
    }

    private Mono<AuthorizationDecision> currentUserMatchesPath(Mono<Authentication> authentication, AuthorizationContext context) {
        return authentication
            .map(a -> context.getVariables().get("user").equals(a.getName()))
            .map(AuthorizationDecision::new);
    }

    @Bean
    public MapReactiveUserDetailsService userDetailsRepository() {
        UserBuilder users = User.withDefaultPasswordEncoder();
        UserDetails user = users.username("user").password("password").roles("USER").build();
        UserDetails admin = users.username("admin").password("password").roles("USER", "ADMIN").build();
        return new MapReactiveUserDetailsService(user, admin);
    }
}

In the above codes:

  1. The @EnableWebFluxSecurity annotation enables Security for a spring-webflux based application.
  2. A SecurityWebFilterChain bean is required to configure the details of Spring Security. ServerHttpSecurity comes from the reactive config support — similar to the servlet-stack HttpSecurity, but it handles ServerWebExchange instead of the Servlet based WebRequest.
  3. A ReactiveUserDetailsService resolves users reactively. The in-memory MapReactiveUserDetailsService is the default choice for demos; you can customize it by implementing the interface yourself — see Customize UserDetailsRepository.
  4. The pathMatchers rules protect the API: GET /posts/** is public, DELETE /posts/** requires the ADMIN role, and every other exchange must be authenticated.

docs.title: With Spring Boot
docs.text:
For Spring Boot applications, add spring-boot-starter-security to the project dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

Then declare the same chain bean — and leave the annotation out:

@Configuration
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
        return http
            .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/posts/**").permitAll()
                .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/posts/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .build();
    }

    // ...
}

The missing @EnableWebFluxSecurity is deliberate. ReactiveWebSecurityAutoConfiguration applies it for you: its nested EnableWebFluxSecurityConfiguration carries the annotation and is @ConditionalOnMissingBean(WebFilterChainProxy.class), so it stands down only if security has already been enabled some other way. Adding the annotation yourself is harmless, but it is not what makes a Boot application secure.

Two defaults are worth knowing, because both are conditional on what you declare:

  1. The fallback chain. With no SecurityWebFilterChain bean of your own, Spring Security builds one that requires authentication for every exchange and enables both httpBasic and formLogin. Declaring the bean above replaces that fallback entirely — the rules you write are the only rules, so a path you forget to mention is still caught by anyExchange().authenticated().
  2. The deny-all authentication manager. Boot contributes a ReactiveAuthenticationManager that rejects every authentication attempt, and it is @ConditionalOnMissingBean on ReactiveAuthenticationManager, ReactiveUserDetailsService, and SecurityWebFilterChain. Until you supply one of those, no credential can succeed. Adding the MapReactiveUserDetailsService bean from the previous section — or any ReactiveUserDetailsService of your own — switches it off and gives the built-in mechanisms something to validate against.

docs.title: Method security needs an explicit declaration
docs.text:
Auto-configuration stops at the filter chain. No Boot auto-configuration enables method security, so @EnableReactiveMethodSecurity has to be declared explicitly even in a Boot application:

@Configuration
@EnableReactiveMethodSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    // ...
}

Without it, @PreAuthorize and the other method constraints are inert — the annotations compile and the application starts, but nothing intercepts the calls. See Method level constraints for applying them to reactive methods.

docs.title: Verify with curl
docs.text:
Start up the application and verify that the Spring Security configuration works as expected.

After it is started, try to add a new post without authentication:

#curl -v -X POST http://localhost:8080/posts -H "Content-Type:application/json" -d "{\"title\":\"My Post\",\"content\":\"content of My Post\"}"
< HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
< WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Realm"

The server side rejects the client request and sends back a 401 error (401 Unauthorized).

Use the predefined user/password credentials to get authenticated and send the request again:

curl -v -X POST http://localhost:8080/posts -u "user:password" -H "Content-Type:application/json" -d "{\"title\":\"My Post\",\"content\":\"content of My Post\"}"
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< set-cookie: SESSION=b99124f7-c0a0-4507-b9be-34718af3d137; HTTPOnly
<
{"id":"59906f9d3c44060e044fb378","title":"My Post","content":"content of My Post"}

The request succeeds and returns the newly created post.

docs.title: Restricting access by path variable
docs.text:
The built-in rules — permitAll(), hasRole(), authenticated() — are static: they say who may call an endpoint, but not whose data the caller may touch. To express a rule like "a user may only access their own resource", replace the static rule with a custom decision via access(...).

The security-data-mongo sample demonstrates this against a Mongo-backed user store. It protects GET /users/{username} so that only the user themselves can read it:

@Bean
SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    return http
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
        .httpBasic(withDefaults())
        .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
            .pathMatchers("/users/{user}/**").access(this::currentUserMatchesPath)
            .anyExchange().authenticated())
        .build();
}

access(...) accepts a ReactiveAuthorizationManager<AuthorizationContext>, which is a functional interface — a method reference fits its single authorize method:

private Mono<AuthorizationResult> currentUserMatchesPath(Mono<Authentication> authentication, AuthorizationContext context) {
    return authentication
            .map(a -> context.getVariables().get("user").equals(a.getName()))
            .map(granted -> (AuthorizationResult) new AuthorizationDecision(granted));
}

Walking through the decision:

  1. Mono<Authentication> supplies the authenticated principal, resolved reactively from the security context. For an anonymous request it is empty: the comparison never runs, no decision is granted, and the authentication entry point rejects the request with 401.
  2. AuthorizationContext wraps the current ServerWebExchange together with the URI template variables of the matched PathPattern. Since the rule is registered for /users/{user}/**, context.getVariables().get("user") is the {user} segment of the request path — e.g. "admin" for GET /users/admin. The trailing /** also matches zero segments, so /users/user itself is covered.
  3. The decision compares the path variable with Authentication.getName() (the username) and wraps the boolean in an AuthorizationDecision. true lets the request continue to the controller; false ends it with 403 Forbidden.

Two details are worth noting:

  • In Spring Security 7, ReactiveAuthorizationManager.authorize returns Mono<AuthorizationResult> — in 6.x the method was named check and returned Mono<AuthorizationDecision>, which is the signature still shown in the commented fragment at the top of this page. AuthorizationDecision implements AuthorizationResult, but Mono is invariant: the cast inside the second map aligns the types. A plain .map(AuthorizationDecision::new) produces Mono<AuthorizationDecision> and no longer compiles as the method reference.
  • The decision is purely name-based; roles play no part. Even admin is denied on /users/user because the names differ. To let admins bypass the check, extend the predicate with an authority check of your own.

Rules are evaluated in registration order and the first match wins, so the specific /users/{user}/** rule must come before the catch-all anyExchange().authenticated(). The sample also enables HTTP Basic (httpBasic(withDefaults())) so credentials can be sent with curl's -u option.

The sample's UserController exposes two endpoints:

Endpoint Rule Result GET /user anyExchange().authenticated() any authenticated user; returns the current principal GET /users/{username} access(this::currentUserMatchesPath) only when {username} equals the authenticated name

Verify with curl — the sample seeds user/password and admin/password into Mongo on startup:

# own path — granted
curl -v http://localhost:8080/users/user -u "user:password"
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK

# someone else's path — denied
curl -v http://localhost:8080/users/admin -u "user:password"
< HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden

SecurityDataMongoTests covers all of these cases — anonymous 401, own path 200, foreign path 403 — with WebTestClient against a Testcontainers-managed Mongo.

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/security-data-mongo. The security sample shows the same rule commented out alongside the classic path-matching rules.

docs.title: Custom authentication
docs.text:
Built-in mechanisms cover the common credential formats. When your clients send something else — a header of your own design, a device id, a signature — Spring Security has no customizer to enable, and you do not need one. The mechanism is assembled from the same four parts httpBasic and formLogin use internally, plus one registration call.

This page builds that mechanism around the security-api-key sample: client applications authenticate with an opaque key in an X-API-KEY header, and nothing else changes about how the chain runs. Note that, unlike form login, these credentials ride every request — there is no login page, no session, and no cookie in the design.

docs.title: The shape of a mechanism
docs.text:
Every authentication mechanism is the same pipeline, so adding one means supplying the pieces that are specific to your credential format:

  1. An Authentication token type — the object that carries the raw credential before validation and the resolved principal after it.
  2. A ServerAuthenticationConverter — reads the credential off the ServerWebExchange and returns the unauthenticated token.
  3. A ReactiveAuthenticationManager — validates the token and returns the authenticated one, or signals failure.
  4. An AuthenticationWebFilter — wires 1-3 together, and decides when they apply at all through a ServerWebExchangeMatcher.
  5. One registration call on ServerHttpSecurity — addFilterAt(filter, SecurityWebFiltersOrder.AUTHENTICATION), or addFilterBefore/addFilterAfter to place it relative to an existing filter.

You write no WebFilter of your own from scratch, no code to save the SecurityContext, and no code to write the rejection response. AuthenticationWebFilter already does that work: it runs the matcher, calls the converter, subscribes to the manager, stores the result through the chain's ServerSecurityContextRepository, and on AuthenticationException hands off to its failure handler. Overriding those four settings is the entire mechanism.

docs.title: Step 1: the token
docs.text:
A key belongs to a client application, not to a user account, so the sample gives the credential its own principal type. ClientApp pairs a name with the opaque secret that stands for it:

record ClientApp(String name, String apiKey) {

    static ClientApp registered(String name) {
        return new ClientApp(name, UUID.randomUUID().toString());
    }

}

ClientAppRepository keeps the applications in a ConcurrentHashMap keyed by the API key, which is exactly the query authentication needs:

@Component
class ClientAppRepository {

    private final Map<String, ClientApp> byApiKey = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    ClientAppRepository() {
        save(new ClientApp("web-client", "web-client-api-key"));
        save(new ClientApp("mobile-client", "mobile-client-api-key"));
    }

    Mono<ClientApp> findByApiKey(String apiKey) {
        return Mono.justOrEmpty(this.byApiKey.get(apiKey));
    }

    Flux<ClientApp> findAll() {
        return Flux.fromIterable(this.byApiKey.values());
    }

    Mono<ClientApp> save(ClientApp clientApp) {
        this.byApiKey.put(clientApp.apiKey(), clientApp);
        return Mono.just(clientApp);
    }

}

ApiKeyAuthentication carries the raw key before validation and the resolved principal after it:

public class ApiKeyAuthentication extends AbstractAuthenticationToken {

    private final String principal;
    private String apiKey;

    private ApiKeyAuthentication(String principal, String apiKey, Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> authorities) {
        super(authorities);
        this.principal = principal;
        this.apiKey = apiKey;
    }

    public static ApiKeyAuthentication unauthenticated(String apiKey) {
        return new ApiKeyAuthentication(null, apiKey, List.of());
    }

    public static ApiKeyAuthentication authenticated(String principal, String apiKey, Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> authorities) {
        ApiKeyAuthentication authentication = new ApiKeyAuthentication(principal, apiKey, authorities);
        authentication.setAuthenticated(true);
        return authentication;
    }

    @Override
    public Object getCredentials() {
        return this.apiKey;
    }

    @Override
    public Object getPrincipal() {
        return this.principal;
    }

    @Override
    public void eraseCredentials() {
        super.eraseCredentials();
        this.apiKey = null;
    }
}
  1. The converter creates the unauthenticated form: the raw key, no principal, and isAuthenticated() false — the state every token must be in before a manager has vouched for it.
  2. The manager returns the authenticated form: the client app name the key maps to, its granted authorities, and the authenticated flag set to true.
  3. eraseCredentials() clears the key so it is not held after the exchange completes. getName() comes from AbstractAuthenticationToken and resolves to the principal, so downstream code reads the authenticated application name with authentication.getName().

docs.title: Step 2: the converter
docs.text:
The converter reads the header and hands the raw value to the token factory:

class ApiKeyAuthenticationConverter implements ServerAuthenticationConverter {

    public static final String API_KEY_HEADER = "X-API-KEY";

    @Override
    public Mono<Authentication> convert(ServerWebExchange exchange) {
        return Mono.justOrEmpty(exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst(API_KEY_HEADER))
            .map(ApiKeyAuthentication::unauthenticated);
    }

}

An empty Mono from convert(...) tells AuthenticationWebFilter that this request carries no credentials for this mechanism, so it moves on unchanged. API_KEY_HEADER is public because the header name is part of the contract with callers — it is what the README, the tests, and the curl transcript below all quote.

docs.title: Step 3: the manager
docs.text:
The manager asks the store who owns the key and grants a single fixed role to every client application:

class ApiKeyAuthenticationManager implements ReactiveAuthenticationManager {

    private static final String ROLE_APP = "ROLE_APP";

    private final ClientAppRepository clientApps;

    ApiKeyAuthenticationManager(ClientAppRepository clientApps) {
        this.clientApps = clientApps;
    }

    @Override
    public Mono<Authentication> authenticate(Authentication authentication) {
        String apiKey = (String) authentication.getCredentials();
        return this.clientApps.findByApiKey(apiKey)
            .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new BadCredentialsException("Invalid API key")))
            .map(clientApp -> ApiKeyAuthentication.authenticated(clientApp.name(), apiKey,
                AuthorityUtils.createAuthorityList(ROLE_APP)));
    }

}
  1. An empty lookup becomes a BadCredentialsException through switchIfEmpty. AuthenticationWebFilter catches AuthenticationException and routes it to its failure handler, so a wrong key never reaches the controller.
  2. The principal is the application name, the authority is ROLE_APP for all of them. Per-application roles would belong to the store, not to the manager; until then, hasRole("APP") is what the /api chain asks for and what every registered application satisfies.

docs.title: Step 4: the filter
docs.text:
The filter collects the collaborators and adds the wiring that makes the mechanism fire only for requests carrying the header:

class ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter extends AuthenticationWebFilter {

    ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter(ClientAppRepository clientApps) {
        super(new ApiKeyAuthenticationManager(clientApps));
        setServerAuthenticationConverter(new ApiKeyAuthenticationConverter());
        setRequiresAuthenticationMatcher(this::apiKeyPresent);
        setAuthenticationFailureHandler(new ServerAuthenticationEntryPointFailureHandler(
            new HttpStatusServerEntryPoint(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)));
    }

    private String extractApiKeyFromHttpHeaders(ServerWebExchange exchange) {
        return exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst(ApiKeyAuthenticationConverter.API_KEY_HEADER);
    }

    private Mono<ServerWebExchangeMatcher.MatchResult> apiKeyPresent(ServerWebExchange exchange) {
        return StringUtils.hasText(extractApiKeyFromHttpHeaders(exchange))
            ? ServerWebExchangeMatcher.MatchResult.match()
            : ServerWebExchangeMatcher.MatchResult.notMatch();
    }

}

ServerWebExchangeMatcher is a functional interface returning a Mono<MatchResult>, so the gate can be a method reference on the filter itself. Three settings matter:

  1. setRequiresAuthenticationMatcher(...) decides whether the filter applies at all, before any conversion happens. A request without the header is left completely alone — no token, no manager call, no failure.
  2. setAuthenticationFailureHandler(...) replaces the default. Left alone, the failure handler calls HttpBasicServerAuthenticationEntryPoint, which would answer a rejected API key with a WWW-Authenticate: Basic challenge — inviting a machine client to retry with credentials it was never meant to have. HttpStatusServerEntryPoint writes a bare 401 instead.
  3. setServerAuthenticationConverter(...) swaps the Basic converter for the header reader above. The repository is passed through to the manager, and the NoOpServerSecurityContextRepository default stays: an API key is resent with every request, so there is nothing worth persisting between them.

docs.title: Step 5: register it
docs.text:
The filter is registered in a chain of its own, matching only the machine-facing paths:

@Configuration
class ApiKeySecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    @Order(1)
    SecurityWebFilterChain apiKeySecurityWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http, ClientAppRepository clientApps) {
        return http
            .securityMatcher(ServerWebExchangeMatchers.pathMatchers("/api/**"))
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .addFilterAt(new ApiKeyAuthenticationFilter(clientApps), SecurityWebFiltersOrder.AUTHENTICATION)
            .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                .anyExchange().hasRole("APP"))
            .exceptionHandling(handling -> handling
                .authenticationEntryPoint(new HttpStatusServerEntryPoint(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED)))
            .build();
    }

}

and the conventional Basic chain takes the rest:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    @Order(2)
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
        return http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .httpBasic(withDefaults())
            .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                .pathMatchers("/clients").hasRole("ADMIN")
                .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .build();
    }

    @Bean
    MapReactiveUserDetailsService userDetailsService() {
        UserDetails user = User.withDefaultPasswordEncoder()
            .username("user").password("password").roles("USER").build();
        UserDetails admin = User.withDefaultPasswordEncoder()
            .username("admin").password("password").roles("USER", "ADMIN").build();
        return new MapReactiveUserDetailsService(user, admin);
    }

}
  1. @EnableWebFluxSecurity belongs to a single configuration class; the other one only contributes its chain bean. ServerHttpSecurity is a prototype-scoped bean, so each chain method receives its own instance to configure — that is what makes several chains possible at all.
  2. securityMatcher(...) restricts a chain to the requests it owns. It takes a ServerWebExchangeMatcher, not a String, hence ServerWebExchangeMatchers.pathMatchers("/api/**"). The first chain whose matcher matches handles the request and the remaining ones are skipped entirely — exclusivity comes from the matcher, not from inspecting headers inside a filter.
  3. @Order is load-bearing. Without it the chains run in bean-definition order, which is not something to rely on; giving the Basic chain the earlier value makes it match every path first and the /api tests fail — a bad key answers with a Basic challenge again and the ROLE_APP rule is never reached.
  4. Because a path is served by exactly one chain, each chain carries one mechanism, and neither mechanism has to know the other exists: Authorization is invisible to /api/** and X-API-KEY is invisible everywhere else. The exceptionHandling entry point on the API chain keeps its rejections free of the WWW-Authenticate: Basic header that httpBasic would otherwise advertise.
  5. Construct the filter with new here rather than declaring it as a bean. WebHttpHandlerBuilder collects all WebFilter beans, so a bean would run once standalone and again inside the security chain.
  6. csrf is disabled in both chains: neither mechanism relies on a cookie a browser could be tricked into sending, which is the attack CsrfWebFilter exists to stop. That exemption is a property of these transports, not a habit to carry into a cookie-based mechanism — see the CSRF discussion in Built-in authentication mechanisms.

docs.title: Registering client apps
docs.text:
Management of the store deliberately lives outside /api/**, so it is guarded by HTTP Basic and an admin role rather than by the keys it hands out:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/clients")
class ClientAppController {

    record Registration(String name) {
    }

    private final ClientAppRepository clientApps;

    ClientAppController(ClientAppRepository clientApps) {
        this.clientApps = clientApps;
    }

    @GetMapping
    Flux<ClientApp> list() {
        return this.clientApps.findAll();
    }

    @PostMapping
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)
    Mono<ClientApp> register(@RequestBody Mono<Registration> registration) {
        return registration
            .map(entry -> ClientApp.registered(entry.name()))
            .flatMap(this.clientApps::save);
    }

}

POST /clients takes only a name, generates the key, and returns both. The new key authenticates against the same repository the manager reads, so the application can call /api/** immediately — adminRegistersClientAppAndNewKeyAccessesApiPath asserts exactly that round trip.

docs.title: Which mechanism answers a request
docs.text:
Path Credentials sent Chain that owns it Result /user none Basic 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: Basic challenge /user valid Authorization Basic 200, authenticated as that user /user valid X-API-KEY Basic 401 — outside /api/** a key is not a credential /api/posts valid X-API-KEY API key 200, authenticated as the client app /api/posts none API key 401 with no challenge header /api/posts invalid X-API-KEY API key 401 — the chain stops at the filter /api/posts valid Authorization API key 401 — this chain has no Basic mechanism /api/posts valid X-API-KEY and Authorization API key 200, authenticated as the client app /clients admin Basic Basic 200 / 201 /clients user Basic Basic 403 — authenticated, but not ROLE_ADMIN

The last row is the distinction worth remembering: credentials that are not accepted at all produce 401 and run the chain's entry point, while an accepted identity that fails a role check produces 403.

SecurityApiKeyTests pins each row down, in validApiKeyIsIgnoredOutsideApiPath, basicCredentialsAreNotCredentialsForTheApiPath, validApiKeyDecidesApiPathWhenBasicCredentialsAreAlsoSent, invalidApiKeyIsUnauthorized, invalidApiKeyChallengeDoesNotAdvertiseBasic, and nonAdminCannotListClientApps.

docs.title: Verify with curl
docs.text:
Start the sample and try each mechanism:

# no credentials — 401 with a Basic challenge
curl -v http://localhost:8080/user
< HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
< WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Realm"

# HTTP Basic — a human user
curl -s http://localhost:8080/user -u "user:password"
{"name":"user","authorities":["ROLE_USER"],"authenticated":true}

# API key on /api/** — authenticated as the client app that owns the key
curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/posts -H "X-API-KEY: web-client-api-key"
[{"title":"post one","content":"content of post one"},{"title":"post two","content":"content of post two"}]

# unknown key — 401, and no Basic challenge to mislead the caller
curl -v http://localhost:8080/api/posts -H "X-API-KEY: no-such-key"
< HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized

# Basic credentials on /api/** — this chain has no Basic mechanism
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080/api/posts -u "admin:password"
401

# an API key outside /api/** — this chain has no key mechanism
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080/user -H "X-API-KEY: web-client-api-key"
401

# administering the store needs an admin user, not a key
curl -s http://localhost:8080/clients -u "admin:password"
[{"name":"mobile-client","apiKey":"mobile-client-api-key"},{"name":"web-client","apiKey":"web-client-api-key"}]
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080/clients -u "user:password"
403

# register a new application and use the key it is given
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/clients -u "admin:password" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"batch-worker"}'
{"name":"batch-worker","apiKey":"b42db08b-f58c-485a-8b64-fe7d096aebcf"}
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080/api/posts -H "X-API-KEY: b42db08b-f58c-485a-8b64-fe7d096aebcf"
200

docs.title: See it in code
docs.text: The security-api-key sample exposes GET /user, which renders the current Authentication as name, authorities, and the authenticated flag; GET /api/posts, the general-purpose API for client applications; and GET/POST /clients, the admin-only registry behind them. The same pipeline is what the built-in mechanisms are built from — compare it against Built-in authentication mechanisms — and once authentication is settled, Method level constraints moves authorization next to the business methods themselves.

docs.title: An introduction to Spring Security
docs.text:
Spring Security is Spring's framework for protecting applications and their resources. It provides authentication (establishing who is making a request) and authorization (deciding what that identity may do), along with protections such as security headers, CSRF defenses, and session integration.

This chapter introduces Spring Security's WebFlux support and shows how to configure these protections without leaving the non-blocking architecture.

docs.title: Security in WebFlux
docs.text:
In a WebFlux application, security participates in the reactive request pipeline. A request passes through a chain of web filters before it reaches a handler. Spring Security installs its own WebFilter integration in that chain; the integration delegates to a SecurityWebFilterChain that applies authentication and authorization rules. A request that is not authenticated or authorized is rejected or redirected before the application handler runs.

The servlet stack uses servlet filters and HttpSecurity; WebFlux uses WebFilter and ServerHttpSecurity. The concepts are familiar, but the APIs and execution model differ. The core mapping looks like this:

Servlet stack Reactive stack SecurityFilterChain SecurityWebFilterChain HttpSecurity ServerHttpSecurity FilterChain WebFilterChain UserDetailsService ReactiveUserDetailsService @EnableWebSecurity @EnableWebFluxSecurity ServletRequest/ServletResponse ServerWebExchange

The underlying idea is the same: a filter chain intercepts each request, authentication resolves a principal, and authorization rules decide whether the request should pass through. The difference is that the entire flow works with reactive primitives and non-blocking exchange objects.

Security also depends on the application's authentication model. A server-rendered site may use a session and form login, while an API may use bearer tokens. CSRF protection is important for browser requests that automatically attach credentials, such as session cookies; do not disable it without considering how clients authenticate and send requests.

docs.title: Add the dependencies
docs.text:
The reactive pieces ship in the standard Spring Security modules — no separate reactive artifact is required. When you are developing a WebFlux application without Spring Boot, add the security dependencies like this (versioning is typically managed by spring-boot-starter-parent):

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-config</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

For Spring Boot applications, a single starter is enough. See Configuration for both variants.

docs.title: How request security is applied
docs.text:
The security filter chain is configured as a Spring bean. Each SecurityWebFilterChain combines security filters with request-matching rules. Spring evaluates the chains in order and uses the first chain whose security matcher applies to the request. Within the selected chain, authorization rules are evaluated in declaration order, so put specific matchers before broad ones and end with an intentional catch-all rule.

For example, route-level rules can allow a public endpoint, require a role for an administrative area, and require authentication for everything else:

@Bean
SecurityWebFilterChain applicationSecurity(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    return http
        .authorizeExchange(exchanges -> exchanges
            .pathMatchers("/about", "/health").permitAll()
            .pathMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyExchange().authenticated()
        )
        .build();
}

These rules protect requests based on their paths and other request attributes. Authentication can be provided by mechanisms such as form login, HTTP Basic, OAuth 2.0 login, or bearer tokens; choose and configure only the mechanisms that match the application.

docs.title: A friendly reading path
docs.text:
This page covers the general security model. A natural way through the rest of the chapter is to move into the concrete configuration pieces:

  • continue with Configuration to see the core ServerHttpSecurity setup, both without Spring Boot and with the starter's auto-configuration
  • explore Built-in authentication mechanisms for the request-level mechanisms Spring Security ships — HTTP Basic, form login, and a tour of the rest
  • move into Method level constraints to protect business logic and endpoints with authorization rules
  • read Customize UserDetailsRepository to see where the credentials those mechanisms check actually come from
  • finish with Custom authentication, which walks an X-API-KEY mechanism end to end and shows how the same pieces are assembled when none of the built-ins fits

The chapters are ordered to build from concept to implementation: first the model, then the configuration, then the practical details that make security feel real in a reactive application.

docs.title: Method level constraints
docs.text:
Like traditional Spring WebMvc applications, you can use a @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") annotation on your methods to prevent the execution of a method when the expression defined in @PreAuthorize evaluates to false.

Path rules are a useful first boundary, but they are not always enough. A route may be open to several roles while a particular operation — or the object an operation touches — needs a more specific permission. Method security puts that check next to the business method it protects.

docs.title: Enable method security
docs.text:
To enable method level security, add @EnableReactiveMethodSecurity to your security configuration class:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
@EnableReactiveMethodSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
                .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)
                .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/posts/**").permitAll()
                        //.pathMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/posts/**").hasRole("ADMIN")//replace this with method level constraints
                        .anyExchange().authenticated())
                .build();
    }

    // ...
}

The annotation applies to Spring-managed beans: the secured method has to be invoked through the proxy that method security creates around the bean, so a call from inside the same bean bypasses the check.

docs.title: Apply constraints on reactive methods
docs.text:
Annotate the methods in your business code — the sample applies the constraint on the repository:

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
Mono<Post> delete(Long id) {
    Post deleted = data.get(id);
    data.remove(id);
    return Mono.just(deleted);
}

@PreAuthorize works on methods returning Mono or Flux because the reactive method security interceptor checks the expression before subscribing to the returned publisher — the decision happens before any data flows.

The expression can also reach the method's own arguments, which is how an ownership check is written:

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #owner == authentication.name")
public Mono<Report> findReport(String owner, String reportId) {
    return reports.findById(reportId);
}

With the URL-level rules replaced by the annotation, a DELETE /posts/{id} call from a non-admin user is rejected with 403 before the repository method runs.

Method security and request-level authorization complement each other rather than compete: keep the broad policy in the SecurityWebFilterChain and put the checks that depend on the arguments or the domain object on the method, where the data needed to decide is in scope.

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/security-method.

docs.title: Customize UserDetailsRepository
docs.text: The authentication manager resolves users through a ReactiveUserDetailsService, whose single method returns a Mono<UserDetails>. The in-memory MapReactiveUserDetailsService covers demos; this page shows two ways to replace it.

docs.title: Load users from a properties file
docs.text:
Spring Security provides a ReactiveUserDetailsServiceResourceFactoryBean which loads users from a properties file and creates the ReactiveUserDetailsService for your applications:

@Bean
public ReactiveUserDetailsServiceResourceFactoryBean userDetailsService() {
    return ReactiveUserDetailsServiceResourceFactoryBean
        .fromResourceLocation("classpath:users.properties");
}

The content of the users.properties file is similar to the following:

user=password,ROLE_USER
admin=password,ROLE_USER,ROLE_ADMIN

The key is the username; the value is the password and its roles.

You can explore the sample in spring-reactive-sample/security-user-properties

docs.title: Load users from a database
docs.text:
For real applications, implement the ReactiveUserDetailsService against your user store. Using Mongo as the backend store, create a User document class that implements the Spring Security UserDetails interface:

@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
@Document
class User implements UserDetails {

    @Id
    private String id;
    private String username;
    private String password;

    @Builder.Default()
    private boolean active = true;

    @Builder.Default()
    private List<String> roles = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    public Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities() {
        return AuthorityUtils.createAuthorityList(roles.toArray(new String[roles.size()]));
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isAccountNonExpired() {
        return active;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isAccountNonLocked() {
        return active;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isCredentialsNonExpired() {
        return active;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isEnabled() {
        return active;
    }
}

Create a UserRepository for User:

public interface UserRepository extends ReactiveMongoRepository<User, String> {

    Mono<User> findByUsername(String username);
}

Replace the in-memory user details service bean with the following, which connects to the real database:

@Bean
public ReactiveUserDetailsService userDetailsService(UserRepository users) {
    return (username) -> users.findByUsername(username).cast(UserDetails.class);
}

The security-data-mongo sample goes one step further and registers a PasswordEncoder:

@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
}

You can explore the sample in spring-reactive-sample/security-data-mongo.

docs.title: Programmatic Bean Registration with BeanRegistrar
docs.text: Most applications declare beans with @Component scanning or @Bean methods, but some wiring is better expressed programmatically — conditional on the environment, assembled from a library's own types, or composed from several independent registration units. Spring Framework 7 introduces BeanRegistrar as a dedicated contract for this, replacing the older context-level registerBean approach with a bean-definition-stage API that participates in the configuration model and AOT processing.

docs.title: Existing alternatives
docs.text:
Before Spring Framework 7, programmatic registration typically went through one of these routes:

  • BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor or ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar — powerful but low-level: you manipulate raw BeanDefinition objects and run at a specific point of the container lifecycle.
  • GenericApplicationContext.registerBean(...) (since Spring Framework 5) — a friendly context-level API, but the registration happens outside the configuration model, and the common usage pattern constructs the objects eagerly before refresh().

The register-bean sample shows the latter:

AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();
PostRepository posts = new PostRepository();
PostHandler postHandler = new PostHandler(posts);
Routes routesBean = new Routes(postHandler);

context.registerBean(PostRepository.class, () -> posts);
context.registerBean(PostHandler.class, () -> postHandler);
context.registerBean(Routes.class, () -> routesBean);
context.registerBean(WebHandler.class, () -> RouterFunctions.toWebHandler(routesBean.routes(), HandlerStrategies.builder().build()));
context.refresh();

The objects are built by hand and captured in supplier lambdas; dependency wiring, lifecycle metadata, and profile conditions are all manual.

docs.title: BeanRegistrar: the Spring Framework 7 alternative
docs.text:
BeanRegistrar (org.springframework.beans.factory) is a single-method contract:

public interface BeanRegistrar {
    void register(BeanRegistry registry, Environment env);
}

Activate it with @Import on any @Configuration class (including the @SpringBootApplication class) — ConfigurationClassPostProcessor picks it up while parsing the configuration model. In a plain Spring application you can also call GenericApplicationContext.register(BeanRegistrar) directly.

Compared with context.registerBean(...), it brings several improvements:

  • Bean-definition stage, not context level. Registrations go through BeanRegistry into bean definitions before the context refreshes. Suppliers are deferred — nothing is constructed at registration time — and the registrations participate in the same configuration-model processing as @Bean methods.
  • Environment access. The Environment argument lets you branch on profiles and properties directly, e.g. env.matchesProfiles("h2").
  • Typed, fluent bean specs. registerBean(Class, Consumer<Spec>) exposes metadata as chainable options: supplier, primary, fallback, order, lazyInit, backgroundInit, prototype, scope, description, infrastructure, and notAutowirable.
  • Deferred dependency resolution. The supplier receives a SupplierContext; ctx.bean(SomeType.class) (or beanProvider(...) for lazy/optional access) resolves collaborators at instantiation time instead of capturing pre-built instances.
  • Composition. registry.register(otherRegistrar) nests registrars, registerAlias adds aliases, and containsBean guards against duplicates.
  • AOT and GraalVM native support. Because registrars are processed as part of the configuration model, ConfigurationClassPostProcessor generates AOT contributions for them — registrations survive ahead-of-time processing and native-image builds.

Note: the Spec API has no qualifier support. For resolution conflicts, use primary(), fallback(), and order(int).

Generic types need a ParameterizedTypeReference so the full type is recorded in the bean definition:

registry.registerBean(new ParameterizedTypeReference<RouterFunction<ServerResponse>>() {}, spec -> spec
        .supplier(ctx -> ctx.bean(Routes.class).routes()));

docs.title: Example: switching repositories by profile
docs.text:
The boot-bean-registrar sample registers a complete WebFlux application — repository, handler, routes, and a data initializer — from a single registrar, and switches between an in-memory store and H2 (R2DBC) with a profile:

public class PostBeanRegistrar implements BeanRegistrar {

    @Override
    public void register(BeanRegistry registry, Environment env) {
        if (env.matchesProfiles("h2")) {
            registry.registerBean(PostRepository.class, spec -> spec
                    .supplier(ctx -> new H2PostRepository(ctx.bean(DatabaseClient.class))));
        } else {
