            registry.registerBean(PostRepository.class, spec -> spec
                    .supplier(ctx -> new InMemoryPostRepository()));
        }

        registry.registerBean(PostHandler.class, spec -> spec
                .supplier(ctx -> new PostHandler(ctx.bean(PostRepository.class))));

        registry.registerBean(Routes.class, spec -> spec
                .supplier(ctx -> new Routes(ctx.bean(PostHandler.class))));

        registry.registerBean(new ParameterizedTypeReference<RouterFunction<ServerResponse>>() {}, spec -> spec
                .supplier(ctx -> ctx.bean(Routes.class).routes()));

        registry.registerBean(CommandLineRunner.class, spec -> spec
                .supplier(ctx -> args -> {
                    var posts = ctx.bean(PostRepository.class);
                    if (posts instanceof InMemoryPostRepository) {
                        Flux.just(
                                new Post(null, "Spring 7", "Content of Spring 7"),
                                new Post(null, "Bean Registrar", "Content of Bean Registrar")
                        ).flatMap(posts::save).then().block();
                    }
                }));
    }
}

Reading the registrar:

  • env.matchesProfiles("h2") selects the repository implementation at registration time. Under the h2 profile, ctx.bean(DatabaseClient.class) resolves the DatabaseClient that Spring Boot's R2DBC auto-configuration provides from spring.r2dbc.url.
  • The RouterFunction<ServerResponse> bean is what Spring Boot's RouterFunctionMapping picks up to serve the functional endpoints — no manual WebHandler/server bootstrap is needed in a Boot application.
  • The CommandLineRunner seeds sample data only for the in-memory variant; the H2 variant is populated by schema.sql/data.sql, which Boot runs automatically for the embedded database.

Import it on the application class:

@SpringBootApplication
@Import(PostBeanRegistrar.class)
public class DemoApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

The profile switch is plain Boot configuration — application.properties sets the default spring.r2dbc.url, and application-h2.properties overrides it with a separate in-memory database. Run with the H2 profile via mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=h2.

The sample verifies both variants with WebTestClient: DemoApplicationTests runs against the default in-memory context, and H2ApplicationTests adds @ActiveProfiles("h2") to exercise the R2DBC-backed repository.

docs.title: Kotlin: BeanRegistrarDsl
docs.text:
Kotlin gets a DSL on top of the same contract — BeanRegistrarDsl — with reified registerBean { }, bean<T>() resolution inside suppliers, and profile("...") { } blocks:

class PostBeanRegistrar : BeanRegistrarDsl({
    registerBean { InMemoryPostRepository() }
    registerBean { PostHandler(bean()) }
    registerBean { Routes(bean()) }
    registerBean { bean<Routes>().routes() }
})

See Kotlin DSLs for the full DSL walkthrough and the boot-bean-registrar-kotlin-dsl sample for a complete coroutine-based application built with it.

docs.title: Create a WebFlux application with Spring Boot
docs.text:
Spring Boot 4.x targets the latest Spring technology stack, including Spring Framework 7, Spring Security 6+, Spring Session 3+, and more.

Spring Boot added a new starter spring-boot-starter-webflux for starting a WebFlux application.

docs.title: Generate project skeleton
docs.text:
Follow the following steps to prepare the project skeleton using Spring initializr.

Open your browser and navigate to http://start.spring.io.

In the Spring Boot Initializr page, fill the following fields.

  1. Select the latest Spring Boot 4.x release (for example, 4.0.0).
  2. In the dependencies box, type reactive and choose Reactive Web to add spring-boot-starter-webflux. Optionally add Lombok, Reactive MongoDB, Reactive Redis, or other starters you need.
  3. Click Generate project (or press ALT+ENTER) to download a ZIP archive containing the project skeleton.

Download the archive and extract it to your disk, then import the source codes into your IDE.

Open the pom.xml, you will see the spring-boot-starter-webflux is added into dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>

And a spring-boot-maven-plugin is added in the initial pom.xml.

Spring Boot starter spring-boot-starter-webflux will handle the spring-webflux related dependencies and enable WebFlux support automatically. It also add logback as default logging handler.

Compare to the former vanilla version,

  1. No need explicit WebConfig, Spring Boot configures it automatically.
  2. The former bootstraping class or AppInitializer is no use now, the Spring Boot built-in @SpringBootApplication annotated class hands over the applicationContext lifecyle and application bootstrap.
@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

By default, Spring Boot will use Reactor Netty as runtime to run a WebFlux application. No need extra configuration for it.

To start the application in your terminal, run the following command in the project root folder.

mvn spring-boot:run

Alternatively, to start Spring Boot applications in your IDEs, run it just like running a general-purpose Java application.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
As an exercise, try to add the similar codes with the former post to expose RESTful APIs for Post.

  1. Add a POJO Post.
  2. Add a dummy PostRepository.
  3. Add a simple PostController.

Restart the application, and test the endpoints.

#curl http://localhost:8080/posts
...

docs.title: Bootstrap
docs.text:
By default, when spring-boot-starter-webflux is included in the classpath, it uses Netty as the embedded server to serve HTTP requests.

It is easy to switch to other embedded servers.

docs.title: Apache Tomcat
docs.text:
If you want to use Apache Tomcat as target runtime environment, just exclude spring-boot-starter-reactor-netty from spring-boot-starter-webflux, and add an extra dependency spring-boot-starter-tomcat into pom.xml.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
     <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-reactor-netty</artifactId>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
</dependency>

The boot-start sample provides Maven profiles to switch between Reactor Netty (default), Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow — activate one with mvn spring-boot:run -Ptomcat.

docs.title: Eclipse Jetty
docs.text:
To use Jetty to replace the default Reactor Netty.

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
  <exclusions>
    <exclusion>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-reactor-netty</artifactId>
    </exclusion>
  </exclusions>
</dependency>

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Undertow (deprecated)
docs.text:
You can use Undertow as the runtime, but note that Undertow examples in this repository are retained for historical reference and are marked deprecated. For new projects prefer Reactor Netty or Jetty.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-reactor-netty</artifactId>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-undertow</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Sample
docs.text: You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/boot-start.

docs.title: Create a WebFlux application from Scratch
docs.text:
A working example is worth a thousand words. Let's write code and explore the reactive programming features introduced in Spring Framework 7.

As an example, I will reuse the same concept in my former Spring Boot sample codes which is a simple blog application.

Note

In this post, we prepare the codes manually and do not use Spring Boot autoconfiguration. I think it will help you to understand the essential configuration in a Spring WebFlux application.

In the following steps we will start with creating RESTful APIs for Post.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before writing some real codes, make sure you have installed the essential software:

  • Java 21. Install a JDK from Eclipse Temurin, Oracle, or your preferred vendor.
  • Apache Maven or Gradle
  • Your favorite IDE:
    • IntelliJ IDEA (Community or Ultimate Edition)
    • Eclipse IDE — with Spring Tools for Spring support
    • Apache NetBeans IDE
    • VS Code with the Java and Spring Boot extensions

Note

Do not forget to add path which includes java and mvn command into your system environment variable PATH .

docs.title: Generate project skeleton
docs.text:
Personally I prefer to use Apache Maven to build Java applications.

Run the following command to create a general web application from the existing Maven archetype.

$ mvn archetype:generate -DgroupId=com.example \
    -DartifactId=demo \
    -DarchetypeArtifactId=maven-archetype-webapp \
    -DinteractiveMode=false \

Note

I would like Unix like bash to run commands in my terminal. Under Windows system, you can choose CygWin or convert it to Windows form.

Import the generated codes into your IDE..

Open pom.xml in your IDE editor, add some modifications:

  1. Add spring-boot-starter-parent as parent POM to manage the versions of all required dependencies for this project.
  2. Add spring-webflux, Jackson 3 (tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind), and Reactor as dependencies to get Spring Web Reactive support
  3. Add logback as logging framework, jcl-over-slf4j is a bridge for Spring jcl and slf4j.
  4. Add Lombok to erase the tedious getters, setters, etc for POJO classes. More details go to Lombok project.

The final pom.xml looks like:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>com.example</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-reactive-sample-vanilla</artifactId>
    <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>

    <name>spring-reactive-sample-vanilla</name>
    <description>Spring Webflux demo(without Spring Boot)</description>

    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>4.0.0</version>
        <relativePath/> <!-- lookup parent from repository -->
    </parent>

    <properties>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
        <project.reporting.outputEncoding>UTF-8</project.reporting.outputEncoding>
        <java.version>21</java.version>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-webflux</artifactId>
        </dependency>

        <dependency>
            <groupId>tools.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
        </dependency>

        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.netty</groupId>
            <artifactId>netty-buffer</artifactId>
        </dependency>

        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.projectreactor.netty</groupId>
            <artifactId>reactor-netty</artifactId>
        </dependency>

        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
            <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
        </dependency>

        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
            <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
            <artifactId>jcl-over-slf4j</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
            <artifactId>logback-core</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
            <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
        </dependency>

    </dependencies>
</project>

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The project skeleton is ready, now let's add some codes to play reactive programming.

Create a new class named Post, it includes three fields: id, title, content.

@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
class Post {

    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private String content;

}

In the above codes, @Data, @ToString, @Builder, @NoArgsConstructor, @AllArgsConstructor are from the Lombok project.

When you compile Post, it will utilize Java compiler built-in Annotation Processing Tooling feature to add extra facilities into the final compiled classes, including:

  1. Getters and setters of the three fields, and overrides equals and hashCode methods.
  2. Overrides toString method.
  3. A builder class for creating the Post instance more easily.
  4. A constructor with no arguments.
  5. A constructor with all fields as arguments.

Create a dummy repository named PostRepository to retrieve posts from and save them back to a repository.

@Component
class PostRepository {

    private static final Map<Long, Post> DATA = new HashMap<>();
    private static long ID_COUNTER = 1L;

    static {
        Arrays.asList("First Post", "Second Post")
            .stream()
            .forEach((java.lang.String title) -> {
                long id = ID_COUNTER++;
                DATA.put(Long.valueOf(id), Post.builder().id(id).title(title).content("content of " + title).build());
            }
            );
    }

    Flux<Post> findAll() {
        return Flux.fromIterable(DATA.values());
    }

    Mono<Post> findById(Long id) {
        return Mono.just(DATA.get(id));
    }

    Mono<Post> createPost(Post post) {
        long id = ID_COUNTER++;
        post.setId(id);
        DATA.put(id, post);
        return Mono.just(post);
    }

}

Currently we have not connected to any database, so this repository uses a Map backed data store instead. When we discuss the reactive features provided by the Spring Data projects, we will replace it with a real Spring Data reactive implementation.

If you have used Spring Data before, you will find these APIs are every similar with Repository interface provided in Spring Data.

The main difference is in the current Repository class all methods return a Flux or Mono.

Flux and Mono are from Reactor, which powers the reactive support in Spring Framework 7 by default.

  • Flux represents a stream of 0..N elements.
  • Mono represents an asynchronous 0..1 result.

Create a controller class named PostController to expose RESTful APIs for the Post entity.

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "")
    public Flux<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") Long id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PostMapping(value = "")
    public Mono<Post> create(Post post) {
        return this.posts.createPost(post);
    }

}

If you have some experience in Spring WebMvc, you will see the above codes are almost same as the existing one, except we return a Flux or Mono as the response body.

Next, create a @Configuration class and add an @EnableWebFlux annotation to activate WebFlux support in this application.

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {

}

The application code is ready. Let's bootstrap the application.

docs.title: Bootstrap
docs.text:
According to the official documentation (see the Web on Reactive Stack section), Spring Framework 7 provides several options to bootstrap a reactive web application: https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/docs/current/reference/html/web-reactive.html#spring-webflux

Quote

Spring WebFlux is supported on Tomcat, Jetty, Servlet 3.1+ containers, as well as on non-Servlet runtimes such as Netty and Undertow.

Every bootstrap variant follows the same three steps, built on a handful of core Spring types (Javadoc links):

  1. Build an HttpHandler from the ApplicationContext with WebHttpHandlerBuilder — the low-level contract for reactive request handling.
  2. Wrap it in a server-specific adapter: TomcatHttpHandlerAdapter, JettyCoreHttpHandlerAdapter, ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter, or UndertowHttpHandlerAdapter. Above the adapter, the WebHandler chain assembles the filters and exception handlers — see An introduction to Reactive Web.
  3. Start the embedded server.

docs.title: Apache Tomcat
docs.text:
Create a general-purpose Application class to start the application manually.

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@PropertySource(value = "classpath:application.properties", ignoreResourceNotFound = true)
public class Application {

    @Value("${server.port:8080}")
    private int port = 8080;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);  // (1)

        Tomcat tomcatServer = context.getBean(Tomcat.class);
        tomcatServer.start();

        System.out.println("Tomcat server is running at port:"
                           + tomcatServer.getConnector().getLocalPort());
        //System.in.read();
    }

    @Bean
    @Profile("default")
    public Tomcat embeddedTomcatServer(ApplicationContext context) {
        HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();

        Servlet servlet = new TomcatHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
        Tomcat tomcat = new Tomcat();

        File base = new File(System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir"));
        Context rootContext = tomcat.addContext("", base.getAbsolutePath());
        Tomcat.addServlet(rootContext, "main", servlet).setAsyncSupported(true);
        rootContext.addServletMappingDecoded("/", "main");

        tomcat.setHostname("localhost");
        tomcat.setPort(this.port);
        tomcat.setBaseDir(System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir"));

        return tomcat;
    }

}

The above codes perform some tasks.

  1. Create a HttpHandler from ApplicationContext.
  2. Use TomcatHttpHandlerAdapter to bridge the Servlet APIs to the reactive based HttpHandler.
  3. Start tomcat server.

Do not forget add the tomcat-embed-core to project dependencies.

 <dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.tomcat.embed</groupId>
    <artifactId>tomcat-embed-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

You can simply run this class in IDEs as java applications.

If you want to package all dependencies into one jar and run the application in command line, eg. java -jar filename, maven-assembly-plugin can help this purpose.

Add maven-assembly-plugin configuration into the pom.xml file.

<!-- Maven Assembly Plugin -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-assembly-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <descriptorRefs>
            <descriptorRef>jar-with-dependencies</descriptorRef>
        </descriptorRefs>
        <!-- MainClass in mainfest make a executable jar -->
        <archive>
            <manifest>
                <mainClass>com.example.demo.Application</mainClass>
            </manifest>
        </archive>

    </configuration>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <id>make-assembly</id>
            <phase>package</phase> <!-- bind to the packaging phase -->
            <goals>
                <goal>single</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

Open your terminal, run the following command in your project root folder:

mvn package

When it is done, switch to the target folder, besides the general jar, you will find an extra fat jar was generated, which filename is ended with jar-with-dependencies.jar.

spring-reactive-sample-vanilla-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT-jar-with-dependencies.jar
spring-reactive-sample-vanilla-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar

Run the following command to run this application.

java -jar target/spring-reactive-sample-vanilla-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT-jar-with-dependencies.jar

When it is started, let's try to verify if it works.

#curl http://localhost:8080/posts
[{"id":1,"title":"First Post","content":"content of First Post"},{"id":2,"title":"Second Post","content":"content of Second Post"}]

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/vanilla-tomcat.

docs.title: Eclipse Jetty
docs.text:
To use a Jetty server instead, replace the Application class with the following:

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@PropertySource(value = "classpath:application.properties", ignoreResourceNotFound = true)
public class Application {

    @Value("${server.port:8080}")
    private int port = 8080;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);
        Server server = context.getBean(Server.class);

        // 4. Starts up application
        server.start();

        System.out.println("Press ENTER to exit.");
        System.in.read();
    }

    @Bean
    public Server jettyServer(ApplicationContext context) throws Exception {
        // 1. Initialize the adapter with Spring's HttpHandler
        HttpHandler httpHandler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();
        // 2. Create the Jetty Core adapter
        JettyCoreHttpHandlerAdapter adapter = new JettyCoreHttpHandlerAdapter(httpHandler);

        // 3. Set up the Jetty 12 Core Path Mappings
        PathMappingsHandler pathMappingsHandler = new PathMappingsHandler();

        // CRITICAL JETTY 12 CHANGE: Bind your adapter explicitly via PathSpec
        // Use "/*" to ensure all sub-paths underneath the root context are matched correctly
        pathMappingsHandler.addMapping(PathSpec.from("/*"), adapter);

        // 4. Initialize server and attach the mapping handler
        Server server = new Server();
        server.setHandler(pathMappingsHandler);

        // 5. Setup Network Connector
        ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server);
        connector.setPort(port);
        server.addConnector(connector);

        return server;
    }

}

Since Jetty 11, the Jetty artifact IDs changed: the servlet support moved into environment-specific modules such as jetty-ee11-servlet (Jetty 12, EE 11 environment), and the servlet-era ServletContextHandler bootstrap is replaced by Jetty Core's PathMappingsHandler. Declare a BOM for the EE 11 environment and use the new coordinates:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty.ee11</groupId>
            <artifactId>jetty-ee11-bom</artifactId>
            <version>${jetty.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty</groupId>
        <artifactId>jetty-server</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty.ee11</groupId>
        <artifactId>jetty-ee11-servlet</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Similarly, you can run the application directly in your IDEs.

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/vanilla-jetty.

Alternatively, you can run the application in Reactor Netty, or JBoss Undertow.

docs.title: Reactor Netty
docs.text:
For Reactor Netty, replace the Application class with:

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@PropertySource(value = "classpath:application.properties", ignoreResourceNotFound = true)
public class Application {

    @Value("${server.port:8080}")
    private int port = 8080;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(
                Application.class)) {
            context.getBean(HttpServer.class)
                    .bindUntilJavaShutdown(Duration.ofSeconds(60), null);
        }
    }

    @Bean
    public HttpServer httpServer(ApplicationContext context) {
        HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();
        ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter adapter = new ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
        return  HttpServer.create()
                .host("localhost")
                .port(this.port)
                .handle(adapter);
    }

}

And add reactor-netty in your project dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.projectreactor.netty</groupId>
    <artifactId>reactor-netty</artifactId>
</dependency>

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/vanilla.

docs.title: Undertow (deprecated)
docs.text:
For Undertow, replace the Application class with:

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@PropertySource(value = "classpath:application.properties", ignoreResourceNotFound = true)
public class Application {

    @Value("${server.port:8080}")
    private int port = 8080;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);  // (1)
        Undertow server = context.getBean(Undertow.class);
        server.start();
        System.out.println("Press ENTER to exit.");
        System.in.read();
    }

    @Bean
    public Undertow undertowServer(ApplicationContext context) {
        HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();  // (2)

        // Undertow
        UndertowHttpHandlerAdapter undertowAdapter = new UndertowHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
        Undertow server = Undertow.builder()
            .addHttpListener(port, "localhost")
            .setHandler(undertowAdapter)
            .build();

        return server;
    }

}

And add undertow-core in your project dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.undertow</groupId>
    <artifactId>undertow-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Standalone Servlet Container
docs.text:
If you prefer traditional web applications and want to package a WAR to deploy into a servlet container, Spring Framework 7 provides AbstractReactiveWebInitializer to help initialize a reactive web application in a Servlet environment. This class implements WebApplicationInitializer and is discovered by the servlet container at startup.

Create a AppInitializer instead of the Application class.

public class AppInitializer extends AbstractReactiveWebInitializer {

    @Override
    protected Class<?>[] getConfigClasses() {
        return new Class[]{
                AppConfig.class,
                WebConfig.class
        };
    }
}

Note

The former AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherHandlerInitializer is problematic, check notes I added in the sample codes spring-reactive-sample/war

Next change the project packaging from jar to war in pom.xml.

<packaging>war</packaging>

And add the Jakarta Servlet API to your project dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>jakarta.servlet</groupId>
    <artifactId>jakarta.servlet-api</artifactId>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>

Now you can run this application on an IDE managed Servlet container directly.

Or package the project into a war format and deploy it into a Servlet based container (Tomcat, Jetty) manually.

Alternatively, if you want to run this application via mvn commands in the development stage, the Jetty EE 11 Maven plugin serves the WAR in place:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty.ee11</groupId>
    <artifactId>jetty-ee11-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <scanIntervalSeconds>10</scanIntervalSeconds>
        <webApp>
            <contextPath>/</contextPath>
        </webApp>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

Run the following command to start it.

mvn jetty:run

Or use the Cargo plugin to package and deploy into an embedded Tomcat controlled by cargo:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-war-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <failOnMissingWebXml>false</failOnMissingWebXml>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.codehaus.cargo</groupId>
    <artifactId>cargo-maven3-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <container>
            <containerId>tomcat10x</containerId>
            <type>embedded</type>
        </container>

        <configuration>
            <properties>
                <cargo.servlet.port>8080</cargo.servlet.port>
                <cargo.logging>high</cargo.logging>
            </properties>
        </configuration>
    </configuration>
</plugin>

mvn verify cargo:run

Check the sample codes: spring-reactive-sample/war.

docs.title: Alternative Bean Registration
docs.text:
In the example above we use ApplicationContext component scanning. For classes that are not part of the component scan, Spring Framework 7 provides a concise registerBean API to programmatically register instances as Spring beans in the ApplicationContext.

public class Application {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();
        PostRepository posts = new PostRepository();
        PostHandler postHandler = new PostHandler(posts);
        Routes routesBean = new Routes(postHandler);

        context.registerBean(PostRepository.class, () -> posts);
        context.registerBean(PostHandler.class, () -> postHandler);
        context.registerBean(Routes.class, () -> routesBean);
        context.registerBean(WebHandler.class, () -> RouterFunctions.toWebHandler(routesBean.routes(), HandlerStrategies.builder().build()));
        context.refresh();

        nettyServer(context).onDispose().block();
    }

    public static DisposableServer nettyServer(ApplicationContext context) {
        HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();
        ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter adapter = new ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
        HttpServer httpServer = HttpServer.create().host("localhost").port(8080);
        return httpServer.handle(adapter).bindNow();
    }

}

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/register-bean.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This section is the entry point for the book. If you are new to reactive programming, start here. If you already know the basics, use it as a quick check of the foundations before moving into the more specialized chapters.

At a high level, this part is about answering three questions:

  • what reactive programming is and why it matters in modern Spring apps
  • how Mono and Flux model asynchronous data streams
  • how to build a first WebFlux application, either manually or with Spring Boot

docs.title: What you will cover
docs.text:
• the Reactive Streams specification and the role of Project Reactor
  • the difference between imperative and reactive code
  • minimal WebFlux applications built with RouterFunction and HandlerFunction
  • the same idea expressed with Spring Boot auto-configuration
  • the repository examples you can run locally while reading

docs.title: Suggested reading path
docs.text:
If you are new to the stack, a sensible order is:

  1. Reactive Streams and Spring WebFlux
  2. Create a WebFlux application from scratch
  3. Create a WebFlux application with Spring Boot

This keeps the learning curve gentle: you understand the reactive model first, then move to the Spring Boot convenience layer.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you start, make sure you have:

  • JDK 21 or newer
  • Apache Maven 3.9+ or Gradle
  • an IDE such as IntelliJ IDEA, VS Code, or Eclipse IDE
  • a basic understanding of Spring and Java web development
  • Docker for the database-backed examples in the repository

docs.title: Running the examples
docs.text:
Every sample in the repository is an independent Maven module. You can run them one by one as you work through the book:

  1. clone the repository
  2. change into the sample directory you want to study, such as vanilla
  3. run it with ./mvnw spring-boot:run for Boot-based samples
  4. use the module's main class or ./mvnw package exec:java for the manual wiring samples

The examples are intentionally small and independent, which makes them useful for experimentation. Once the basics are clear, the later chapters on Reactive Web, Data Operations, and Security show how these ideas work in larger applications.

docs.title: Reactive Streams and Spring WebFlux
docs.text:
Spring WebFlux is the reactive web framework of Spring Framework. It embraces asynchronous, non-blocking I/O and the Reactive Streams specification to build scalable, resource-efficient applications for modern cloud and microservice environments.

This page introduces the Reactive Streams specification and its implementations (Project Reactor, RxJava 3, SmallRye Mutiny, and the Java Flow API), and shows how Spring WebFlux uses them. Everything is demonstrated with short code fragments that you can run with a plain Java main method — no server required.

Audience and scope

This page is for developers new to reactive programming who want to understand the building blocks before writing a WebFlux application. For the application itself, continue to Create a WebFlux application from scratch or Create a WebFlux application with Spring Boot.

docs.title: Reactive Streams: the specification
docs.text:
Reactive Streams — official site reactive-streams.org — is an initiative to provide a standard for asynchronous stream processing with non-blocking backpressure. It encompasses efforts aimed at runtime environments (JVM and JavaScript) as well as network protocols.

The JVM specification is a small set of four interfaces, defined in the org.reactivestreams package:

  • Publisher<T> — produces a potentially unbounded number of sequenced elements, publishing them according to the demand received from its Subscriber(s).
  • Subscriber<T> — receives the signals produced by a Publisher: onSubscribe, then zero or more onNext, and finally onComplete or onError.
  • Subscription — represents the one-to-one lifecycle between a Subscriber and a Publisher. It carries the demand signal (request(long n)) and cancel().
  • Processor<T, R> — a processing stage that is both a Subscriber and a Publisher, obeying the contracts of both.

The interfaces are intentionally tiny:

public interface Publisher<T> {
    void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> s);
}

public interface Subscriber<T> {
    void onSubscribe(Subscription s);
    void onNext(T t);
    void onError(Throwable t);
    void onComplete();
}

public interface Subscription {
    void request(long n);
    void cancel();
}

public interface Processor<T, R> extends Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> {
}

Nothing is delivered until the Subscriber signals demand. This is the essence of backpressure: the consumer controls the flow of data, so a fast producer cannot overwhelm a slow consumer.

docs.title: A minimal Publisher and Subscriber
docs.text:
The following fragment wires a simple Publisher to a Subscriber by hand. It demonstrates the full signal protocol — no reactive library required, only the org.reactivestreams interfaces:

// A Publisher that emits 1, 2, 3 and completes.
Publisher<Integer> publisher = subscriber ->
        subscriber.onSubscribe(new Subscription() {
            private int value = 1;

            @Override
            public void request(long n) {
                for (long i = 0; i < n && value <= 3; i++) {
                    subscriber.onNext(value++);
                }
                if (value > 3) {
                    subscriber.onComplete();
                }
            }

            @Override
            public void cancel() {
            }
        });

publisher.subscribe(new Subscriber<Integer>() {
    @Override
    public void onSubscribe(Subscription s) {
        s.request(3); // signal demand explicitly
    }

    @Override
    public void onNext(Integer item) {
        System.out.println("received: " + item);
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(Throwable t) {
        System.err.println("error: " + t);
    }

    @Override
    public void onComplete() {
        System.out.println("done");
    }
});

Running it prints:

received: 1
received: 2
received: 3
done

In practice you never assemble these interfaces by hand — a reactive library such as Project Reactor does it for you — but the protocol explains what happens behind every Flux and Mono you will use in WebFlux.

Implementations are validated by a conformance test kit (the Reactive Streams TCK), which guarantees the interoperability of any compliant library.

docs.title: Project Reactor
docs.text:
The Reactor project works closely with the Spring team, and Reactor is the reactive library that Spring WebFlux uses by default. Useful entry points: the reference documentation and the API Javadoc for Flux and Mono.

Reactor provides two types that implement org.reactivestreams.Publisher:

  • Flux<T> — a Publisher that emits 0 to N elements, and then completes either successfully or with an error.
  • Mono<T> — a Publisher that emits at most one item via onNext and then terminates with an onComplete signal (a successful Mono, with or without a value), or emits only a single onError signal (a failed Mono).
Concept Reactor Analogy 0..1 result, maybe asynchronous Mono<T> CompletableFuture<T> / Optional<T> 0..N results, streamed Flux<T> Stream<T> / Iterable<T>

docs.title: Creating a Flux and a Mono
docs.text:
Add Reactor to your project (the coordinates are managed by spring-boot-starter-parent):

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.projectreactor</groupId>
    <artifactId>reactor-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

The most common factory methods are static:

Flux<String> flux = Flux.just("a", "b", "c");          // fixed data
Flux<Long> interval = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // ticks every second
Flux<Integer> generated = Flux.range(1, 5);            // 1..5

Mono<String> mono = Mono.just("hello");                // single value
Mono<String> empty = Mono.empty();                     // completes without a value
Mono<String> fromCallable = Mono.fromCallable(() -> expensiveBlockingCall()); // lazily wrap blocking code

docs.title: Subscribing: nothing happens until you subscribe
docs.text:
Reactive types are lazy by default. Assembling operators builds a pipeline; subscribing executes it:

Flux.just("a", "b", "c")
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .subscribe(
        data -> System.out.println("onNext: " + data),
        err -> System.err.println("onError: " + err),
        () -> System.out.println("onComplete")
    );

Output:

onNext: A
onNext: B
onNext: C
onComplete

Common pitfall

A Flux or Mono that is never subscribed emits nothing. Inside a WebFlux @RestController you return the reactive type and Spring subscribes for you; in plain Java code you must call subscribe() (or a blocking method such as block()) yourself.

docs.title: Transforming and combining streams
docs.text:
The operator style reads like the Java Stream API, but the operations are asynchronous:

Flux.just(1, 2, 3)
    .map(i -> i * 10)                 // transform each element
    .filter(i -> i > 10)              // keep elements matching a predicate
    .flatMap(i -> fetchRelated(i))    // 1-to-N async transformation
    .concatWith(Flux.just(100))       // append another stream
    .take(2)                          // only the first 2 elements
    .subscribe(System.out::println);

Combine several streams with zip — this pattern appears throughout the sample repository, for example to pace a data stream with a timer:

Flux.zip(Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)), Flux.just("a", "b", "c"))
    .map(Tuple2::getT2)
    .subscribe(System.out::println);
// prints "a", then "b", then "c" — one per second

docs.title: Backpressure: demand in action
docs.text:
Reactor manages demand for you, and exposes it when you want to control it explicitly:

Flux.range(1, 100)
    .subscribe(new BaseSubscriber<Integer>() {
        @Override
        protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription subscription) {
            request(1); // ask for one item at a time
        }

        @Override
        protected void hookOnNext(Integer value) {
            System.out.println("received: " + value);
            request(1);
        }

        @Override
        protected void hookOnComplete() {
            System.out.println("done");
        }
    });

Operators such as limitRate, buffer, and onBackpressureDrop reshape demand when the default behavior does not fit.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Errors are signals, not exceptions thrown at the caller:

Flux.just("a", "b")
    .map(s -> { if (s.equals("b")) throw new IllegalStateException("boom"); return s; })
    .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just("fallback"))
    .subscribe(System.out::println);
// prints: a, fallback

For tests, reactor-test provides StepVerifier, which verifies the exact sequence of signals:

StepVerifier.create(Flux.just("a", "b"))
    .expectNext("a")
    .expectNext("b")
    .verifyComplete();

See Testing for a full treatment.

docs.title: Other implementations
docs.text: Spring WebFlux is unopinionated about the reactive library. Any Publisher implementation can be a controller return type, and Spring adapts between supported reactive types automatically.

docs.title: RxJava 3
docs.text:
RxJava 3 implements Reactive Streams with Flowable (backpressured), Observable (unbackpressured), Single, Maybe, and Completable. RxJava 2 is end of life and removed from Spring's supported adapters; prefer RxJava 3 for new work.

// io.reactivex.rxjava3:rxjava
Flowable.just("a", "b", "c")
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .subscribe(System.out::println);

See RxJava 3 for the WebFlux integration.

docs.title: SmallRye Mutiny
docs.text:
SmallRye Mutiny is a Reactive Streams implementation from Red Hat, supported by Spring since Framework 5.3.10. Its two core types are Uni<T> (0..1, similar to Mono but accepts null) and Multi<T> (0..N, similar to Flux).

// io.smallrye.reactive:mutiny
Uni.createFrom().item("hello")
    .onItem().transform(String::toUpperCase)
    .subscribe().with(System.out::println);

See SmallRye Mutiny for the WebFlux integration.

docs.title: The JDK Flow API
docs.text:
The JDK ships java.util.concurrent.Flow, which packages the Reactive Streams interfaces inside the JDK and adds a ready-made SubmissionPublisher implementation. The JDK also includes a reactive java.net.http.HttpClient built on the Flow API.

SubmissionPublisher<String> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>();
publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<>() {
    @Override
    public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription subscription) {
        subscription.request(Long.MAX_VALUE);
    }

    @Override
    public void onNext(String item) {
        System.out.println("received: " + item);
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(Throwable throwable) {
    }

    @Override
    public void onComplete() {
        System.out.println("done");
    }
});

publisher.submit("hello");
publisher.close();

Spring adapts between Flow.Publisher and Reactive Streams types — see The JDK Flow API and the runnable java9 sample.

docs.title: Choosing an implementation
docs.text:
Library Core types Backpressure Notes Project Reactor Mono, Flux Yes Default in Spring; richest operator set; reactor-test for verification RxJava 3 Flowable, Observable, Single, Maybe, Completable Flowable only Adapted types supported in WebFlux controllers SmallRye Mutiny Uni, Multi Yes Simple, event-first API; Uni accepts null JDK Flow Flow.Publisher Yes JDK-native; minimal operators; useful for interop

For new Spring projects, start with Project Reactor: it is what Spring Data, Spring Security, Spring Session, and the WebFlux server internals are built on.

docs.title: How Spring WebFlux uses the reactive stack
docs.text:
Spring WebFlux builds on Reactive Streams and Project Reactor by default, but stays unopinionated about the reactive runtime. The key integration points:

  • Reactive return types. Controller methods and handler functions may return Mono<T>, Flux<T>, CompletableFuture<T>, or any org.reactivestreams.Publisher<T>. Spring adapts between supported reactive types automatically.
  • Two programming models. Annotated controllers (@RestController with @GetMapping, @PostMapping, and friends) or functional handlers (RouterFunction + HandlerFunction) — see the Reactive Web chapter.
  • A reactive HTTP client. WebClient performs non-blocking HTTP requests and integrates with Reactor and other reactive types — see WebClient.
  • Server runtimes. Reactor Netty is the default server for Spring Boot's WebFlux starter; Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow are also supported — see the bootstrapping options in Create a WebFlux application from scratch.
  • The wider ecosystem. Spring Data (R2DBC, reactive repositories), Spring Security (ServerHttpSecurity, reactive user details), and Spring Session (reactive WebSession storage) all accept and return Reactive Streams types — the following chapters cover each of them.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Specification

  • Reactive Streams specification — the JVM specification, TCK, and examples
  • reactive-streams.org — the official site
  • org.reactivestreams Javadoc — Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription, Processor

Projects

  • Project Reactor — reference docs, API Javadoc, Flux, Mono
  • RxJava 3 — 3.x Javadoc
  • SmallRye Mutiny — Javadoc
  • Reactor Netty — the default WebFlux server runtime
  • Spring WebFlux reference — the official framework documentation

JDK

  • java.util.concurrent.Flow and SubmissionPublisher
  • java.net.http.HttpClient — the JDK's reactive HTTP client

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Create a WebFlux application from scratch — the low-level building blocks (HttpHandler, WebHttpHandlerBuilder, Reactor Netty).
  • Create a WebFlux application with Spring Boot — the fast path with starters and auto-configuration.
  • An introduction to Reactive Web — the WebHandler and HttpHandler architecture of WebFlux.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Reactive code is not tested in the same way as blocking code. Instead of asserting one final value, you typically verify a sequence of events: what was emitted, in what order, whether the stream completed, and whether an error appeared at the right time.

This is why the reactive stack comes with a dedicated testing toolkit. The examples in this repository use it throughout the stack, from repository tests to full web integration tests.

docs.title: A friendly reading path
docs.text:
For reactive testing, the easiest way to learn is to move from simple web assertions to the more realistic integration scenarios:

  • start with Testing Web Components to learn how to test controllers, filters, and routing with WebTestClient
  • move to Testing Spring Security when you want to verify protected endpoints and request-level authorization
  • continue with Data Operations with Testcontainers for realistic database-backed tests with real containers
  • then read Spring Test Context and Slices to understand the broader testing support available in Spring itself
  • finish with Testing in Kotlin for coroutine-aware and Kotlin-native testing patterns

This order keeps the learning curve gentle: you first validate the web layer in isolation, then add security and real infrastructure, and finally explore the Kotlin-specific testing tools.

docs.title: StepVerifier: verify a Publisher
docs.text:
StepVerifier is the foundation of reactive testing. It subscribes to a Publisher and asserts the exact sequence of signals — the values produced, the completion signal, and any error.

StepVerifier.create(posts.findAll())
    .consumeNextWith(p -> assertEquals("post one", p.getTitle()))
    .consumeNextWith(p -> assertEquals("post two", p.getTitle()))
    .expectComplete()
    .verify();

This pattern is used all over the repository:

postClient.allPosts()
        .as(StepVerifier::create)
        .expectNextCount(2)
        .verifyComplete();

counter.getInvocationCount()
        .as(StepVerifier::create)
        .consumeNextWith(count -> assertThat(count).isGreaterThan(0))
        .thenCancel()
        .verify();

posts.findByTitleLike("one")
    .as(StepVerifier::create)
    .consumeNextWith(p -> assertEquals("Post one", p.getTitle()))
    .verifyComplete();

The most useful methods are:

  • expectNext(...) / expectNextCount(...) — assert values or counts
  • consumeNextWith(...) — run a custom assertion against each emitted element
  • expectError(...) / verifyComplete() — validate completion or failure behavior
  • thenCancel() — cancel a subscription mid-stream
  • as(StepVerifier::create) — adapt any existing Mono or Flux chain for verification

StepVerifier is the workhorse for repository tests in the Data Operations chapter and for HTTP client tests in Testing Web Components. The next page moves one level up: testing the web layer itself.

docs.title: Testing in Kotlin
docs.text:
Kotlin tests keep the same layered structure as the Java ones — StepVerifier, WebTestClient, Testcontainers — with a Kotlin-native toolkit on top: Kotest assertion matchers, MockK for suspending functions, Spring MockK for bean overrides, and kotlinx-coroutines-test for coroutine lifecycles.

The samples referenced here are kotlin-co and boot-kotlin-co in this repository.

docs.title: Test dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlinx</groupId>
    <artifactId>kotlinx-coroutines-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.kotest</groupId>
    <artifactId>kotest-assertions-core-jvm</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.mockk</groupId>
    <artifactId>mockk-jvm</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.ninja-squad</groupId>
    <artifactId>springmockk</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

docs.title: MockK: mocking suspending functions
docs.text:
MockK mirrors the Mockito vocabulary for coroutines: coEvery stubs a suspend call, coVerify asserts it, and coEvery { ... } throws ... drives the error paths:

coEvery { postRepository.findByTitleContains(any()) } returns
        flowOf(Post(id = 1, title = "test title", content = "test content"))

coEvery { postRepository.findById(any()) } throws PostNotFoundException(id)

coVerify(exactly = 0) { postRepository.findByTitleContains(any()) }

Flow-returning methods are stubbed with flowOf(...), and clearAllMocks() resets between tests.

docs.title: Spring MockK: @MockkBean and @MockkSpyBean
docs.text:
Spring MockK is the Kotlines counterpart of @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean (see Testing Web Components):

  • @MockkBean — replace a bean with a MockK mock; stub it with coEvery { ... } returns ...
  • @MockkSpyBean — wrap the real bean in a spy: real behavior by default, coEvery overrides selected calls

The boot-kotlin-co sample uses @MockkBean inside a @WebFluxTest slice:

@WebFluxTest(controllers = [PostController::class])
class PostControllerTests {

    @Autowired
    private lateinit var client: WebTestClient

    @MockkBean
    private lateinit var posts: PostRepository

    @Test
    fun `get all posts`() = runTest {
        coEvery { posts.findAll() } returns
                flowOf(
                    Post(id = "1", title = "post one", content = "content of post one"),
                    Post(id = "2", title = "post two", content = "content of two")
                )
        client.get()
            .uri("/posts")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk
            .expectBody().jsonPath("$.size()").isEqualTo(2)

        coVerify(exactly = 1) { posts.findAll() }
    }

    @Test
    fun `get post by id when not found`() = runTest {
        val id = UUID.randomUUID().toString()
        coEvery { posts.findById(any()) } returns null

        client.get()
            .uri("/posts/$id")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound

        coVerify(exactly = 1) { posts.findById(any()) }
    }
}

docs.title: kotlinx-coroutines-test: runTest
docs.text:
Every test that touches coroutine code runs under runTest { } — it skips real delays and completes when the coroutine tree settles, even for the WebTestClient exchange calls above. The repository tests use the same shape:

@Test
fun `test save and query`() = runTest {
    val saved = template.insert(Post(title = "test", content = "content of test")).awaitSingle()
    saved.id shouldNotBe null

    val postById = posts.findById(saved.id!!)
    postById shouldNotBe null
    postById!!.title shouldBe "test"
}

The awaitSingle() extension (from kotlinx.coroutines.reactor) bridges the reactive Mono into the coroutine; awaitSingleOrNull(), awaitFirst(), and awaitToList() cover the other shapes — see the transaction extensions in Coroutines.

docs.title: Kotest assertions
docs.text:
Kotest contributes the infix assertion matchers used across the Kotlin samples — shouldBe, shouldNotBe, shouldContain, and friends:

import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe
import io.kotest.matchers.shouldNotBe

posts shouldNotBe null
postById!!.title shouldBe "test"

Kotest matchers compose with everything above — inside runTest, inside StepVerifier.consumeNextWith, or alongside AssertJ in mixed codebases. They work on plain JUnit 5 tests (as the samples do) or inside Kotest's own spec styles if you prefer a full Kotest test framework.

docs.title: A complete plain Spring test
docs.text:
The kotlin-co sample assembles the pieces — SpringJUnitConfig, a manually registered MockK bean, bindToController, and Kotest matchers — without Boot:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = [TestConfig::class])
class PostControllerTest {

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    @ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = [PostController::class])
    internal class TestConfig {

        @Bean
        @Primary
        fun mockPostRepository(): PostRepository = mockk<PostRepository>()
    }

    @Autowired
    lateinit var posts: PostRepository

    lateinit var client: WebTestClient

    @BeforeEach
    fun setup() {
        client = WebTestClient.bindToController(PostController(posts))
            .configureClient()
            .build()
    }

    @AfterEach
    fun teardown() {
        clearAllMocks()
    }

    @Test
    fun `get post by id`() = runTest {
        val id = UUID.randomUUID().toString()
        coEvery { posts.findById(any()) } returns
                Post(id = id, title = "test title", content = "content of test title")

        client.get().uri("/posts/$id")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk
            .expectBody().jsonPath("$.title").isEqualTo("test title")
    }
}

When Boot's bean-override machinery is available, prefer @MockkBean over the manual @Primary mock bean — the manual registration shown here is what makes the same test work in plain Spring modules.

docs.title: Testing Spring Security
docs.text:
Secured endpoints change what a web-layer test means: an unauthenticated request should get 401, a wrong-role request 403, and a valid one should pass. Spring Security's test support (spring-security-test, shipped as spring-boot-starter-security-test in Boot) provides the tools — mock users, JWT/OIDC authentication, CSRF handling, and ways to skip the security layer entirely.

The samples referenced here are security, security-method, session-header, and boot-exception-handler.

docs.title: Add the test dependency
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

For a plain Spring (non-Boot) application, use org.springframework.security:spring-security-test instead.

docs.title: Wire security into WebTestClient
docs.text:
A WebTestClient bound to an application context does not apply the security filters by default. Activate them with the springSecurity() configurer — this installs the WebFilterChainProxy into the mock environment, exactly as at runtime:

@BeforeEach
public void setup() {
    this.rest = WebTestClient
            .bindToApplicationContext(this.context)
            .apply(springSecurity())
            //.apply(csrf())
            .configureClient()
            .build();
}

From this point, the test client behaves like a real browser: the HTTP Basic challenge, form login redirect, and CSRF protection all apply, and the following sections authenticate against them.

docs.title: HTTP Basic credentials
docs.text:
The simplest approach against an HTTP Basic-protected API — send real credentials as headers, which exercises the whole authentication path including the ReactiveUserDetailsService:

@Test
public void savingPostsWhenInvalidCredentialsThenUnauthorized() {
    this.rest
            .post()
            .uri("/posts")
            .body(BodyInserters.fromValue(Post.builder().title("title test").content("content test").build()))
            .headers(invalidCredentials())
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().is4xxClientError();
}

private Consumer<HttpHeaders> invalidCredentials() {
    return httpHeaders -> httpHeaders.setBasicAuth("user", "INVALID");
}

The session-header sample uses the same pattern with the Authorization header built explicitly.

docs.title: mutateWith(mockUser())
docs.text:
To bypass authentication and inject a principal directly, use SecurityMockServerConfigurers.mockUser() — it authenticates the request as an in-memory user without touching the ReactiveUserDetailsService:

@Test
public void deletingPostsWhenUserCredentialsThenForbidden_mutateWith() {
    this.rest
            .mutateWith(mockUser().password("password"))
            .delete()
            .uri("/posts/1")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().is4xxClientError();
}

mockUser() defaults to username "user" with role USER; customize with .username(...), .roles(...), .authorities(...), or pass a prepared UserDetails.

docs.title: @WithMockUser
docs.text:
The annotation-driven variant sets the authentication for a whole test class or a single method:

@SpringBootTest(classes = {DemoApplication.class, TestcontainersConfiguration.class})
@WithMockUser
public class DemoApplicationTests {
    // every test in this class runs as the default mock user
}

@Test
@WithMockUser()
public void deletingPostsWhenUserCredentialsThenForbidden_withMockUserAnnotation() {
    this.rest
            .delete()
            .uri("/posts/1")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().is4xxClientError();
}

@WithMockUser(username = "admin", roles = "ADMIN") elevates the principal; @WithAnonymousUser and @WithSecurityContext cover the remaining cases.

docs.title: Testing method-level security
docs.text:
@PreAuthorize rules are exercised by driving the request with a user of the wrong role and asserting 403 — the security-method sample protects delete with hasRole('ADMIN') and verifies a plain USER cannot reach it, both with mutateWith and with @WithMockUser:

@Test
public void deletingPostsWhenUserCredentialsThenForbidden_mutateWith() {
    this.rest
            .mutateWith(mockUser().password("password"))   // role USER
            .delete()
            .uri("/posts/1")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().is4xxClientError();            // 403, not 401
}

The distinction matters: 401 means unauthenticated, 403 means authenticated but not authorized — mockUser() should always produce the latter on an authorization failure.

docs.title: Mocking JWTs and OIDC
docs.text:
For resource servers validating JWTs or OIDC tokens, the mutators fabricate a token without a real issuer:

import static org.springframework.security.test.web.reactive.server.SecurityMockServerConfigurers.mockJwt;

@Test
public void readWithJwtScope() {
    this.rest
            .mutateWith(mockJwt().jwt(jwt -> jwt
                    .subject("test-subject")
                    .claim("scope", "read")))
            .get()
            .uri("/posts")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk();
}

mockJwt() authenticates as a JwtAuthenticationToken; control the token with the Jwt.Builder consumer (subject, claim, audience, expiresAt, ...) or build a complete Jwt and pass it to mockJwt(jwt). The OIDC counterpart is mockOidcLogin() — it authenticates as an OidcUser with a configurable ID token and user-info claims:

import static org.springframework.security.test.web.reactive.server.SecurityMockServerConfigurers.mockOidcLogin;

this.rest
        .mutateWith(mockOidcLogin().idToken(token -> token.subject("alice")))
        .get()
        .uri("/profile")
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isOk();

Both mutators need the JOSE machinery on the test classpath — add org.springframework.security:spring-security-oauth2-jose with test scope when the application itself is not a resource server.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
CSRF protection rejects mutating requests (POST/PUT/DELETE) that lack the token. Tests that authenticate real users should add the CSRF configurator — either once on the client builder or per request:

// once for all requests
this.rest = WebTestClient.bindToApplicationContext(this.context)
        .apply(springSecurity())
        .apply(csrf())
        .configureClient()
        .build();

// or per request
this.rest.mutateWith(csrf()).post().uri("/posts")...

When tests authenticate with mockUser()/mockJwt() the CSRF filter is already satisfied — you need the explicit token mainly for tests that exercise real authentication (Basic, form login).

docs.title: Skipping security
docs.text: Some web-layer tests should not deal with security at all. Two verified ways to skip it:

docs.title: Exclude the security auto-configuration
docs.text:
In a Boot test, remove the security configuration from the slice — the Boot 4 reactive auto-configuration classes live in org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure:

@WebFluxTest(controllers = PostController.class, excludeAutoConfiguration = {
        org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.web.reactive.ReactiveWebSecurityAutoConfiguration.class,
        org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.SecurityAutoConfiguration.class,
        org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.ReactiveUserDetailsServiceAutoConfiguration.class
})
class PostControllerWithoutSecurityTest {
    // no security filters in this context — every request passes through
}

The property form works for @SpringBootTest too:

spring.autoconfigure.exclude=\
  org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.web.reactive.ReactiveWebSecurityAutoConfiguration,\
  org.springframework.boot.security.autoconfigure.SecurityAutoConfiguration

docs.title: Override the filter chain with a permissive one
docs.text:
Alternatively, keep the auto-configuration and supply a SecurityWebFilterChain bean that permits everything — a user-declared chain always replaces the Boot default:

@TestConfiguration
static class PermitAllSecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain permitAll(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
        return http
                .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)
                .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange.anyExchange().permitAll())
                .build();
    }
}

@WebFluxTest(controllers = PostController.class)
@Import(PermitAllSecurityConfig.class)
class PostControllerOpenTest {
}

Prefer mock users for security tests

Excluding security verifies that your controllers work — it does not verify your security rules. Use the exclusion for tests focused on other concerns, and the mockUser()/mockJwt() mutators from the sections above when the rules themselves are under test.

docs.title: Spring Test Context and Slices
docs.text: Spring Test provides a spectrum of test contexts, from a targeted slice to the full application. This page maps the spectrum as the samples use it: SpringJUnitConfig for plain Spring modules, @SpringBootTest for full Boot contexts, and the Boot test slices that load only what a layer needs.

docs.title: SpringJUnitConfig: plain Spring without Boot
docs.text:
Non-Boot samples test with SpringJUnitConfig — the JUnit 5 extension that builds an ApplicationContext from the given configuration classes without any Boot machinery:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
@ActiveProfiles("test")   // disables the Netty @Profile("default") server bean
public class ApplicationTests {

    @Autowired
    ApplicationContext context;

    WebTestClient rest;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup() {
        this.rest = WebTestClient
                .bindToApplicationContext(this.context)
                .configureClient()
                .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk() {
        this.rest
                .get()
                .uri("/posts")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}

This pattern runs across the plain Spring samples — the integration sample's ApplicationTests and PostControllerTest show it with bindToApplicationContext and the narrower bindToController:

this.rest = WebTestClient.bindToController(this.ctrl)
        .configureClient()
        .build();

docs.title: SpringBootTest: the full context
docs.text:
@SpringBootTest boots the complete application. With WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT it starts the real server on a free port, and @AutoConfigureWebTestClient injects a client ready to talk to it:

@AutoConfigureWebTestClient
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient client;

    @Test
    public void getAllPosts() {
        client.get().uri("/posts")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk()
                .expectBody().jsonPath("$.size()").isEqualTo(2);
    }
}

Combine it with the Testcontainers styles from Data Operations with Testcontainers (@ServiceConnection or @DynamicPropertySource) and the full stack — web layer, data layer, real database — runs in one test.

docs.title: Integration tests over a real server
docs.text:
Some contracts only exist over the wire. The integration sample binds its own Reactor Netty server bean and a server-bound WebTestClient:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    HttpServer httpServer;

    private DisposableServer disposableServer;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup() {
        this.disposableServer = this.httpServer.bindNow();
        this.client = WebTestClient
                .bindToServer()
                .responseTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(5000))
                .baseUrl("http://localhost:" + this.port)
                .build();
    }

    @AfterEach
    public void tearDown() {
        this.disposableServer.disposeNow();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk_viaIntegration() {
        this.client
                .get()
                .uri("/all")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}

This is the shape to use for SSE streams, WebSocket handshakes, and cookie/header contracts — see session-header for a worked example.

docs.title: Test slices
docs.text:
Boot's test slices load only the auto-configuration a layer needs, keeping tests fast and focused:

Slice Loads Typical use @WebFluxTest WebFlux infrastructure for the given controllers Controller and filter tests with mocked dependencies — see Testing Web Components @JsonTest JSON serializers/deserializers only (Jackson, and @JsonTester injection) Round-trip serialization assertions without any web layer @DataMongoTest Spring Data Mongo repositories and ReactiveMongoTemplate Repository tests against a real Mongo — pair with Testcontainers @DataR2dbcTest Spring Data R2DBC repositories, DatabaseClient R2DBC repository tests @DataNeo4jTest Spring Data Neo4j repositories Neo4j repository tests — see Neo4j — Testing

A @DataMongoTest repository test from the boot-data-mongo sample — the slice plus a @ServiceConnection container gives a complete database test with no web layer loaded:

@DataMongoTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
@ActiveProfiles("test")
public class PostRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    ReactiveMongoTemplate reactiveMongoTemplate;

    @Autowired
    PostRepository postRepository;
}

Slices and transactions

Reactive slices are not transactional by default. When a slice (for example @DataNeo4jTest) applies test-managed transactions that the reactive stack cannot drive, add @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NEVER) — the Neo4j — Testing page walks through the details.

A @JsonTest follows the same recipe — the slice auto-configures the JSON beans and injects a tester:

@JsonTest
class PostJsonTest {

    @Autowired
    JacksonTester<Post> json;

    @Test
    void serialize() throws Exception {
        var post = new Post(UUID.randomUUID(), "test title", "content");
        assertThat(json.write(post)).extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.title").isEqualTo("test title");
    }
}

The slices pair naturally with the bean-override annotations: @WebFluxTest + @MockitoBean for the web layer, data slices + Testcontainers for the persistence layer.

docs.title: Data Operations with Testcontainers
docs.text:
Repository tests need a real database. Testcontainers starts the store in a Docker container for the duration of the test and tears it down afterwards. The samples use two wiring styles — one for plain Spring applications and one for Spring Boot — plus Boot's automatic @ServiceConnection variant.

Tip

Pair Testcontainers with StepVerifier (see Testing) to assert the reactive query results.

docs.title: Plain Spring: ApplicationContextInitializer
docs.text:
The non-Boot samples (cache, the r2dbc-* modules) implement an ApplicationContextInitializer that starts the container, maps its properties into the environment, and stops it when the context closes:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class ContainersConfiguration implements ApplicationContextInitializer<ConfigurableApplicationContext> {

    private static final PostgreSQLContainer POSTGRES = new PostgreSQLContainer(
            DockerImageName.parse("postgres:18.4-alpine"))
            .withCopyFileToContainer(
                    MountableFile.forClasspathResource("init.sql"),
                    "/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql");

    @Override
    public void initialize(ConfigurableApplicationContext context) {
        if (!POSTGRES.isRunning()) {
            POSTGRES.start();
        }
        context.addApplicationListener((ContextClosedEvent event) -> POSTGRES.stop());
        TestPropertyValues.of(
                "r2dbc.host=" + POSTGRES.getHost(),
                "r2dbc.port=" + POSTGRES.getFirstMappedPort(),
                "r2dbc.username=" + POSTGRES.getUsername(),
                "r2dbc.password=" + POSTGRES.getPassword(),
                "r2dbc.database=" + POSTGRES.getDatabaseName()
        ).applyTo(context.getEnvironment());
    }
}

The initializer is applied through @ContextConfiguration, so it is reusable across test classes:

@ContextConfiguration(initializers = { ContainersConfiguration.class })
@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = { PostRepositoryTest.TestConfig.class })
public class PostRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    PostRepository posts;

    @Test
    public void testSaveAll() {
        var post = posts.save(Post.of("test", "content")).block();
        assertThat(posts.findById(post.id()).block()).isNotNull();
    }
}

Because the properties use the application's own keys (r2dbc.* in the samples), no container library knowledge leaks into the configuration classes — see the cache sample for the complete pattern, and the r2dbc-connection-factories tests for raw-driver variants.

docs.title: Spring Boot with @DynamicPropertySource
docs.text:
For Boot applications, the @Testcontainers + @Container + @DynamicPropertySource combination starts the container with the JUnit lifecycle and maps its runtime values into arbitrary property keys. From the boot-data-mongo-template sample:

@DataMongoTest
@Import({PostRepository.class, TestcontainersConfiguration.class})
public class PostRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    static MongoDBContainer mongoDBContainer = new MongoDBContainer(DockerImageName.parse("mongo:latest"));

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void mongoProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.data.mongodb.uri", mongoDBContainer::getReplicaSetUrl);
    }

    @Autowired
    ReactiveMongoTemplate reactiveMongoTemplate;

    @Autowired
    PostRepository postRepository;
}

Notes:

  • @Testcontainers (class level) enables the JUnit extension; a static @Container field starts before all tests and stops after them.
  • The @DynamicPropertySource method receives a DynamicPropertyRegistry — register the connection properties as suppliers, resolved lazily once the container is up.
  • Any property key works here: spring.data.mongodb.uri, spring.r2dbc.url, spring.neo4j.uri, or custom keys.

docs.title: Spring Boot with @ServiceConnection
docs.text:
Boot 3.1+ removes even the property mapping: a container bean annotated with @ServiceConnection contributes the connection properties automatically — Boot recognizes the container type and registers the right properties. From the boot-data-mongo sample:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    MongoDBContainer mongoDbContainer() {
        return new MongoDBContainer(DockerImageName.parse("mongo:latest"));
    }
}

@DataMongoTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
@ActiveProfiles("test")
public class PostRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    ReactiveMongoTemplate reactiveMongoTemplate;

    @Autowired
    PostRepository postRepository;
}

No @DynamicPropertySource, no property names — Boot wires spring.data.mongodb.uri (or spring.r2dbc.url for a PostgreSQLContainer, spring.neo4j.uri for a Neo4jContainer, and so on) from the container itself. The same pattern appears with CassandraContainer, CouchbaseContainer, ElasticsearchContainer, and Neo4jContainer across the Boot data samples — see the Data Operations chapter pages for each store's snippet.

docs.title: Choosing a style
docs.text: Style Use when ApplicationContextInitializer + TestPropertyValues Plain Spring (no Boot) tests; reusable initializer shared by many test classes @Testcontainers + @DynamicPropertySource Boot tests needing explicit control of property keys or container options @ServiceConnection Boot tests with a supported container type — the least code, zero property names

docs.title: Testing Web Components
docs.text:
The web layer is tested with WebTestClient, which mirrors the WebClient API and adds response assertions. This page covers testing annotated controllers, exception handling, RouterFunctions, and filters — with the dependencies mocked or spied through Spring's bean overriding annotations.

The tests run on JUnit 5 with Mockito for stubbing; for the Kotlin equivalents see Testing in Kotlin.

docs.title: A controller test with a mocked dependency
docs.text:
@WebFluxTest(controllers = ...) loads only the web configuration for the given controller — no database, no full context. The controller's dependencies are replaced with @MockitoBean (from org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito), and Mockito stubs their publisher-returning methods:

@WebFluxTest(controllers = PostController.class)
public class PostControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient client;

    @MockitoBean
    PostRepository posts;

    @Test
    public void getAllPosts() {
        when(this.posts.findAll()).thenReturn(Flux.just(
                Post.builder().id(UUID.randomUUID()).title("post one").content("content of post one").build(),
                Post.builder().id(UUID.randomUUID()).title("post two").content("content of post two").build()
        ));
        client.get().uri("/posts")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk()
                .expectBody().jsonPath("$.size()").isEqualTo(2);

        verify(this.posts, times(1)).findAll();
        verifyNoMoreInteractions(this.posts);
    }
}

Notes:

  • @WebFluxTest auto-configures a WebTestClient bound to the mock web environment — inject it with @Autowired.
  • @MockitoBean replaces the bean in the context with a Mockito mock; when(...)/given(...) stub the reactive methods to return Flux.just(...) or Mono.just(...).
  • The BDD style works too: given(this.posts.findAll()).willReturn(Flux.just(post1, post2)).

Boot 3 vs Boot 4

Spring Boot 3 used @MockBean (deprecated and removed in Boot 4); Spring Framework 6.2+ / Boot 4 use @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean from org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.

docs.title: Mocks and spies
docs.text:
• @MockitoBean — replace a bean entirely with a mock. Unstubbed publisher-returning methods return empty publishers.
  • @MockitoSpyBean — wrap the real bean in a spy: real methods run unless explicitly stubbed, and interactions are still verifiable. Use it when the collaborator's real behavior matters and you only need to observe or tweak a few calls:
@MockitoSpyBean
PostRepository posts;

Both annotations live in the same package as @MockitoBean and work in any Spring test — slices, @SpringBootTest, or plain SpringJUnitConfig tests.

docs.title: Exception handling and status codes
docs.text:
Exception handlers are exercised by driving the client into the error path and asserting the mapped status — here a not-found domain exception maps to 404 through the controller's @ExceptionHandler:

@Test
fun `get post that not found`() = runTest {
    val id = 1L
    coEvery { postRepository.findById(any()) } throws PostNotFoundException(id)

    client.get().uri("/$id")
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isNotFound

    coVerify(exactly = 1) { postRepository.findById(any()) }
}

The Java pattern is identical with Mockito: stub the dependency to return Mono.error(new PostNotFoundException(id)), then expectStatus().isNotFound(). Assert the body of RFC 9457 ProblemDetail responses with expectBody(ProblemDetail.class) when a handler returns one.

docs.title: Testing RouterFunctions
docs.text:
Functional routes are tested by binding the client to the RouterFunction bean. From the boot-start-routes sample:

@AutoConfigureWebTestClient
@SpringBootTest
// create a `WebTestClient` with essential options from application context automatically,
// it works on both mock env or a real server.
public class ApplicationTest {

    @Autowired
    RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routerFunction;

    @MockitoBean
    PostRepository posts;

    WebTestClient client;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
