        this.client = WebTestClient.bindToRouterFunction(this.routerFunction)
                .configureClient()
                .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPosts() {
        // stub the repository, call client.get().uri("/posts")...
    }
}

bindToRouterFunction handles a single RouterFunction; bindToApplicationContext(context) loads the full handler infrastructure (filters, exception handlers) without a socket, and bindToWebHandler(...) sits between the two.

docs.title: Testing filters
docs.text:
Filters are verified by importing them into a @WebFluxTest slice and asserting the outcome with and without the triggering condition — for example, a security-check filter that requires a user query parameter:

@WebFluxTest(controllers = HelloController.class)
class WebFilterTests {

    @TestConfiguration
    @Import(value = SecurityWebFilter.class)
    class TestConfig

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient client;

    @Test
    void `authentication failed with no user params`() = runTest {
        client.get().uri("/hello")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isUnauthorized
    }

    @Test
    void `authentication passed with user params`() = runTest {
        client.get().uri("/hello?user=Hantsy")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk
    }
}

A Java WebFilter test follows the same shape: @Import the filter, request a route the filter protects, assert 401 without the precondition and 200 with it.

docs.title: Against a running server
docs.text: Slice tests exercise the request-handling stack only. When a test needs the real HTTP contract — SSE, WebSocket, cookies — bind the client to a live server instead; see Spring Test Context and Slices.

docs.title: Mocking a target HTTP API with WireMock
docs.text:
The mirror image of the tests above: when your application is the client, stub the remote API with WireMock and assert the reactive call chain. The client sample tests its PostClient wrapper with @WireMockTest(httpPort = 8080) — the same port the client targets — and StepVerifier for the assertions:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = { ClientConfig.class, Jackson2ObjectMapperConfig.class })
@WireMockTest(httpPort = 8080)
public class PostClientTest {

    @Autowired
    PostClient postClient;

    @SneakyThrows
    @Test
    public void testGetAllPosts() {
        var data = List.of(
                new Post(UUID.randomUUID(), "title1", "content1", Status.DRAFT, LocalDateTime.now()),
                new Post(UUID.randomUUID(), "title2", "content2", Status.PUBLISHED, LocalDateTime.now())
        );
        stubFor(get("/posts")
                .willReturn(aResponse()
                        .withHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
                        .withResponseBody(Body.fromJsonBytes(Json.toByteArray(data)))));

        postClient.allPosts()
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .expectNextCount(2)
                .verifyComplete();

        verify(getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/posts"))
                .withHeader("Accept", equalTo("application/json")));
    }

    @SneakyThrows
    @Test
    public void testCreatePost() {
        var id = UUID.randomUUID();
        var data = new Post(null, "title1", "content1", Status.DRAFT, null);

        stubFor(post("/posts")
                .willReturn(aResponse()
                        .withHeader("Location", "/posts/" + id)
                        .withStatus(201)));

        postClient.save(data)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(entity -> {
                    assertThat(entity.getHeaders().getLocation().toString()).isEqualTo("/posts/" + id);
                    assertThat(entity.getStatusCode().value()).isEqualTo(201);
                })
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

Reading the wiring:

  • @WireMockTest(httpPort = 8080) starts WireMock on the port the WebClient under test points at — no code changes between test and production.
  • stubFor(...) registers the expected request and response; verify(...) asserts the client actually sent the expected headers and payload.
  • The reactive result is asserted with .as(StepVerifier::create) — see Testing for the signal-level assertions.

The dependency is com.github.tomakehurst:wiremock-standalone (test scope). You can explore the complete codes in the client sample's PostClientTest.

docs.title: API Versioning
docs.text:
API versioning is usually introduced only when an application has already grown enough to need contract changes without breaking older clients. Spring Framework 7 makes this easier by adding built-in versioning support on both the server and the client side.

A version can be carried in:

  • a URI path segment
  • a request parameter
  • an HTTP header
  • a media type parameter

The server can then route requests using a version attribute on the mapping annotations. This page looks at the WebFlux flavor of the feature.

The examples referenced here live in this repository: api-versioning (manual configuration) and boot-api-versioning (Spring Boot auto-configuration and properties).

docs.title: Server-side configuration
docs.text:
Implement WebFluxConfigurer and override configureApiVersioning to declare where the version is read from and which versions the service supports:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
public class WebConfig implements WebFluxConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void configureApiVersioning(ApiVersionConfigurer configurer) {
        configurer
                //.usePathSegment(0)
                .useRequestHeader("X-API-Version")
                //.useRequestParam("version")

                .setDefaultVersion("1.0")
                // When a defaultVersion is also set, this is automatically set to false.
                // .setVersionRequired(true)

                // default is SemanticApiVersionParser
                //.setVersionParser(new SemanticApiVersionParser())

                // set detectSupportedVersions(false) when adding supported versions
                .detectSupportedVersions(false)
                .addSupportedVersions("1.0", "1.1", "2.0");
    }
}

The version resolution strategies are mutually exclusive:

  • usePathSegment(0) — read the version from a URI path segment, such as /api/v1/resource
  • useRequestHeader("X-API-Version") — read it from an HTTP header, such as X-API-Version: 1
  • useRequestParam("version") — read it from a query parameter, such as /api/resource?version=1
  • useMediaTypeParameter(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON, "version") — read it from the media type, such as application/json;version=1

SemanticApiVersionParser is the default parser, and setDefaultVersion("1.0") handles requests that do not specify a version at all.

docs.title: Versioned routes
docs.text:
Mapping annotations accept a version attribute. Requests without a version fall through to the default route, while versioned requests resolve to the matching method.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/hello")
public class GreetingController {

    @GetMapping
    public String helloDefault() {
        return "Hello v1.0 (default)";
    }

    @GetMapping(version = "1.1")
    public String helloV1_1() {
        return "Hello v1.1";
    }

    @GetMapping(version = "2.0")
    public String helloV2_0() {
        return "Hello v2.0";
    }
}

In a Spring Boot 4 WebFlux application, the same configuration can be expressed entirely with spring.webflux.apiversion.* properties, as the boot-api-versioning example shows:

spring.webflux.apiversion.use.header=X-API-Version
spring.webflux.apiversion.supported=1.0,1.1,2.0
spring.webflux.apiversion.detect-supported=false
spring.webflux.apiversion.default=1.0

The WebMVC counterpart uses spring.mvc.apiversion.* properties.

docs.title: Client-side versioning with WebClient
docs.text:
WebClient participates in the same strategy via ApiVersionInserter, and defaultApiVersion gives clients a fallback when a specific version is not requested:

this.client = WebClient.builder()
        .baseUrl("http://localhost:" + this.port)
        .defaultApiVersion("1.0")
        .apiVersionInserter(ApiVersionInserter.builder()
                .useHeader("X-API-Version")
                //.usePathSegment(0)
                //.useQueryParam("version")
                //.withVersionFormatter(ApiVersionFormatter)
                .build())
        .build();

The client-side strategies mirror the server side: useHeader, usePathSegment, useQueryParam, or custom formatting with withVersionFormatter. The server and client must agree on the same versioning mechanism.

Per-request versions override the default:

this.client.get().uri("/hello")
        .apiVersion("1.1")
        .retrieve()
        .bodyToMono(String.class);

A full integration test can drive all versions against the running server:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    HttpServer httpServer;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup() {
        this.disposableServer = this.httpServer.bindNow(Duration.ofMillis(5_000));
        this.client = WebClient.builder()
                .baseUrl("http://localhost:" + this.port)
                .defaultApiVersion("1.0")
                .apiVersionInserter(ApiVersionInserter.builder()
                        .useHeader("X-API-Version")
                        .build())
                .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void testHello1_1() {
        this.client.get().uri("/hello")
                .apiVersion("1.1")
                .retrieve()
                .bodyToMono(String.class)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .expectNext("Hello v1.1")
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

docs.title: Testing with WebTestClient
docs.text:
WebTestClient supports the same contract. In a @WebFluxTest slice, customize the client builder with the API versioning settings used by the app:

@WebFluxTest(controllers = GreetingController.class)
public class GreetingControllerTest {

    @TestConfiguration
    static class TestConfig {

        @Bean
        WebTestClientBuilderCustomizer testClientBuilderCustomizer() {
            return builder -> builder.defaultApiVersion("1.0")
                    .apiVersionInserter(ApiVersionInserter.useHeader("X-API-Version"))
                    .build();
        }
    }

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient webTestClient;

    @Test
    void testHello1_1() {
        this.webTestClient.get().uri("/hello")
                .apiVersion("1.1")
                .exchange()
                .expectBody(String.class).isEqualTo("Hello v1.1");
    }
}

For the complete code, see api-versioning and boot-api-versioning in this repo.

docs.title: WebClient and Reactive HTTP Clients
docs.text:
If RestTemplate was the usual client in the Servlet era, WebClient is the equivalent in the reactive stack. It is non-blocking, composable, and integrates naturally with Reactor streams.

In practice, you use WebClient for:

  • calling other HTTP services from a reactive app
  • streaming request or response bodies
  • composing asynchronous flows without blocking a worker thread
  • replacing imperative client code with a reactive API that fits the rest of the application

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The simplest client is created from a base URL:

WebClient client = WebClient.create("http://localhost:8080");
client
    .get()
    .uri("/posts")
    .retrieve()
    .bodyToFlux(Post.class)
    .log()
    .subscribe(post -> System.out.println("post: " + post));

This pattern is enough when you want a quick ad hoc call. For anything larger than a tiny sample, it is worth wrapping the client in a dedicated class.

docs.title: Building a client
docs.text:
The builder gives you more control over the underlying connector, codecs, exchange strategies, default headers, and filters.

var reactorHttpClient = HttpClient.create()
        .wiretap("reactor.netty.http.client.HttpClient", LogLevel.DEBUG,
                AdvancedByteBufFormat.TEXTUAL)
        .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 5000);

WebClient client = WebClient.builder()
    .clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(reactorHttpClient))
    .codecs(clientCodecConfigurer -> {
        // use defaultCodecs() to apply the default codecs
        // clientCodecConfigurer.defaultCodecs();

        // alter a registered encoder/decoder based on the default config.
        // clientCodecConfigurer.defaultCodecs().jacksonJsonEncoder(...)

        // or use customCodecs to register codecs from scratch.
        clientCodecConfigurer.customCodecs().register(new JacksonJsonDecoder(objectMapper));
        clientCodecConfigurer.customCodecs().register(new JacksonJsonEncoder(objectMapper));
    })
    .exchangeStrategies(ExchangeStrategies.withDefaults())
    .baseUrl("http://localhost:8080")
    .build();

The value here is not just configuration. It means the client can match the runtime requirements of the service it talks to while staying reusable in the rest of the application.

docs.title: A typed client class
docs.text:
A nicer pattern is to create a dedicated client wrapper instead of calling WebClient directly from multiple services. The sample below uses exchangeToMono and exchangeToFlux to inspect response status and convert error responses into proper reactive results:

@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PostClient {

    private final WebClient client;

    Flux<Post> allPosts() {
        return client.get()
                .uri("/posts")
                .accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .exchangeToFlux(response -> response.bodyToFlux(Post.class));
    }

    Mono<Post> getById(UUID id) {
        return client.get()
                .uri(uriBuilder -> uriBuilder.path("/posts/{id}").build(id))
                .accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .exchangeToMono(response -> {
                    if (response.statusCode().equals(HttpStatus.OK)) {
                        return response.bodyToMono(Post.class);
                    }
                    return response.createError();
                });
    }

    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> save(Post post) {
        return client.post()
                .uri("/posts")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .bodyValue(post)
                .exchangeToMono(response -> {
                    if (response.statusCode().equals(HttpStatus.CREATED)) {
                        return response.toBodilessEntity();
                    }
                    return response.createError();
                });
    }

    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> update(UUID id, Post post) {
        return client.put()
                .uri(uriBuilder -> uriBuilder.path("/posts/{id}").build(id))
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .bodyValue(post)
                .exchangeToMono(response -> {
                    if (response.statusCode().equals(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)) {
                        return response.toBodilessEntity();
                    }
                    return response.createError();
                });
    }

    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> delete(UUID id) {
        return client.delete()
                .uri(uriBuilder -> uriBuilder.path("/posts/{id}").build(id))
                .exchangeToMono(response -> {
                    if (response.statusCode().equals(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)) {
                        return response.toBodilessEntity();
                    }
                    return response.createError();
                });
    }
}

Then the application can use the client without worrying about low-level transport details:

public static void main(String[] args) {
    var applicationContext = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);
    var postClient = applicationContext.getBean(PostClient.class);

    postClient.allPosts().subscribe(data -> log.debug("post: {}", data));

    postClient.save(new Post(null, "test", "test content", Status.DRAFT, null))
            .log()
            .flatMap(saved -> {
                var uri = saved.getHeaders().getLocation().toString();
                var strings = uri.split("/");
                return client.getById(UUID.fromString(strings[strings.length - 1]));
            })
            .flatMap(post -> client.update(post.id(),
                    new Post(null, "updated test", "updated content", Status.PENDING_MODERATION, null)))
            .subscribe(responseEntity -> log.debug("updated status: {}", responseEntity));
}

You can explore the complete code in spring-reactive-sample/client.

To remove the request-building code entirely, declare the same operations as an annotated interface — see HTTP Interfaces with @HttpExchange.

docs.title: Choosing the HTTP client connector
docs.text:
The ClientHttpConnector abstracts the actual HTTP implementation underneath WebClient. By default, Spring uses Reactor Netty, but you can switch to other connectors without changing the client code itself.

Connector Underlying client Extra dependency ReactorClientHttpConnector (default) Reactor Netty none (included with WebFlux) JettyClientHttpConnector Jetty Reactive HttpClient org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-reactive-httpclient JdkClientHttpConnector JDK java.net.http.HttpClient none HttpComponentsClientHttpConnector Apache HttpClient 5 org.apache.httpcomponents.client5:httpclient5

docs.title: Reactor Netty (default)
docs.text:
var reactorHttpClient = HttpClient.create()
        .wiretap("reactor.netty.http.client.HttpClient", LogLevel.DEBUG,
                AdvancedByteBufFormat.TEXTUAL)
        .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 5000);

var connector = new ReactorClientHttpConnector(reactorHttpClient);

docs.title: Jetty Reactive HttpClient
docs.text:
var jettyHttpClient = new org.eclipse.jetty.client.HttpClient();
jettyHttpClient.setConnectTimeout(5000L);
jettyHttpClient.start();
var connector = new JettyClientHttpConnector(jettyHttpClient);

Add the dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty</groupId>
    <artifactId>jetty-reactive-httpclient</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: JDK HttpClient
docs.text:
The built-in JDK java.net.http.HttpClient needs no extra dependency:

var jvmHttpClient = java.net.http.HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .executor(Executors.newCachedThreadPool())
        .version(java.net.http.HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
        .build();
var connector = new JdkClientHttpConnector(jvmHttpClient);

docs.title: Apache HttpClient 5
docs.text:
var httpAsyncClient = org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.async.HttpAsyncClients.createHttp2Default();
var connector = new HttpComponentsClientHttpConnector(httpAsyncClient);

Add the dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.httpcomponents.client5</groupId>
    <artifactId>httpclient5</artifactId>
</dependency>

Each connector swaps in with one builder call — .clientConnector(connector) — while the PostClient layer above stays unchanged. You can explore each variant in client-jetty, client-jdk11-httpclient, and client-apache-httpclient5.

docs.title: Testing the client
docs.text: The PostClient above is tested by stubbing the remote API with WireMock and asserting the reactive sequences — see Mocking a target HTTP API with WireMock in the Testing chapter. The chapter also covers WebTestClient for the server side and StepVerifier for publisher-level assertions.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: a page served from one origin may not freely call an API on another origin. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) relaxes this through response headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For requests that are not "simple", the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request carrying Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method, and only proceeds when the server answers with matching Access-Control-Allow-* headers.

WebFlux offers three levels of CORS configuration:

  • a CorsWebFilter bean — global rules applied in the WebFilter chain, before handler mapping
  • WebFluxConfigurer#addCorsMappings — global rules applied at the handler-mapping level
  • @CrossOrigin — fine-grained rules on a controller class or handler method

The examples referenced here live in this repository: cors (manual configuration) and boot-cors (Spring Boot customization).

docs.title: Manual configuration with CorsWebFilter
docs.text:
CorsWebFilter is a WebFilter that evaluates a CorsConfigurationSource for every request. Pair it with UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource to map path patterns to CORS rules:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
public class WebConfig {

    @Bean
    public CorsWebFilter corsWebFilter() {
        var config = new CorsConfiguration();
        config.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://allowed-origin.com"));
        config.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
        config.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("*"));
        config.setAllowCredentials(true);
        config.setMaxAge(3600L);

        var source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
        source.registerCorsConfiguration("/**", config);
        return new CorsWebFilter(source);
    }
}

Both WebHttpHandlerBuilder and Spring Boot pick up WebFilter beans automatically, so no further registration is needed. Requests from any other origin are rejected with 403 FORBIDDEN; requests without an Origin header pass through untouched.

docs.title: Alternative: WebFluxConfigurer
docs.text:
If the application already implements WebFluxConfigurer, CORS mappings can be declared through addCorsMappings instead of a filter bean:

public class CorsWebFluxConfigurer implements WebFluxConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/**")
                .allowedOrigins("https://allowed-origin.com")
                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS")
                .allowedHeaders("*")
                .allowCredentials(true)
                .maxAge(3600);
    }
}

These mappings are applied by the handler mappings rather than the filter chain. In the cors example this class is deliberately not registered as a Spring configuration — annotate it with @Configuration (or @Import it from WebConfig) to activate it in place of the CorsWebFilter bean.

docs.title: Spring Boot customization
docs.text:
Spring Boot 4 has no spring.webflux.cors.* properties; CORS is customized with beans and annotations. A CorsWebFilter bean is detected automatically, and the rules can be scoped to specific paths:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class CorsConfig {

    @Bean
    public CorsWebFilter corsWebFilter() {
        var config = new CorsConfiguration();
        config.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://allowed-origin.com"));
        config.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
        config.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("*"));
        config.setAllowCredentials(true);
        config.setMaxAge(3600L);

        var source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
        source.registerCorsConfiguration("/posts/**", config);
        return new CorsWebFilter(source);
    }
}

For individual handlers, @CrossOrigin declares the allowed origins directly on the controller method:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/hello")
public class HelloController {

    @GetMapping
    @CrossOrigin(origins = "https://hello-origin.com")
    public Mono<String> hello() {
        return Mono.just("Hello CORS");
    }
}

Note

Keep filter-level and annotation-level rules on distinct paths when demonstrating both. In boot-cors the filter covers /posts/** while @CrossOrigin applies to /hello, so each mechanism can be observed independently.

docs.title: Testing with WebTestClient
docs.text:
A preflight test asserts the negotiated headers:

this.rest
        .options().uri("/posts")
        .header(HttpHeaders.ORIGIN, "https://allowed-origin.com")
        .header(HttpHeaders.ACCESS_CONTROL_REQUEST_METHOD, "POST")
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isOk()
        .expectHeader().valueEquals(HttpHeaders.ACCESS_CONTROL_ALLOW_ORIGIN, "https://allowed-origin.com")
        .expectHeader().valueEquals(HttpHeaders.ACCESS_CONTROL_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS, "true")
        .expectHeader().valueEquals(HttpHeaders.ACCESS_CONTROL_MAX_AGE, "3600");

A disallowed origin is rejected for both preflight and actual requests:

this.rest
        .get().uri("/posts")
        .header(HttpHeaders.ORIGIN, "https://disallowed-origin.com")
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isForbidden();

Note

As of Spring Framework 7.1, the CORS processor validates the Origin against the request URI's scheme, host, and port. When binding WebTestClient to an application context, set a base URL such as .baseUrl("http://localhost:8080") — otherwise the mock request has no scheme or host and every CORS request is rejected as a malformed origin. Tests against a running server (@SpringBootTest with RANDOM_PORT) are not affected.

For the complete code, see cors and boot-cors in this repo.

docs.title: Handling Web Exceptions
docs.text:
When exposing RESTful APIs you can choose between @RestController and functional RouterFunction routes.

The former is simple. If you have some experience with Spring WebMvc, it is easy to update your knowledge. Just need to use newer Reactor specific Mono and Flux instead in your codes.

The exception handling in reactive @RestController is similar to the one in WebMVC.

  1. Create an Exception class.

    public class PostNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public PostNotFoundException(Long id) {
        super("Post:" + id +" is not found.");
    }
}

  2. Throw exception in your codes.

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}")
public Mono<Post> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") Long id) {
    return this.posts.findById(id).switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new PostNotFoundException(id)));
}

  3. Create a standalone @ControllerAdvice annotated class or @ExceptionHandler annotated method in your controller class to handle the exceptions.

    @RestControllerAdvice
@Slf4j
class RestExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(PostNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<?> postNotFound(PostNotFoundException ex) {
        log.debug("handling exception: {}", ex.toString());
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }

}

@RestControllerAdvice only works for @RestController.

If you are using RouterFunction, create a WebExceptionHandler bean to handle it manually.

@Bean
public WebExceptionHandler exceptionHandler() {
    return (ServerWebExchange exchange, Throwable ex) -> {
        if (ex instanceof PostNotFoundException) {
            exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
            return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
        }
        return Mono.error(ex);
    };
}

Note

WebExceptionHandler is a low-level API. It also works for the exception handling in the annotated controller case — the @ExceptionHandler mechanism itself is implemented as a chain of WebExceptionHandlers.

docs.title: Registering a WebExceptionHandler in Spring Boot
docs.text:
In a Spring Boot application, register the handler as a @Component with an explicit @Order(-2) so it runs before the default ErrorWebExceptionHandler (which has order -1):

@Component
@Order(-2)
class RestWebExceptionHandler implements WebExceptionHandler {

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> handle(ServerWebExchange exchange, Throwable ex) {
        if (ex instanceof PostNotFoundException) {
            exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);

            // marks the response as complete and forbids writing to it
            return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
        }
        return Mono.error(ex);
    }
}

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/exception-handler and spring-reactive-sample/boot-exception-handler.

Tip

Spring supports the standard error response format defined by RFC 9457. See Problem Details for the ProblemDetail based approach.

docs.title: RouterFunction
docs.text:
Functional routing provides a concise, fluent alternative to @RestController. Introduced in the Spring 5 era, RouterFunction remains fully supported in Spring Framework 7. It lets you compose routes and handlers using a functional API instead of controller classes.

For example, there is a simple controller class.

@RestController
@RequestMapping
class MessageController {

    @GetMapping
    Flux<Message> allMessages(){
        return Flux.just(
            Message.builder().body("hello Spring Framework 7").build(),
            Message.builder().body("hello Spring Boot 4").build()
        );
    }

}

You can write the same functionality with a RouterFunction bean instead.

@Bean
public RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes() {
    return route(GET("/"),(ServerRequest req)-> ok()
                 .body(
                     BodyInserters.fromValue(
                         Arrays.asList(
                             Message.builder().body("hello Spring Framework 7").build(),
                             Message.builder().body("hello Spring Boot 4").build()
                         )
                     )
                 )
                );
}

The route (from RouterFunctions) accepts a RequestPredicate and a HandlerFunction. HandlerFunction is a @FunctionalInterface.

RouterFunctions and RequestPredicates are helpers to make it easy to assemble the request routes and predicates.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface HandlerFunction<T extends ServerResponse> {
    Mono<T> handle(ServerRequest var1);
}

You can extract the handler codes into a new class.

The following code fragments demonstrates the same features of PostController but written in RouterFunction.

@Bean
public RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes(PostHandler postController) {
    return route(GET("/posts"), postController::all)
        .andRoute(POST("/posts"), postController::create)
        .andRoute(GET("/posts/{id}"), postController::get)
        .andRoute(PUT("/posts/{id}"), postController::update)
        .andRoute(DELETE("/posts/{id}"), postController::delete);
}

The implementations of HandlerFunction are centralized in a PostHandler class.

@Component
class PostHandler {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostHandler(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> all(ServerRequest req) {
        return ServerResponse.ok().body(this.posts.findAll(), Post.class);
    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> create(ServerRequest req) {
        return req.bodyToMono(Post.class)
            .flatMap(post -> this.posts.save(post))
            .flatMap(p -> ServerResponse.created(URI.create("/posts/" + p.getId())).build());
    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> get(ServerRequest req) {
        return this.posts.findById(req.pathVariable("id"))
            .flatMap(post -> ServerResponse.ok().body(Mono.just(post), Post.class))
            .switchIfEmpty(ServerResponse.notFound().build());
    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> update(ServerRequest req) {

        return Mono
            .zip(
                (data) -> {
                    Post p = (Post) data[0];
                    Post p2 = (Post) data[1];
                    p.setTitle(p2.getTitle());
                    p.setContent(p2.getContent());
                    return p;
                },
                this.posts.findById(req.pathVariable("id")),
                req.bodyToMono(Post.class)
            )
            .cast(Post.class)
            .flatMap(post -> this.posts.save(post))
            .flatMap(post -> ServerResponse.noContent().build());

    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> delete(ServerRequest req) {
        return ServerResponse.noContent().build(this.posts.deleteById(req.pathVariable("id")));
    }

}

Note

The RouterFunction is ported back to the Servlet stack since Spring Framework 5.2 — check my example hantsy/spring-webmvc-functional-sample.

docs.title: Sample
docs.text: You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/boot-start, spring-reactive-sample/boot-start-routes, and spring-reactive-sample/routes.

docs.title: HTTP Interfaces with @HttpExchange
docs.text:
A typed client wrapper, as shown in the WebClient chapter, keeps HTTP details in one class — but you still write the request-building code yourself. Spring's HTTP interface approach removes that last layer: you declare a Java interface annotated with @HttpExchange, and Spring creates a proxy that performs the requests through WebClient.

The interface becomes the contract with the remote API. Method annotations describe the HTTP method, URL, and media types; return types stay reactive (Mono, Flux, or ResponseEntity wrappers), so the client composes with the rest of a WebFlux application exactly like hand-written WebClient code.

Spring Boot 4 adds auto-configuration for these HTTP service clients: @ImportHttpServices registers the interfaces, and spring.http.serviceclient.* properties configure each group.

The examples referenced here live in this repository: httpexchange-webclient (manual configuration), boot-httpexchange-webclient (Boot starter and properties), and boot-httpexchange (a shared contract implemented by the server and proxied by the client).

docs.title: Declare an HTTP interface
docs.text:
The domain model is a simple record:

public record Post(UUID id,
                   String title,
                   String content,
                   Status status,
                   LocalDateTime createdAt
) {
}

The interface maps each operation to an HTTP request. @HttpExchange on the type sets the common URL prefix, and the method-level annotations (@GetExchange, @PostExchange, @PutExchange, @DeleteExchange) describe individual calls:

@HttpExchange(url = "/posts")
public interface PostHttpService {
    @GetExchange(accept = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    Flux<Post> allPosts();

    @GetExchange(value = "/{id}", accept = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    Mono<Post> getById(@PathVariable("id") UUID id);

    @PostExchange(contentType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> save(@RequestBody Post post);

    @PutExchange(value = "/{id}", contentType = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> update(@PathVariable UUID id, @RequestBody Post post);

    @DeleteExchange(value = "/{id}")
    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> delete(@PathVariable UUID id);
}

The familiar WebMVC annotations @PathVariable and @RequestBody bind method arguments to URI templates and request bodies. Returning Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> keeps access to status codes and headers — useful for reading the Location header of a 201 Created response.

docs.title: Manual configuration
docs.text:
Without Spring Boot, create the proxy yourself. Build a WebClient, wrap it in a WebClientAdapter, and let HttpServiceProxyFactory create the interface implementation:

@Configuration
public class ClientConfig {

    @Bean
    WebClient webClient(JsonMapper mapper) {
        var reactorHttpClient = HttpClient.create()
                .wiretap("reactor.netty.http.client.HttpClient", LogLevel.DEBUG,
                        AdvancedByteBufFormat.TEXTUAL)
                .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 5000);

        return WebClient.builder()
                .clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(reactorHttpClient))
                .codecs(clientCodecConfigurer -> {
                    clientCodecConfigurer.customCodecs()
                            .register(new JacksonJsonDecoder(mapper));
                    clientCodecConfigurer.customCodecs()
                            .register(new JacksonJsonEncoder(mapper));
                })
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_TYPE, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
                .baseUrl("http://localhost:9090")
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    PostHttpService postHttpService(WebClient webClient) {
        var proxyFactory = HttpServiceProxyFactory
                .builderFor(WebClientAdapter.create(webClient))
                .build();
        return proxyFactory.createClient(PostHttpService.class);
    }
}

The JsonMapper bean configures Jackson 3 (tools.jackson) — the codecs JacksonJsonEncoder and JacksonJsonDecoder use it for request and response bodies. From this point on, inject PostHttpService like any other bean; no WebClient call sites remain in the application code:

var postHttpService = applicationContext.getBean(PostHttpService.class);

postHttpService.allPosts()
        .subscribe(post -> log.debug("post: {}", post));

postHttpService.save(new Post(null, "test", "test content", Status.DRAFT, null))
        .flatMap(saved -> {
            var uri = saved.getHeaders().getLocation().toString();
            var strings = uri.split("/");
            return postHttpService.getById(UUID.fromString(strings[strings.length - 1]));
        })
        .subscribe(post -> log.debug("saved post: {}", post));

You can explore the complete code in httpexchange-webclient.

docs.title: Spring Boot auto-configuration
docs.text:
In a Boot application, the starter and a registration annotation replace the manual proxy setup. Add the dependencies:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webclient</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jackson</artifactId>
</dependency>

Register the interface with @ImportHttpServices, assigning it to a named group and selecting the reactive client type:

@SpringBootApplication
@ImportHttpServices(
        value = PostHttpService.class,
        group = "post",
        clientType = HttpServiceGroup.ClientType.WEB_CLIENT
)
public class DemoApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

Boot creates the proxy bean and applies the group's settings from application.properties:

spring.http.serviceclient[post].base-url=http://localhost:9090

# shared settings for the reactive HTTP client
#spring.http.reactiveclient.connect-timeout=3s
#spring.http.reactiveclient.read-timeout=1s
#spring.http.reactiveclient.redirects=dont_follow

# requires the Jetty reactive HTTP client on the classpath
#spring.http.reactiveclient.connector=jetty

The group name in @ImportHttpServices(group = "post") is the key in spring.http.serviceclient[post].*, so each group can point at a different service.

To tune the underlying WebClient — codecs, default headers, filters — contribute a WebClientCustomizer bean instead of building the client by hand:

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class WebClientConfig {

    @Bean
    WebClientCustomizer webClientCustomizer(JsonMapper mapper) {
        return builder -> builder
                .codecs(c -> c.defaultCodecs().jacksonJsonEncoder(new JacksonJsonEncoder(mapper)))
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_TYPE, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE);
    }

    @Bean
    ClientHttpConnectorBuilder<?> clientHttpConnectorBuilder() {
        return ClientHttpConnectorBuilder.reactor();
    }
}

You can explore the complete code in boot-httpexchange-webclient.

docs.title: Share the contract between server and client
docs.text:
The same interface can play both sides of the conversation: the server implements it as a controller, and the client consumes it as a proxy. The boot-httpexchange example runs both roles in one application — the client group points back at the server's own address:

spring.http.serviceclient[post].base-url=http://localhost:8080

On the server side, a @RestController implements the interface. The @HttpExchange annotations on the interface methods drive the request mapping, so the controller carries no mapping annotations of its own:

@RestController
public class PostApiController implements PostApi {
    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostApiController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @Override
    public Flux<Post> allPosts() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @Override
    public Mono<Post> getById(UUID id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    // save, update, delete follow the same pattern
}

Because the controller and the client proxy both implement PostApi, the context holds two beans of that type. Inject the proxy by its registered name — GROUP#INTERFACE — to disambiguate:

public ClientExampleInitializer(
        @Qualifier("post#com.example.demo.PostApi") PostApi client) {
    this.client = client;
}

Error responses stay structured. The server converts PostNotFoundException into a ProblemDetail body (spring.webflux.problemdetails.enabled=true), and the client decides how to surface it through a status handler on a WebClientCustomizer:

@Bean
WebClientCustomizer webClientCustomizer() {
    return builder -> builder
            .defaultStatusHandler(HttpStatusCode::is4xxClientError, ClientResponse::createError);
}

The default handler raises a WebClientResponseException in the calling reactive flow. Alternatively, parse the ProblemDetail body in the handler and restore the original PostNotFoundException, so client code catches the same exception type the server threw.

When you customize the shared JsonMapper, contribute a JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer rather than replacing the mapper bean — Boot applies its own settings, including the ProblemDetail serialization mixin, through the same customizer chain.

docs.title: Testing with WireMock
docs.text:
The proxy is a normal bean, so tests stub the remote API with WireMock and assert the reactive sequences with StepVerifier — the same approach as the typed client in the WebClient chapter. In the Boot example, @SpringBootTest loads the auto-configured proxy; in the manual example, @SpringJUnitConfig(ClientConfig.class) loads the hand-built beans:

@SpringBootTest
@WireMockTest(httpPort = 9090)
public class PostHttpServiceTest {

    @Autowired
    PostHttpService client;

    @Test
    public void testGetAllPosts() {
        var data = List.of(
                new Post(UUID.randomUUID(), "title1", "content1", Status.DRAFT, LocalDateTime.now()),
                new Post(UUID.randomUUID(), "title2", "content2", Status.PUBLISHED, LocalDateTime.now())
        );
        stubFor(get("/posts")
                .willReturn(
                        aResponse()
                                .withHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
                                .withResponseBody(Body.fromJsonBytes(Json.toByteArray(data)))
                )
        );

        client.allPosts()
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .expectNextCount(2)
                .verifyComplete();

        verify(getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/posts"))
                .withHeader("Accept", equalTo("application/json")));
    }
}

The WireMock port matches the configured base-url, so the proxy calls the stub server without any test-specific client configuration. See Mocking a target HTTP API with WireMock in the Testing chapter for the general pattern, and StepVerifier for publisher-level assertions.

docs.title: An introduction to Reactive Web
docs.text:
The reactive web stack in Spring is not just a different controller style. It is a different execution model built around non-blocking I/O, backpressure-friendly stream processing, and Reactor primitives such as Mono and Flux.

At the heart of the stack are two important abstractions:

  • WebHandler — the high-level entry point that assembles the pieces of a web request, including filters, exception handlers, and routing logic
  • HttpHandler — the lower-level bridge between Spring's web layer and the runtime, such as Reactor Netty or a Servlet container with async support

You can see both abstractions working together in the bootstrap code from the Getting Started chapter:

HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();
ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter adapter = new ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
HttpServer httpServer = HttpServer.create().host("localhost").port(this.port);
return httpServer.handle(adapter);

Base projects for this chapter

The examples in this section extend the two applications introduced earlier in the book: the vanilla application (manual wiring, no Spring Boot) and the Spring Boot application built with spring-boot-starter-webflux. Each page points to the exact sample in the repository.

docs.title: Enabling WebFlux
docs.text:
To activate the reactive web stack, create a @Configuration class and add @EnableWebFlux:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {}

If you are familiar with the traditional WebMvcConfigurer, you will feel at home with WebFluxConfigurer. It gives you a place to customize validation, CORS, resource handling, and other built-in web behaviors:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig implements WebFluxConfigurer {}

Note

If you are using Spring Boot, there is usually nothing additional to do: adding spring-boot-starter-webflux is enough to activate the stack.

docs.title: Alternative reactive types
docs.text:
WebFlux is deliberately library-agnostic. Controller methods can return Flux, Mono, or types from RxJava 3, SmallRye Mutiny, or the JDK Flow API, and Spring adapts them automatically.

The runnable examples for these alternative reactive libraries live in the Reactive libraries section of the ecosystem chapter:

  • RxJava 3
  • SmallRye Mutiny
  • The JDK Flow API

docs.title: Multipart Support
docs.text:
In Spring, the Servlet stack supports multipart requests through the Servlet 3.0+ built-in multipart feature or Apache Commons IO. The WebFlux stack also adds multipart support — backed by non-blocking stream processing instead of buffering whole files in memory.

The Part abstraction represents a part in a multipart/form-data request. A part is either a FilePart (uploaded file content) or a FormFieldPart (a simple form field), whether the request comes from a browser form or any other client.

docs.title: Reading parts in a controller
docs.text:
The reactive controllers accept Part parameters wrapped in Mono or Flux. The following variants are supported:

@PostMapping("/requestBodyMap")
Mono<String> requestBodyMap(
    @RequestPart("fileParts") FilePart fileParts,
    @RequestPart("fileParts") Mono<FilePart> filePartsMono,
    @RequestPart("fileParts") Flux<FilePart> filePartsFlux,
    @RequestBody Mono<MultiValueMap<String, Part>> partsMono) {
    // ...
}

For a streaming approach, consume all parts as a Flux<Part> — this is the variant the sample implements:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/uploads")
public class MultipartController {

    @PostMapping(value = "", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
    Mono<String> requestBodyFlux(@RequestBody Flux<Part> parts) {
        return partFluxDescription(parts);
    }

    private static Mono<String> partFluxDescription(Flux<? extends Part> partsFlux) {
        return partsFlux.log().collectList().map(MultipartController::partListDescription);
    }

    private static String partDescription(Part part) {
        return part instanceof FilePart fp ? part.name() + ":" + fp.filename() : part.name();
    }

    // partListDescription(...) joins the part descriptions into a single string
}

You can explore the complete codes in spring-reactive-sample/multipart.

docs.title: Streaming with PartEvent
docs.text:
Beyond the aggregated forms above, WebFlux can consume a multipart request as a stream of PartEvent messages — one event per form field and a pair of events (start/content) per file part. This processes parts as they arrive instead of buffering them, and scales to large uploads.

From the multipart sample of the spring6-sandbox repository, the controller consumes Flux<PartEvent>, splits the stream at each part boundary with windowUntil(PartEvent::isLast), and dispatches on the event type:

@PostMapping("partevents")
public ResponseEntity<Flux<String>> handlePartsEvents(@RequestBody Flux<PartEvent> allPartsEvents) {
    var result = allPartsEvents
            .windowUntil(PartEvent::isLast)
            .concatMap(p -> {
                        return p.switchOnFirst((signal, partEvents) -> {
                                    if (signal.hasValue()) {
                                        PartEvent event = signal.get();
                                        if (event instanceof FormPartEvent formEvent) {
                                            String value = formEvent.value();
                                            // handle form field
                                            log.debug("form value: {}", value);
                                            return Mono.just(value + "
");

                                        } else if (event instanceof FilePartEvent fileEvent) {
                                            String filename = fileEvent.filename();
                                            log.debug("upload file name:{}", filename);

                                            return partEvents.map(PartEvent::content)
                                                    .map(DataBufferUtils::release)
                                                    .then(Mono.just(filename + "
"));
                                        }

                                        return Mono.error(new RuntimeException("Unexpected event: " + event));
                                    }
                                    return Flux.empty(); // either complete or error signal
                                }
                        );
                    }
            );

    return ok().body(result);
}

Reading the flow:

  1. windowUntil(PartEvent::isLast) groups the event stream into windows, one per part.
  2. switchOnFirst inspects the first event of each window: a FormPartEvent carries the field value directly, a FilePartEvent opens the file — the content events that follow stream the file data (partEvents.map(PartEvent::content)), where you would write to storage instead of releasing the buffers.
  3. DataBufferUtils::release frees the buffer memory once the content is consumed.

The controller also demonstrates the other multipart consumption styles — a form command object, @RequestPart parameters, and Mono<MultiValueMap<String, Part>>:

@PostMapping("form")
public ResponseEntity handleFileUploadForm(FileUploadCommand form, BindingResult errors) {
    var result = Map.of(
            "name", form.getName(),
            "filename", form.getFile().filename()
    );
    return ok().body(result);
}

@PostMapping("requestparts")
public ResponseEntity handleRequestParts(@RequestPart("name") String name,
                                         @RequestPart("file") FilePart file) {
    var result = Map.of(
            "name", name,
            "filename", file.filename()
    );
    return ok().body(result);
}

@PostMapping("multivalues")
public ResponseEntity handleMultivalues(@RequestBody Mono<MultiValueMap<String, Part>> parts) {
    var partNames = parts.map(p -> p.keySet().stream().map(key -> p.getFirst(key).name()).toList()).log();
    return ok().body(partNames);
}

A test builds the PartEvent stream on the client side with FormPartEvent.create(...) and FilePartEvent.create(...):

@Test
public void testHandlePartEvents() {
    this.client
            .post().uri("/partevents")
            .contentType(MULTIPART_FORM_DATA)
            .body(
                    Flux.concat(
                            FormPartEvent.create("name", "test"),
                            FilePartEvent.create("file", new ClassPathResource("spring.png"))
                    ),
                    PartEvent.class
            )
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBodyList(String.class).hasSize(2);
}

For the complete codes, check the multipart module of the spring6-sandbox repository.

docs.title: File upload and download
docs.text: For file upload/download backed by a store, stream the FilePart content into the backend of your choice. The Mongo GridFS example stores uploads in MongoDB via ReactiveGridFsTemplate and streams them back on download; the R2DBC FilePart example maps upload content to Postgres bytea (byte[], ByteBuffer, or R2DBC Blob).

docs.title: Problem Details
docs.text:
When building REST API backends, developers often invent custom wrappers such as ApiResult or ErrorResponse to standardize responses. Those formats are rarely portable, and consuming a different one for every third-party API quickly becomes frustrating.

Spring HATEOAS adopted the vnd.error draft proposal for representing errors, but it is primarily aimed at hypermedia APIs.

The widely accepted cross-language alternative is Problem Details for HTTP APIs, standardized by the IETF as RFC 9457 (originally RFC 7807). It defines a consistent, human-readable structure for error conditions so that clients can interpret errors uniformly. It is served as media type application/problem+json (or application/problem+xml).

Spring 6 added native support for Problem Details and Spring Boot builds on it, so there is usually no reason to hand-roll an error envelope any more.

docs.title: The ProblemDetail class
docs.text:
ProblemDetail is a POJO that models the RFC 9457 members:

Member Description type A URI reference identifying the problem type. Defaults to about:blank when omitted. title A brief, human-readable summary of the problem type. status The HTTP status code. detail A human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence. instance A URI reference identifying this specific occurrence, usually the request path. properties An extension point for adding custom members.

Create an instance with one of the factory methods:

ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Post was not found.");

Any additional data goes into the properties map:

var problemDetail = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "The request is invalid.");
problemDetail.setProperty("errors",
        List.of(Map.of("path", "title", "details", "Cannot be empty"))
);

When Jackson is used, Spring registers ProblemDetailJacksonMixin; the entries of properties are written as top-level JSON members instead of being nested under a properties key:

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "The request is invalid.",
  "instance": "/posts",
  "errors": [
    { "path": "title", "details": "Cannot be empty" }
  ]
}

docs.title: Producing Problem Details
docs.text:
In both Spring WebMvc and WebFlux, error responses can be assembled in @ExceptionHandler methods within a @ControllerAdvice / @RestControllerAdvice bean. The handler may return ProblemDetail directly, or wrap it in a ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> when it needs to control headers or the response status explicitly:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class RestExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(PostNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleNotFoundException(PostNotFoundException exception) {
        var problemDetail = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, exception.getMessage());
        problemDetail.setProperty("id", exception.getPostId());
        problemDetail.setProperty("entity", "POST");
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(problemDetail);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class)
    public ProblemDetail handleIllegalArgumentException(IllegalArgumentException exception) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, exception.getMessage());
    }
}

The response is rendered with Content-Type: application/problem+json, and the response status is taken from the ProblemDetail.

docs.title: Problem Details in a manual WebFlux application
docs.text:
The sample project problem-details bootstraps Spring WebFlux without Spring Boot, stores posts in PostgreSQL with R2DBC, and returns ProblemDetail bodies for errors.

A domain exception can carry the extra data that should be exposed:

public class PostNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {

    private final UUID postId;

    public PostNotFoundException(UUID postId) {
        super("Post #" + postId + " was not found.");
        this.postId = postId;
    }

    public UUID getPostId() {
        return postId;
    }
}

The controller converts an empty result into that exception:

@GetMapping("{id}")
public Mono<ResponseEntity<Post>> get(@PathVariable UUID id) {
    return this.posts.findById(id)
            .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new PostNotFoundException(id)))
            .map(ResponseEntity::ok);
}

Then a @RestControllerAdvice maps it to a ProblemDetail and adds extension members:

@RestControllerAdvice
public class RestExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(PostNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleNotFoundException(PostNotFoundException exception) {
        var problemDetail = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, exception.getMessage());
        problemDetail.setType(URI.create("https://example.com/errors/post-not-found"));
        problemDetail.setProperty("id", exception.getPostId());
        problemDetail.setProperty("entity", "POST");
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(problemDetail);
    }
}

A request for a missing post returns:

{
  "type": "https://example.com/errors/post-not-found",
  "title": "Not Found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "Post #4c2f9f0c-2b8a-5d1e-4c73-7f1b3c9a8f6e was not found.",
  "instance": "/posts/4c2f9f0c-2b8a-5d1e-4c73-7f1b3c9a8f6e",
  "id": "4c2f9f0c-2b8a-5d1e-4c73-7f1b3c9a8f6e",
  "entity": "POST"
}

docs.title: Handling validation errors
docs.text:
@Valid on a @RequestBody argument raises a WebExchangeBindException in WebFlux. Extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler and override handleWebExchangeBindException to enrich the framework-provided ProblemDetail with the field errors:

@Override
protected Mono<ResponseEntity<Object>> handleWebExchangeBindException(
        WebExchangeBindException exception,
        HttpHeaders headers,
        HttpStatusCode status,
        ServerWebExchange exchange) {
    return super.handleWebExchangeBindException(exception, headers, status, exchange)
            .map(entity -> {
                if (entity.getBody() instanceof ProblemDetail problemDetail) {
                    problemDetail.setProperty("errors",
                            exception.getFieldErrors().stream()
                                    .map(error -> Map.of(
                                            "path", error.getField(),
                                            "details", error.getDefaultMessage()))
                                    .toList()
                    );
                }
                return entity;
            });
}

A validation failure now includes an errors extension member:

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "Invalid request content.",
  "instance": "/posts",
  "errors": [
    { "path": "content", "details": "must not be blank" }
  ]
}

docs.title: Problem Details in a Spring Boot application
docs.text:
Enable the built-in support in application.properties:

# For Spring WebMvc
spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true

# For Spring WebFlux
spring.webflux.problemdetails.enabled=true

Spring Boot then registers a ProblemDetailsExceptionHandler that converts framework exceptions such as ResponseStatusException, MethodArgumentNotValidException, and MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException into Problem Details responses. The built-in error handling also renders errors in the same format.

Application-specific exceptions can still be customized with a @RestControllerAdvice. Give it the highest precedence so it runs before Spring Boot's advice, and only handle the exceptions you care about — everything else falls through to the built-in handler:

@RestControllerAdvice
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
public class RestExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(PostNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleNotFoundException(PostNotFoundException exception) {
        var problemDetail = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, exception.getMessage());
        problemDetail.setType(URI.create("https://example.com/errors/post-not-found"));
        problemDetail.setProperty("id", exception.getPostId());
        problemDetail.setProperty("entity", "POST");
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(problemDetail);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(WebExchangeBindException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleWebExchangeBindException(WebExchangeBindException exception) {
        var problemDetail = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
                HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "The request is invalid.");
        problemDetail.setProperty("errors",
                exception.getFieldErrors().stream()
                        .map(error -> Map.of(
                                "path", error.getField(),
                                "details", error.getDefaultMessage()))
                        .toList()
        );
        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(problemDetail);
    }
}

The Boot variant, boot-problem-details, uses Spring Data R2DBC instead of a hand-written DatabaseClient repository:

public interface PostRepository extends ReactiveCrudRepository<Post, UUID> {

    Flux<Post> findByTitleContains(String title);
}

Because of the built-in handler, an invalid path variable is also converted into a Problem Details response without any application code:

GET /posts/not-a-uuid

{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "Failed to convert 'id' with value: 'not-a-uuid'",
  "instance": "/posts/not-a-uuid"
}

docs.title: Testing with WebTestClient
docs.text:
WebTestClient exposes the response status, headers, and body, so the media type and extension members can be asserted directly:

this.client
        .get().uri("/posts/{id}", postId)
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isNotFound()
        .expectHeader().contentTypeCompatibleWith(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON)
        .expectBody()
        .jsonPath("$.type").isEqualTo("https://example.com/errors/post-not-found")
        .jsonPath("$.id").isEqualTo(postId.toString())
        .jsonPath("$.entity").isEqualTo("POST");

docs.title: Alternative: Zalando Problem
docs.text:
Before Spring 6, applications that wanted the Problem Details format typically used Zalando Problem together with its Spring Web integration, which supports both Spring WebMvc and WebFlux.

Note

Zalando's library still offers deeper integration with the Spring ecosystem than the built-in support — for example it handles Spring Security exceptions and Jakarta Validation errors automatically. It remains a reasonable choice for applications that need those integrations out of the box.
